title: llm 0.37.3
content:
Release:

llm 0.37.3

A bug fix release for
LLM
, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.

Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite,
3.54.1
, which includes
a fix
that
broke LLM's logging code
.

Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:

select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))

Returns this:

{"a":[1]}

But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:

{"a":"[1]"}

According
to D. Richard Hipp
:

That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.

The workaround looks like this:

select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))

title: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0
content:
Release:

datasette-maplibre 0.1a0

The first new Datasette geospatial plugin in quite a while! This one combines the excellent
MapLibre GL
library with
OpenFreeMap
, the free vector map server operated by Zsolt Ero (you should
sponsor Zsolt on GitHub
.)

I built most of this with a single prompt to Claude Fable 5.2:

Look at datasette-cluster-map and datasette-leaflet-geojson plugins, then look at ~/dev/tools/openfreemap-demo.html - then build a brand new Datasette plugin that uses maplibreGL and openfreemap and combines the features of those other two plugins - but be creative and think outside the box for other useful features the plugin might have

"Be creative and think outside the box" resulted in a few neat ideas - my favorite is that it displays SVG previews of GeoJSON shapes, then loads a WebGL preview only when they scroll into view.

I also had Claude build a comprehensive demo which works in the latest Datasette Lite, so you can
visit this link
to load the plugin and a demo database in your browser via Pyodide and WebAssembly.

title: datasette 1.0a43
content:
Release:

datasette 1.0a43

I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the
1.0 milestone
, which is now 53% complete.

The biggest 1.0 item in this release is
streaming support for output renderers
- the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new
Response.stream()
method.

There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed
deserving of a GitHub advisory
: private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed).

There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation
finally has a design suitable for 1.0
. A new
<datasette-copy-button>
Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new
DatasetteModal.confirm()
JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by
Zihan Dai
,
Peter Olkhovets
,
Ilya Khalafi
, and
Ankita Advitot
.

The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette!
Here's the commit
- key CSS is as follows:

/* Enable cross-document view transitions,

for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */

@media

(
prefers-reduced-motion
:
no-preference
)

{

@view-transition

{

navigation
:
auto
;

}

}

/* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */

html
:
active-view-transition

.
content

>

.
facet-results

{

view-transition-name
:
facet-results
;

}

/* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */

html
:
active-view-transition

.
table-wrapper
:
has
(
>

table
.
rows-and-columns
)

{

view-transition-name
:
rows-table
;

}

With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in
Firefox 162
on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.)

title: datasette-apps 0.4a0
content:
Release:

datasette-apps 0.4a0

Datasette Apps are sandboxed HTML and JavaScript applications that live inside Datasette - think Claude Artifacts, but these ones can run SQL queries against your data.

0.4a0 adds support for linking: you can link to an app with
#fragments
in the URL and the app can see and use those, plus supported URL schemes are reported back to Datasette Agent so it can help write apps that link to each other.

This means you can have e.g. an app that shows details about a specific record, and a completely separate app that searches those records and links to their representations in the first app.

title: datasette-llm 0.1a11
content:
Release:

datasette-llm 0.1a11

datasette-llm
is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins.

This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol.

This means that if you're running local models with
LM Studio
or
Ollama
or
llama.cpp
(which just hit
v1.0.0
) you can run Datasette via
uvx
like this:

wget https://datasette.io/content.db

uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \
--root --secret 1 \
-s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model
'
{

"model": "lmstudio-qwen",

"model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b",

"api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1"

}
'
content.db

And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model!

title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
content:
Release:

datasette-leaflet 0.3

OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server
should send a referrer header
. Datasette table pages used the
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer
HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy.

datasette-leaflet
is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to
strict-origin-when-cross-origin
, passing the host but not the full path to the page.

title: llm-gemini 0.37
content:
Release:

llm-gemini 0.37

Google launched
Gemini 4 Hydrogen
today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.

It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing
really
confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

Model

Dates

Input ($/M)

Cached input

Output

Gemini 4 Carbon

Through Nov 30, 2026

$2.00

$0.10

$10.00

From Dec 1, 2026

$4.00

$0.20

$20.00

Gemini 4 Argon

Through Nov 30, 2026

$2.00

$0.10

$10.00

From Dec 1, 2026

$4.00

$0.20

$20.00

Gemini 4 Hydrogen

$1.50

$0.075

$7.50

Carbon and Argon are
the same price
, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models?
Google says
that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.

Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.

I had Hydrogen
generate some pelicans
. Here's a
full comparison grid
showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:

Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.

Here's
how Google describe
Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

title: Gemini Decisions API
content:
Gemini Decisions API

Google join
Jev
and
OpenAI
in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question.

It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million.

Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.

I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my
Yonkers stomping robot
video file:

dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it?
robot: Does this video have a robot in it?
france: Is this video set in France?
usa: Is this video set in the USA?

title: aws-emulator
content:
aws-emulator

Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so.

It's written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents - 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project. Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian wrote about

It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms.

title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
content:
Anthropic's IPO roadshow video

Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.

The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's
one that I extracted
using MacWhisper. Highlights below:

We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]

As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work
This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention
. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]

The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.

Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack.
We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself
, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.

We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their
postmortem of three recent issues
, where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
content:
Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember

Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as:

[...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.

For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is
80x that price
at $8/$40.

The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking
that
threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others:

Model

Prompt size

Input ($/M)

Cached input

Output

GPT-6 Luna

≤272k

$0.10

$0.01

$0.50

>272k

$0.20

$0.75

Muse Ember 1.0

≤200k

Claude Haiku 5.5

≤100k

$2.50

But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem.

For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis.

And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models:

The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement:

It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.

(That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!)

Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I
rendered six pelicans riding bicycles
. The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response.

Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too:

The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those
I got from Muse Wonder
, which is
40x the price
of Muse Ember.

title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
content:
Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked.

If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own:

You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you.

The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it.

—
Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
, Anthropic documentation

title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
content:
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started
intermittently beeping
. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build
Beep Locator
, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.

Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.

Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.

The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.

How it works

When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up
BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices
, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see
detector.js
), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.

How I built it

I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's
that shared starter session
, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve

There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it

I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from

There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app

Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?

That got me
this problem.md file
. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.

The research looked good, so I told it:

Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else

That got me
to this point
- most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.

I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then
Fable 5.2 was released
, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening
and
make live changes to the software as it ran.

This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an
installModule()
method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate

This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]

Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps

That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.

each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp

That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays

Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for

Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is

At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.

And since I had one spare device, I then said:

add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far

Giving Claude Code ears

I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to
give Claude Code ears
.

Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.

Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where
Martin Woodward
told me he had been debugging the
GitHub Universe Badge computers
by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.

Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
content:
Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions.

They're too good at describing the work

The problem is that they are
too
good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb.

It's not necessarily slop, but it
reads
like slop!

It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!

I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention.

I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right.

Hide most of it in a details/summary

The HTML
<details><summary>
elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this:

<
details
>

<
summary
>
Claude Opus 5.5
</
summary
>

<
h2
>
The hook
</
h2
>

Plugins implement
<
code
>
register_agent_reference_types(datasette)
</
code
>
...

</
details
>

When rendered, it looks
like this
:

Crucially,
<details><summary>

is supported in GitHub Markdown
. You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow.

I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests.

The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed.

I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature.

The full agent-written essay then follows in a
<details><summary>
. I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example.

My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details.

I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time.

Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used:

datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields
- "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub
repos
table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot)

datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page
- "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot)

datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader
- "
edit-tools.js
(~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)."

datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook
- "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the
#
tagging in the chat composer using a new
register_agent_reference_types(datasette)
plugin hook." - pictured above.

llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands
- "Adds commands for managing the records in
extra-openai-models.yaml
, so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied
--help
output.

The mnemonic

I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it
<details><summary>
or
<summary><details>
?

Here are two tricks that helped me.

First, and most obviously, the
<summary>
is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the
<details>
element must then wrap everything else.

An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary".

"details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details".

Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again.

(I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.)

title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
content:
Research:

parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust

I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a
parse_number()
function for turning strings like
-$1,234.56
or
'12.5%'
into numeric values that could be summed and sorted.

I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5)
and prompted
:

I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse

Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting
.so
(or whatever) file

This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using
Rusqlite
) and 298 KB (using
sqlite-loadable-rs
), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster!

Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's
strtod
is "twice as fast". So I prompted:

Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation

And it did, using "Clinger's fast path":

Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better:

first C

new C

rusqlite

sqlite-loadable

Mixed data

67 ns

19 ns

46 ns

41 ns

Integers only

25 ns

16 ns

36 ns

32 ns

Decimals only

106 ns

18 ns

55 ns

47 ns

Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in
simonw/research
by prompting this:

Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder

Here's
the resulting report
.

title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
content:
datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages

I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an
HTTP prefetch
to the next page of rows in that table.

This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP
link
header like this:

link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next"

This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away.

I dug in and learned that Firefox has
an issue
that has been open for 24 years about this behavior...

And one of the early comments on that issue links to
my blog post from 2002
complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely!

title: Terry Pratchett's Study
content:
My comment
on
Terry Pratchett's Study
— Hacker News.
Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich:
https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin...

But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it.

(Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.)

title: Quoting Nilay Patel
content:
The products aren't good enough to sell people on the costs.

You cannot tell people that you have to listen to the whine of a data center in their backyard for AI overviews and some of the most hilarious deep fake slop in history.

It's not worth it. It just isn't worth it to anyone. And agents aren't real and they might not be being used the way that anyone wants them to yet. All these companies are spending more than they're making on these products. Refrigerators holding blood storage in Europe are being hacked.

The costs are too high. The benefits are not real. And if you connect that to corruption, you're like, in order to impose these costs on me, these CEOs are in the White House shaking Trump's hand, renaming it to the Gulf of America, paying for this ballroom that we don't want. It's obvious crypto-corruption, and it's still slop.

The AI industry will not get out of it until they make
better products
. Until everyone can see without needing to be convinced, without needing an ad campaign, without any of this stuff that just using these products makes your life better.

—
Nilay Patel

title: GitHub availability report: October 2026
content:
We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October:
we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same:
availability, then capacity, then features.

October 05 19:11 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 38 minutes)

Duration:
approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

What went wrong and why?

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How did we respond?

A partial networking failure began, and actions jobs started backing up.

Alerts flagged errors and slow job assignment, and we declared an incident.

We redeployed the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners, but it did not recover. We traced the failures to the networking issue.

We failed over the affected databases and storage to healthy regions, one service at a time, and added capacity. Actions recovered, but some other affected services kept failing even after failover.

We worked with our cloud provider to resolve the networking failure. The remaining services recovered, and we resolved the incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We are making the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners better able to handle sudden increases in load, so it keeps up when another region shifts extra jobs to it.

We now have expanded prioritization of runner assignment based on customer profile when available runner capacity is degraded.

We are changing the behavior of GitHub-hosted runners to reduce recovery time when job assignment services are degraded for a period of time.

We are improving how quickly we detect and locate partial network failures between our datacenters and the cloud-hosted services they depend on.

October 06 19:57 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 43 minutes)

Duration:
approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

What went wrong and why?

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How did we respond?

A surge of migration work overloaded a shared database, causing requests across github.com to fail or slow down.

Automated monitoring detected the failures and paged our on-call engineers.

The errors stopped on their own within minutes.

We declared an incident and paused enterprise migrations to prevent a recurrence while we investigated the cause.

Once a mitigation was deployed, we resumed migrations and resolved the incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We optimized the query GitHub Enterprise Importer sends to the database so that each one stays small and fixed in size.

We are automating importer backoff when the database is under strain, easing load before it can affect other GitHub services.

We are adding database alerts that flag queries doing much more work than usual and identify which query is responsible, so we can find and fix problems like this one faster.

October 07 15:14 and 17:17 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 11 minutes, and 47 minutes, respectively)

Duration:
two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

What went wrong and why?

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How did we respond?

Automated monitoring alerted us to failing writes, and we declared an incident.

Writes recovered when an established machine with correct records became leader and published correct settings.

We traced the cause to the new machine, resolved the first incident, and paused automated maintenance to prevent a repeat.

When a maintenance task did not honor the pause and the outage repeated, we declared a second incident.

Writes recovered when an established machine became leader again. We removed the new machine and resolved the second incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We improved how we retire database servers, so outdated records aren’t left behind.

We tightened controls on adding new machines that manage database routing, and making sure automated maintenance honors a pause.

We strengthened validation of database routing settings, so incorrect settings are caught before they take effect.

October 19 15:49 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 7 minutes)

Duration:
approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

What went wrong and why?

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How did we respond?

Automated alerts detected the failures, we declared an incident, and we traced the problem to the shared network link.

We routed the actions service away from some of its cache servers in that region, but the link was still over capacity.

We routed it away from the rest of those cache servers, and the link recovered.

We raised processing limits to clear the actions backlog, and we resolved the incident once all affected services had recovered.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We have limited how quickly this actions service can open new connections to its cache servers.

We are alerting on spikes in new connections from this service to identify and address the source sooner.

October 21 14:52 UTC (lasting 4 hours and 30 minutes)

Duration:
approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

What went wrong and why?

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How did we respond?

We declared an incident and moved some traffic off an overloaded server, but more servers became overloaded soon after.

We split the busiest traffic into more partitions and moved it to less-loaded servers. All affected features except audit logs gradually recovered.

Once the audit log service stopped restarting, we raised the rate at which it could write events so the backlog would clear faster.

We resolved the incident once audit log delays were back within the healthy range, and the remaining backlog cleared afterward.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We added randomized delays to reconnects after a failed request, so servers that are already slow don’t get hit with a burst of new connections.

We are alerting earlier on server memory use, so we can move traffic before a server slows down.

We are adding a second destination for webhook delivery data that we can switch to, so we can keep webhook deliveries moving if our event streaming platform slows down.

We have improved our playbooks to move hot partitions for similar situations in the future

October 28 14:12 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 16 minutes)

Duration:
approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

What went wrong and why?

Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How did we respond?

A credential we use with an upstream model provider stopped working, and requests to the affected models began to fail.

Alerts flagged rising errors on the affected models, and we declared an incident.

We posted a public status update and recommended choosing another model in the meantime.

We traced the errors to our own credential and created a replacement.

We began deploying the new credential, and requests started to recover once the first environment was updated.

We completed the deployment in the remaining environments, confirmed that requests to the affected models had recovered, and resolved the incident.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We improved how our service handles authentication failures from upstream model providers, so requests can be retried instead of failing.

We are strengthening how we manage credentials for upstream model providers.

We are adding alerts for authentication failures from upstream model providers, so we can identify and address this kind of problem faster.

October 30 14:31 UTC (lasting 31 minutes)

Duration:
approximately 9 minutes.

Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

What went wrong and why?

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

The pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How did we respond?

Requests used up every connection in the shared database pool, and requests across github.com began to fail.

We declared an incident after seeing failures, and on-call engineers for the affected services were paged.

The pool drained and error rates returned to normal. Shortly after, we confirmed that the full connection pool had caused the errors and posted a public status update.

We verified that database connections were back to normal and resolved the incident after monitoring for stability.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

We are now running the slow lookup before these update requests start writing a change, so they no longer hold a database connection while they wait.

We are evaluating limits on how long a pooled database connection can be held, so a slow request pattern is less likely to tie up the pool.

Follow our
status page
for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the
GitHub Blog
.

GitHub availability report: October 2026
appeared first on

title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
content:
How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline.

An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a
SKILL.md
file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database.

I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled
“Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills”
.

Define one job and when it applies

A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With
Proof Agent
, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose:

---
name: proof-agent
description: Adversarial verification of AI-generated work. Spawns an independent verifier to check for false claims, broken code, and security issues.
---

At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification.

The
When to Verify
section in Proof Agent’s
SKILL.md
says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings.

Coordinate multiple skills for a larger workflow

When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data.
Data Forge
is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together.

In the
support-desk pipeline example
, we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the
forge-init
skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need.

The
forge-builder
skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses
forge-dbx
to query the data platform and
forge-lint
to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests.

Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone.

Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit.

Keep project configuration out of the skill

We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a
manifest
describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions:

project:
name: "support-desk"
store_name: "support_metric_store"

platform:
engine: "duckdb"
pipeline_framework: "spark_python"
duckdb_dir: "warehouse"

With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project.

Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The
forge-init
initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the
forge-lint
skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them?

Share execution paths between skills

The
forge-dbx
skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic.

The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access.

Put checks and approval points in the workflow

The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The
workflow overview
shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval.

The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns
PASS
,
FAIL
, or
PARTIAL
and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set
block-on-fail: false
so findings were advisory. By default, a
FAIL
fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules.

Package for each agent client, then verify its setup

Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync. In the Data Forge example, we keep
skills/*/SKILL.md
as the source and use a packaging script to generate client-specific files:
.claude-plugin/plugin.json
for Claude Code,
.cursor-plugin/plugin.json
for Cursor, and
.github/agents/*.agent.md
for GitHub Copilot. The script also includes a check mode for CI:

node scripts/package.mjs --check

Clients can differ in their available models, tools, credentials, and permissions. After installing a skill, check that the client recognizes it for the intended task, loads its references, can use the required tools, and returns the evidence the skill calls for.

Three practices for building agent skills

Put business context in one file.
Keep project-specific names, schemas, and conventions in a manifest, and have each skill read it instead of duplicating those facts. This gives the team one visible place to update configuration.

Give related skills one consistent way to use the platform.
Have related skills use the same path to run queries, jobs, and schema changes instead of each defining its own commands and connection logic. This makes the workflow’s access easier to understand and its behavior easier to check in each client.

Use instructions to guide the work, and checks to verify it.
A skill can tell an agent which standards to follow and when to ask for approval. Add human review at decisions that need context or judgment, and use tests and CI checks to catch issues before a change moves forward. If a check must block a merge or deployment, configure that requirement in your repository’s rules.

Start with the task you’re tired of explaining. Write down what it needs, where it stops, and what a reviewer sees. Then try it with another agent and improve it as you learn what works.

Add an agent skill to GitHub Copilot >

The post
Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
appeared first on
The GitHub Blog
.

title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
content:
Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in
Git 2.56.1
, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Vulnerabilities in Git

CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.

An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s
.git
file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or
hooks
. When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone.

The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

[
Advisory
]

CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a
HEAD
symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

[
Advisory
]

CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

[
Advisory
]

CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

[
Advisory
]

CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large
conflict-marker-size
attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

[
Advisory
]

CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams

git fast-import
reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The
rewrite-submodules-from
and
rewrite-submodules-to
features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The
export-pack-edges
option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables
--allow-unsafe-features
. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

[
Advisory
]

Additional hardening

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Protecting GitHub users

We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible.

We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git.

GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git.

Update Git

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Get an updated version of Git >

Git security vulnerabilities announced

The GitHub Blog
