title: Mem Is Shutting Down
content:
After a lot of thought, we’ve made the difficult decision to bring Mem to a close.
Mem will shut down on January 15, 2027.

Over the years, you’ve trusted us with your ideas, meeting notes, unfinished drafts, and things you wanted to remember. Thank you for that trust. We know a notes app can become part of your daily life, and moving away from one takes time and care.

Our focus during these final weeks is helping you take your notes with you.

What happens next

December 18, 2026: notes become read-only.
You won’t be able to create or edit notes, but you can still read and export your existing notes.

January 15, 2027: Mem shuts down.
You won’t be able to access Mem after this date. Please download your notes beforehand.

You won’t be charged again.
All charging has been paused. The paid features, functionality, and limits you previously paid for will be honored for the remainder of Mem’s availability, with notes becoming read-only on December 18.

You don’t need to choose your next app right away. Start by saving a copy of your library. Our
migration guide
walks you through that download and moving to Apple Notes, Notion, Google Docs, Obsidian, OneNote, and other apps. It also explains what to check afterward, including attachments, collections, and meeting transcripts.

Move your notes from Mem →

A few moments we’ll remember

We built Mem around a question: what if your notes could do more than sit in a folder? What if they could help you remember, make connections, and use what you already knew?

From catching a thought with a keyboard shortcut to finding connections, writing with AI, and having a conversation with your knowledge, each step grew out of that same question. These moments come from our original newsletters, product walkthroughs, and launch emails, with the interfaces and demos we shared along the way.

April 2021
Catch a thought without breaking your flow
Mem Spotlight let you create a note from anywhere on your Mac with a keyboard shortcut. Capture first, get back to what you were doing, and find the thought waiting in your Timeline later. That small interaction captured a lot of what we wanted Mem to feel like.
Creating a note from Spotlight, from our April 2021 announcement.
Original launch post →
August 2021
Finding notes in your own words
Search began understanding clues like dates, links, and people. You could ask for “mems that contain Twitter links from July 2021,” instead of remembering an exact title.
The search demo from our August 2021 launch post.
Original launch post →
June 2022
Connections you didn’t have to organize
Mem X used embeddings to find notes by meaning and surface related ideas. Similar Mems could bring back a thought you’d forgotten, without asking you to maintain a perfect filing system.
Similar Mems in use, from Srini Rao’s August 2022 guest walkthrough.
Original walkthrough →
December 2022
AI writing that knew your context
Smart Write & Edit brought generative AI into your notes. It could help draft a message, prepare for a meeting, or develop an idea using the knowledge you had already saved.
The Smart Edit interface from our February 2023 product walkthrough, following the December rollout.
Original walkthrough →
March 2023
From tags to Collections
Collections grew out of the tags people were already using. Mem suggested relevant Collections as you wrote and found notes you might have forgotten to include. You could rename, merge, and organize them in bulk as your thinking changed.
Suggested Collections in the March 2023 launch demo.
Original launch post →
April 2024
Letting new themes find their own home
The next step was helping you notice themes you hadn’t named yet. When you wrote about something new, Mem could suggest a new Collection—not just an existing one. You could accept it, change its name, or keep writing.
New Collection suggestions from the April 2024 release.
Original launch post →
July 2024
A conversation with what you knew
With Mem Chat, your notes became something you could ask questions of. Our summer walkthrough showed how a simple question could surface a specific fact from your saved knowledge, with Smart Cards linking back to the notes behind an answer.
Chat in use in July 2024. This walkthrough followed its 2023 debut.
Original walkthrough →
October 2025
A fresh start with Mem 2.0
We rebuilt Mem around dependable, offline-first capture and recall. Voice Mode turned spoken thoughts and meetings into notes, and a new Chrome extension made saving from the web easier. The two arrows in our new logo represented you and Mem thinking together.
Voice Mode, as shown in the Mem 2.0 announcement.
Original launch post →
November 2025
Meeting notes on autopilot
Mem could detect when you joined a call and offer to start taking notes with one click, without a bot joining the meeting. It also detected the end of the call, so you didn’t have to remember to stop recording.
The meeting-detection screenshot sent on November 24, 2025.
Original launch email →
March 2026
Your notes, there when the conversation needed them
We introduced Heads Up Live and Meeting Briefings in beta for Mem Pro. One surfaced relevant context during a recorded meeting; the other helped you prepare before a calendar-linked meeting began.
Meeting Briefings from the March 26, 2026 beta announcement.
Original launch email →
April 2026
Bringing your notes into ChatGPT
The Mem app for ChatGPT brought your saved knowledge into another place you were already thinking and working. Alongside our MCP connector, it was another way to make your notes useful beyond Mem itself.
The graphic from our April 23, 2026 newsletter.
Original launch email →
July 2026
An Agent that reached out first
Mem Agent arrived in iMessage, WhatsApp, email, and Slack. It connected the context in your notes with proactive follow-ups, bringing back a useful next step when it was time to act.
The notification example from the July 23, 2026 Agent launch email.
Original launch email →

Behind each launch were people trying it, telling us where it fell short, and helping us make it better. The release posts record what we shipped. Your feedback shaped what those things became.

Thank you

To everyone who used Mem, shared it with a friend, sent us a thoughtful bug report, or trusted us with an idea before it was fully formed: thank you.

And to the team and the people who supported us along the way, thank you for the care you put into building this product.

We’re proud of the ideas we explored together. More than anything, we want the work you put into Mem to remain useful to you wherever you go next.

Save your notes and find your next home for them →

— Kevin

Founder and CEO

title: Stop Filming in Log?
content:
I may ruffle some feathers with that title; but after years as a colorist, log-encoded clips can be an unnecessary challenge. Using camera log profiles is often a crutch for location and studio set-ups. Or it’s simply used because the internet tells you log = film. That’s just not true. Many times a videographer will shoot log incorrectly – generally underexposed – expecting to ‘fix it in post’. The same issues apply to shooting in camera raw or HDR.

In the video world, camera raw was introduced by the
RED Digital Cinema Camera Company
in 2007, borrowing from still photo concepts. Log (logarithmic) videography came to the forefront when
ARRI introduced the Alexa in 2010
, which offered a Log-C profile. ARRI’s camera raw format wasn’t post-friendly, so Log-C was a better fit. The goal of both manufacturers was to shoot video with a wide dynamic range that could be recovered and adjusted in post production.

ARRI was able to do this with a mathematical approach that resulted in Log-C, which looked flat or with very, low contrast when viewed on a monitor. To correct this, a LUT file (color look-up table) was applied in post (or on-set) that used the inverse math to correct the image. However, ARRI cameras were and are generally used where there’s a specific color pipeline and workflow that’s discussed between production and post. A log image is also designed with a ‘sweet spot’. So if you under or overexpose the image, you will still encounter issues when you grade (color correct) the video.

Other camera manufacturers followed suit, including even Apple and its iPhones. The down side of this covers many facets. First, there are a plethora of inconsistent log schemes among the camera manufacturers. Second, the workflow and discipline in big budget shoots doesn’t usually exist in the kind of run-and-gun shoots that use these smaller form-factor cameras. On many projects that I post, I don’t know the videographer, have never had a conversion prior to the shoot about the grade, and almost never get notes as to how the cameras were set up. This becomes very problematic with Sony camera in particular. But they are not alone.

The earliest digital films were shot using
Sony F900 (modified by Panavision)
and
Thomson Viper FilmStream cameras
. These gave us films like
Attack of the Clones
,
Collateral
,
Zodiac
, and
Benjamin Button
. The Sony image was basically a standard Rec. 709 profile, whereas the Viper used a different color science. While the image wasn’t log or raw as we know it today, it did generate a green cast that had to be corrected in the color grade.

In reality, film doesn’t have an equivalent to log or raw. Motion picture film negative is typically shot with proper exposure and then color corrected when going to print. A film timer does the color correction, but the tools and looks are nowhere near as surgical as modern video color correction. While film negative might be scanned in the Cineon color space, this isn’t exactly the same as video log. If the film was transferred using some type of film scanner (
like the modern Cintel Scanner from Blackmagic Design
), then the result will be an image that’s close to standard or HDR video.

The Alexa’s introduction created many copy-cat cameras that each used different color profiles in log. These all required different LUTs (color look-up tables) to get you back to a Rec. 709 image. Quite frankly, I haven’t been too happy with the majority of these. The ARRI and Panasonic implementations look pretty good to me. Everyone else? Not so much.

Unfortunately, Sony made things even more confusing by introducing various profiles, including camera raw, s709, several iterations of S-Log, S-Cinetone, and, of course, Rec. 709. I’ve worked various projects shot in S-Log and it’s always a toss-up whether or not you can grade a good-looking image from the footage.
Of these options, I like S-Cinetone the best
.
It can make a wonderful image
.

From the
WhoIsMatt website
, “According to Sony, the base S-Cinetone curve is Rec. 709, but adds some filmic qualities. It has high contrast tone in low luminance levels and low contrast tone in the high luminance levels. The black level is lower than s709 and Rec. 709. With a low highlight contrast, S-Cinetone will have softer and lighter highlights, but higher contrast levels in low luminance levels will give you a more saturated look.”

Case in point. I’m currently editing and grading a project shot primarily with Sony A7S3 and FX9 cameras using a range of color settings. Some low contrast, some S-log of some sort. Zero info from the videographer. I’ve tried various Sony LUTs and color space conversions and none look as good as simply grading the shots manually. In fact, when I do apply a Sony LUT, I pick up noticeable noise artifacts in the shadow areas that simply isn’t there when I grade the shot without using a LUT.

This brings us to camera raw. Most users will only deal with camera raw from either
RED
or
Blackmagic Design cameras
. Each take different approaches, which have evolved over time. While camera raw can be useful in post, it’s not essential. If you shoot correctly with 709 in mind, then the raw result will fall right into line and be easily correctable, even if you don’t adjust the raw settings.

If you question the idea of using Rec. 709 under the false belief that it’s only limited to 8-bit, you would be mistaken.
Rec. 709 can also be 10-bit, assuming the camera supports it and you are using the proper codec.
Many of the small cameras record an H.264 or H.265 file. These files can be 8 or 10-bit. However, if you record in ProRes, ProResHQ, or ProRes4444, the signal can be 10-bit or higher. On top of that, these MP4 files (H.264/5) are highly compressed. This means if you record a log signal and then ‘expand’ it to full range, you run the risk of noise. Recording standard video in H.265 (10-bit) and then transferring it to ProRes for post will make your life so much easier in the edit and in the grade.

I’ll wrap this up with HDR (high dynamic range). Understand that HDR video is not the same thing as HDR photography.
An HDR still photo is created in-camera by capturing and combining multiple, simultaneous exposures.
These might be automatically ‘composited’ together as is (like in some iPhone software) – or can be extracted in post. The latter allows a photo retouching artist to shift the emphasis of the exposure. That’s how you get hyper-real-looking photos that fit into sRGB color space. HDR video simply captures the full linear range of the sensor as a single signal. So, they use different science and apply different technologies to the sensor image. HDR video is based largely on
Dolby
and
Canon’s
push to sell more display systems.

Many cameras can shoot in an HDR mode, which provides a peak brightness that far exceeds Rec. 709. However, in spite of all the marketing that tells you HDR is the image your eyes see, that simply isn’t true. Assume that you are in a dark room with bright sunlight visible through a window at the far end. Your eyes do not see all the information in the dark corners of the room and at the same time all the puffy clouds in the blue sky outside. Your eye ‘stops down’ for the window, or opens up for the room detail, making the window painful to look at. Yet, HDR videography and display systems reproduce exactly that. The result is a very painful-to-watch image on the display device.
RED actually tried to approach HDR capture like a still photo camera, but their solution never caught on
.

Smart phone cameras have become HDR-video-capable, even though most users have no idea what it is or how to set it correctly. Hence, you occasionally see an HDR video pop up on someone’s YouTube channel, making in nearly impossible to watch in a dim room. Also, in spite of the efforts of Canon and Dolby, true HDR has really not taken hold more broadly. Yes, there are camera and displays capable of some level of HDR – and yes, some streaming services, such as Netflix and YouTube, support it. But, it really is not a factor in the large amount of content that’s created globally.

Add to this feature films. There is a theatrical version of HDR, but it’s not nearly at the extreme levels of video HDR. Few if any films that I’ve seen use it. Whether or not HDR will be more of a factor in the future is an unknown. Nevertheless, in the context of this blog post, don’t shoot anything in a video HDR mode unless you specifically have been tasked to deliver HDR content.

Boiling this down: shooting in some version of Rec. 709, especially if it’s correctly lit and uses a low-contrast profile, will often yield much better results. Dealing with these clips will be easier in post than all the other recommendations that the internet puts in front of you.

©2026 Oliver Peters

title: Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force
content:
Here’s a demo video:
https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA
We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly.
The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors.
When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here:
https://axonnic.com/benchmarks
.
We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies.
Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension.
Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings.
So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG.
If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks!
https://axonnic.com

title: Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix
content:
saas

Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix

Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back

Richard Speed

Richard

Speed

MICROSOFT ECOSYSTEM REPORTER

Published

mon 16 Nov 2026 // 11:15 UTC

READ MORE

Microsoft fixes Windows activation as admins pick through Exchange outage wreckage

15 hours ago

Microsoft Outlook outage blamed after 15 injured in hotel pool chlorine incident

18 hours ago

We don't need no education platform evolution. Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone

23 hours ago

Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads

1 day ago

Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China

1 day ago

Microsoft has blamed last week's
epic outage
on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email.
According to a preliminary post incident report
published
by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact.
However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted."

REG AD

"The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware."

REG AD

The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued.
It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive."
So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again.
"Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old.
Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.
The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues.
At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in.
It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over.

REG AD

"Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report says. "But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons."
Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many users, Outlook) was out of action.
By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled.
However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation –  an update that reverted the defective change."
At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer update.
A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An update applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control?
The engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an update with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ®

title: Do Repeat Yourself
content:
← All articles
You are Lisa. You work at Megabank. Your team builds the account management part of the website - transaction lists with filters and queries, charts for account levels, and statement exports in .csv and .pdf. You’ve built a sleek backend in Go and a frontend in Svelte, all running on a Kubernetes cluster that you manage.
Your buddy Steve, two floors up, builds the investment banking part of the customer portal. Portfolio lists with filters and queries, charts for market prices, and order exports in CSV and PDF. They used Node for WebSocket connections, Erlang for the processing side, and React for a smoother frontend experience.
Hanna, on floor five, handles credit cards. Her team has developed a nice customer portal featuring a list of credit card charges that can be filtered and queried. Pretty charts allow you to track debt levels over time. And, for extra convenience, you can export your charges in CSV and PDF. Hanna’s team implemented all this in PHP running on Apache servers, with a frontend in Angular.
All three teams adhered to the corporate branding guidelines, so their products look and feel reasonably similar. They also work fairly well and were shipped on time.
But - great news! Megabank has hired some new top talent. Mike comes from the mythical lands of tech and management consultancy. He’ll be the super senior VP of platform at Megabank.
Good Inefficiencies
It takes Mike just two days to realise that work at Megabank is highly inefficient. Each team has reimplemented the same functionality over and over again. They are also relying on their own stacks, so transferring people between teams is much harder. Sure, they shipped quality products on time - but with Mike’s process improvement expertise, imagine how much more they could be doing…
Mike creates a fourth team-the platform team. That team has two tasks:
Set standards that every other team has to adhere to. The platform team will conduct careful research and then decide on one stack that all other teams have to use and one standard they have to follow. This will allow for knowledge sharing and inter-team transfers.
Create a shared component library for other teams to use. This will include a generic list with filters and queries, a time-series data model with an abstract chart library, and universal export to CSV and PDF.
Soon, the platform team goes to work. They decide that backend functionality will be implemented in Go from here on, frontends in React, and everything will be hosted on Kubernetes. As far as platform teams go, this is a very modern and common-sense decision.
The other teams start learning these technologies. Some already have some experience; others have to learn from scratch - but those are just temporary teething pains. Soon, everyone will have adjusted to the new reality and efficiency will skyrocket.
Except maybe for the investment banking team. They really need their Erlang architecture for decentralized networking - after all, they process fast-moving market data, order execution, and the like.
It also turns out that Go is overkill for the credit card guys. They just need a simple model-view-controller architecture like PHP provides. Having pointers to memory addresses and managing concurrency via goroutines rather than just writing linear PHP that Apache runs in parallel is really much more than they bargained for.
But at least on the frontend side, a lot of time will be saved. The new list components and charts are well designed and can just be dropped into a customer portal, saving lots of development time. Except for the investment banking team - they need candlestick charts that were supported by their chart library but haven’t made it into the generic charting component yet. They raise a ticket with the platform team, but it gets deprioritised since the CSV and PDF exports have to be implemented first.
The credit card team is also really struggling with porting their backend to Go. They ask if they could use the transaction list from the platform team but send the same data format from their existing PHP implementation. The platform team doesn’t want to be seen as the obstacle, so they agree. But writing documentation for the internal data structure of the transaction list component hasn’t been planned for - after all, it was never meant to be available externally. And really, the focus right now is on building the PDF and CSV exports.
Unfortunately, this year, none of the teams will be shipping much. But Mike made an amazing presentation called “Megabank platform vision 2028 – a road to global efficiency”. So his bonus will be fine.
This story has played out too many times. You were probably part of it at some point. And it makes sense on its face. The inefficiencies are real. But-they are necessary. Different requirements need different solutions. Different people know different things. Standardisation and abstraction seem like good solutions on their face but are hard to implement in practice. Minor differences multiply into large, unwieldy problems.
Service-Oriented Architecture
The solution is often the opposite of what good software design teaches. Do Repeat Yourself. At least, allow for some level of repetition. But more importantly, create clear boundaries within which teams can be flexible, and clear interfaces and protocols to interact and combine their services.
This idea is as old as the internet - and is often called Service-Oriented Architecture, or SOA for short.
Think of service-oriented architecture like going to a street food market. Each vendor has a little booth with a menu of available options. If you want to order something, you know you need to talk to the vendor, request your option, and pay using a shared currency or card. That’s the common interface. How the vendor prepares the food, where they source their ingredients from, which kitchen appliances they use - all of that is not your concern. You interact with the common interface.
For our three teams, that means that each can continue using their stack and approach and ship at their own cadence. But Mike also had a point with his platform team. There are things that are necessary for a user experience to not feel disjointed. And there are capabilities, such as DevOps, that are best handled centrally. So, rather than prescribing an exact technology stack and building shared components, Mike shifts the platform team’s responsibility. It now:
Standardizes that all backend functionality has to be shipped as Docker Containers and all frontend functionality has to be compiled into static files that can be loaded via CDN.
Prescribes standards for API design and structure. All teams have to offer their services through a clear RESTful HTTP API, documented with Swagger and following common conventions. How that API is implemented is each team’s decision.
Provides a shared CSS framework for UI elements. This can be applied to HTML created by any framework and creates a common look and feel.
Provides the outer framework for the user portal: navigation, asset loading, and module bundling. This accepts some pretty major inefficiencies-whenever the user switches from the account view to the investing tab, a whole new JS framework is loaded. But, given all other factors, this is an acceptable trade-off.
Creates a universal documentation base that all other teams contribute to. This provides transparency and knowledge sharing and helps to keep teams from becoming siloed.
With these changes, efficiency rises back up. Not because the teams stopped rebuilding the same thing, but because they’ve stopped getting in each other’s way. Some code is duplicated. Some problems are solved three different ways. And that’s fine. Minimizing the amount of code written or the number of technologies used isn’t a goal in itself - but building good products, shipping them on time, and allowing teams to work effectively together is. Sometimes, the most efficient thing you can do is to let people repeat themselves.

title: How to Break into Security, Ptacek Edition (2012)
content:
At least once a month, sometimes more, readers write in to ask how they can break into the field of computer security. Some of the emails are from people in jobs that have nothing to do with security, but who are fascinated enough by the field to contemplate a career change. Others are already in an information technology position but are itching to segue into security. I always respond with my own set of stock answers, but each time I do this, I can’t help but feel my advice is incomplete, or at least not terribly well-rounded.

I decided to ask some of the brightest minds in the security industry today what advice they’d give. Almost everyone I asked said they, too, frequently get asked the very same question, but each had surprisingly different takes on the subject. Today is the first installment in a series of responses to this question. When the last of the advice columns have run, I’ll create an archive of them all that will be anchored somewhere prominently on the home page. That way, the next time someone asks how they can break into security, I’ll have more to offer than just my admittedly narrow perspectives on the matter.

Last month, I interviewed
Thomas Ptacek
, founder of
Matasano Security
, about how companies could beef up password security in the wake of a week full of news about password leaks at
LinkedIn
and other online businesses.
Ptacek’s provocative advice
generated such a huge amount of reader interest and further discussion that I thought it made sense to begin this series with his thoughts:

Ptacek:
“Information security is one of the most interesting, challenging, and, if you do it carefully, rewarding fields in the technology industry. It’s one of the few technology jobs where the most fun roles are well compensated. If you grew up dreaming of developing games, the laws of supply and demand teach a harsh lesson early in your career: game development jobs are often tedious and usually pay badly. But if you watched “Sneakers” and ideated a life spent breaking or defending software, great news: infosec can be more fun in real life, and it’s fairly lucrative.

I’m a software developer. I try to look at security through the lens of computer science. To me, the most attractive thing about the field is the opportunity it provides to work with lots of different concepts at lots of different levels. Computer security might be the best way to work professionally with compiler theory, or to spend time understanding computer microarchitecture, or to apply advanced mathematics.

Other people get involved in security for different reasons, and those reasons are probably equally valid. Some people really like the “good guys / bad guys” narrative that comes with security. Some people see security as an opportunity to save the world. Other people are drawn to the competitive nature of the field: at the higher levels, it really is a cat-and-mouse game. It also comes closer to meritocracy than most of technology: you can either break in or you can’t; your defenses either work or they don’t.

But for me, it’s just one of the best development jobs you can get, and with that in mind, here’s my advice for people interested in pursuing a career in it.

First: I want you to learn how to program.
Clearly, you can get through college and get a good-paying steady job without ever learning to love programming. But no one factor gives you as much control over your career, as much of an ability to write your own ticket, as the ability to solve problems using programming languages. A lot of very smart technology professionals have concluded that they just don’t enjoy writing software. Those people should reconsider. Try different languages, or different application domains, but find a way to make programming stick in your head.

Second: the best jobs in our field are in application security.
You can get good steady work designing firewall deployments, setting up desktop agents, or responding to incidents. But all those roles are fundamentally reacting to what’s happening in appsec. The next generation of security products — along with the org charts of security teams at the savviest companies — are being designed now, by accident, by application security practitioners.

Appsec roles are roles that involve attacking software or devising fixes and countermeasures for those attacks. Two good ways to “come up” in appsec: become a penetration tester, or contribute to (or start) a secure software development practice in your company.

A good way to move into penetration testing: grab some industry standard tools and use an
Amazon EC2
account to set up a “shooting range” to attack. Some of the best-known tools are available for free: the
Nessus scanner
, for instance, while not an application security tool, is free and can land you a network penetration testing role that you can use as a springboard to breaking applications.

When people reach out to Matasano asking how to get a foot in the door attacking software, we have a few simple steps to offer:

0. Learn to love programming in at least one language. The C Programming Language has the most cachet in application security, but for this step-by-step list, Java or Python or Ruby will do fine.

1. Grab a copy of
The Web Application Hacker’s Handbook
.

2. Go to the “previous releases” archive at
WordPress.org
and grab very old versions of WordPress; install them at EC2.

3. Download
OWASP WebScarab
or
Burp Suite Free Edition
, both of which are free, and use them to find bugs in ancient WordPress.

If you’re already in an IT role, and want to come up on the defensive side of appsec, try to position yourself near custom software development. Most large firms build “line of business” applications. As a rule, building “line of business” isn’t particularly fun. But defending those apps can be; sometimes, the most boring applications turn out to be surprisingly sensitive.

And the good news for doing appsec in BigCo’s: most companies have very immature security programs. If you can get a role in QA, or in what the cool kids are calling “DevOps”, you can end up with a lot of influence in security. At Matasano, we’ve watched lots of ops people successfully transition to appsec and senior security management just by instituting basic security testing processes on their company’s software.

To me, the whole field boils down to studying, understanding, and manipulating technology. Like most software security practices, we’ve gotten our hands dirty with a fascinating cross-section of the whole technology industry. We’ve written attack tools that target the control registers of device chipsets, we’ve done custom RF work, we’ve written low-level debuggers for different CPU architectures, and we’ve seen and beaten up on products built in almost every programming language and every platform you can imagine. If crawling through the ventilation ducts of the world’s most important technology is something you think might make you tick like we do… well, appsec! Learn to code. Spend a couple days Starbucks money on an EC2 account and deploy some broken apps to break. Find opportunities to practice in your job.

And, uh, come talk to us? People like you are hard to find!”

title: Squircles
content:
Squircles

A squircle is a shape intermediate between a square and a circle.
There is no single mathematical definition, rather there are a number of curves that fit this shape.
All general squircles are parametrized, and can vary between circle and square.

Loading the interactive tester…

Superellipse

The best known squircle is the superellipse, popularized by Piet Hein.
Martin Gardner wrote a detailed narrative of its origin in a
Scientific American column
in 1977.
The text is replicated in
https://piethein.com/superellipse/
but that’s missing equations and figures.

The superellipse has the formula $|x|^n + |y|^n = 1$ (we’ll use a unit radius for convenience).
When $n=2$ it is a circle, and it approaches a square asymptotically as $n \rightarrow \infty$.

Measurement

There is no standard measurement for squircles.
For superellipses, the exponent is the most common parameter.
A good choice is the coordinates of the midpoint of the quadrant, assuming a unit radius; here $x$ and $y$ are equal.
The conversion formula is simple and intuitive: $x = 0.5^{1/n}$.
This measurement is called "gauge" in the interactive demo above, and is the primary parameter; with the exception of some unreachable regions of parameter space, it should be possible to compare different squircle variants with similar gauge.

Flat-sided squircles

There are two basic approaches to squircle creation.
One is a single analytic curve, where curvature reaches zero at the poles, but is otherwise nonzero.
The other is mixing straight line segments with corners.
A significant advantage of the latter approach is that it can adapt to rectangles of arbitrary aspect ratio without distorting the corner shape.

The Apple squircle shape

Squircles received renewed attention when Apple changed the icon shape from rounded rectangle to their own squircle in iOS 7 in 2013.
There were several blog posts to analyze and recreate the shape.
An early analysis suggested that it was a superellipse of exponent 5, but when people extracted the Béziers and looked more closely, that was found to be inaccurate.
Rather, it’s a flat-sided squircle.

For the raw Bézier path data of the Apple shape, the best source is the
PaintCode blog
.
This blog correctly points out some bugs in that logic, and also has some details on behavior for oval rather than square aspect ratios.

The Apple shape has a number of flaws, including one extraneous straight line segment, and a lack of symmetry.
However, those flaws are minor, and really only reveal themselves under close analysis.

The Apple shape has no additional parameter, so its variation is controlled entirely by the length of the flat side.
With no flat side, it has a gauge fixed at 0.809.

An extremely detailed analysis of the Apple shape is in
The Art of Continuous Corners
.

The Figma squircle

Figma published a blog post,
Desperately Seeking Squircles
, with an analysis of the Apple squircle and their own approximation.
It is influential because Figma is an important design tool, because their writeup was compelling, and because there are any number of open source implementations of it, mostly TypeScript/JavaScript.

squircle-path-kit
from msurguy

figma-squircle
from phamfoo

corner-smoothing
from sanalabs (uses figma-squircle)

squircle-js
from bring-shrubbery (uses figma-squircle)

figma_squircle
from aloisdeniel (Dart/Flutter)

Lisse
from JaceThings

The Figma blog contains a plot of the Béziers comprising a cleaned up version of iOS 7 rounded rectangle, revealing three Bézier segments per quadrant.
It fixes the straight-line segment and the asymmetry, so is not an exact match.
The middle segment is very close to an arc.
The other segments are more problematic.
They have zero curvature at the endpoints, so are G2 continuous with flat sides, but there is a curvature discontinuity with the middle (arc) section, and their curvature profile is not especially smooth.
A reasonable guess is that it was drawn by hand to be approximately smooth.

Without a flat side, the Figma squircle is only capable of a gauge between $\sqrt{0.5}$ (0.707) and 0.854.
Gauges up to 1 are of course attainable by adding the flat side.

Clothoid squircles

The Figma blog suggests “smoothed curvature profiles” which have a piecewise linear relationship between arc length and curvature.
It then goes on to approximate them with cubic Bézier segments, but their approximation has fairly significant curvature discontinuities when joining to the circular arc.
The clothoid squircle is worth describing explicitly, as it has G2 continuity (as opposed to G1 for the Figma approximation).

The behavior is generally similar to the Figma variant.
Without a flat side, it is only capable of a gauge between $\sqrt{0.5}$ (0.707) and 0.790.

The box decorations corner-shape spec

Squircles got a big boost as they’re now standardized in CSS, as the
corner-shape
property of the
box decorations spec
.
These specify real superellipse corners, with additional tweaks and support for animation.

The Chromium superellipse approximation

While the CSS spec mandates the actual superellipse shape, practical implementations will generally use a Bézier approximation.
A blog post,
The corner cases of implementing CSS corner-shape in Blink
, gives an efficient closed-form approximation, with two Bézier segments per quadrant.
This formula, determined using symbolic regression, is parametrized, and handles exponents 2 and above well.
It is exact for placing the midpoint (this is part of the formula), so is well calibrated in that regard.

Apple-like behavior with the corner-shape spec

The early analysis of the Apple squircle shape as being approximately an exponent 5 superellipse was based on coarse shape only and didn't take into account its flat side.
A much better match to the Apple shape is attainable using a superellipse with exponent 3 and a corresponding flat side length to match the gauge.
This has G2 continuity and a similar curvature profile.
This illustration was made using the Chromium approximation, so it should match the browser.

Here's the CSS to accomplish the "close to Apple" squircle shape.
Note that the parameter to the
superellipse()
function is the base-2 log of the exponent, so the value for an exponent of 3 is 1.585.

.
icon
{

aspect-ratio:
1
;

border-radius:
46.2%
;

corner-shape: superellipse(
1.585
);

}

Continuity

A superellipse of exponent $n$ has continuity $G(\lceil n \rceil - 1)$.
This includes the flat-sided variants, as, for exponent > 2, the endpoint of the quadrant has zero curvature.
A perfect circle (and indeed, any even integer exponent) without flat sides is of course the exception, as it has an infinitely high order of continuity.

As a general observation, for visual smoothness, the shape should have G2 continuity.
Of the variants discussed, only the clothoid and superellipse (for n > 2) have this property.
The Chromium approximation comes close; it doesn't have zero curvature by construction when joining the flat part, but does at the corner join by symmetry (unlike the Figma approximation, which has an additional arc there).

Other squircles

Quite a number of other curves can be pressed into service as squircles if need be.

The polynomial spiral (“spiro”) curve can do a reasonable flat-sided squircle with G2 continuity.
See the “suitcase corners” section of
Raph's thesis
, figure 7.2.

Conic sections (hyperbolas).
These approximate a sharp corner but are only G1 continuous (if flat sided).

Fernández-Guasti squircle, defined by $x^2 + y^2 - s^2x^2y^2 = 1$.
This is used in engineering but likely not in graphic design.

The
Wikipedia page on squircles
has a “periodic squircle” which has very similar behavior to the Fernández-Guasti one (they are visually near indistinguishable).

The offset curve of a squircle is not a squircle, but (a) it’s close, and (b) concentric squircles might be visually just as appealing or more so; for example a slightly rounded inner corner might look better than a sharp one if the curvature exceeds the stroke half-width.

The
blurred rounded rectangle approximation
is based on applying shading to a superellipse; each iso-line is in fact a superellipse.

Today Anthropic, PBC launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock.
The proposed offering consists of 825,000,000 shares of Class A common stock. Of these, 801,351,354 shares are being offered by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares are being offered by certain existing stockholders. Anthropic will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders. Anthropic also expects to grant the underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to an additional 123,750,000 shares of its Class A common stock.
The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.”
The proposed offering will be made only by means of a prospectus. Copies of the preliminary prospectus may be obtained from: Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 200 West Street, New York, NY 10282, by telephone at (866) 471-2526, or by email at prospectus-ny@ny.email.gs.com; or Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 180 Varick Street, 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10014.
A registration statement relating to these securities has been filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission but has not yet become effective. title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2
content:
We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.
Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded
Life Sciences
and
Cyber
Verification Programs.
Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.
Safety and alignment.
To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.
We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the
Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card
.
When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2.
Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of
Advisor
(where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or
Orchestrator
(where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).

Effort and efficiency.
On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested.
Agentic coding: FrontierCode 2.0
Agentic search: WANDR
Hardware engineering: BenchCAD 2.1
Multidisciplinary reasoning: Humanity’s Last Exam
Visual chart recognition: Chartography
FrontierCode 2.0
Accuracy vs. cost
FrontierCode measures whether a model’s code changes would be merged by the maintainers of open-source repositories. At High effort, Fable 5.2 scores about the same as Opus 5.5’s best score (45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task, and ahead of GPT-6 Astra’s best score (42.8%) at about the same cost. At Xhigh effort, Fable 5.2 reaches 49.1%, the highest score of any released model we’ve tested.
WANDR (relaxed score)
Accuracy vs. cost
Perplexity’s WANDR benchmark measures agents on large data-collection tasks. At Medium effort, Fable 5.2 matches Opus 5.5’s top score for about 40% of the cost per task.
BenchCAD 2.1 (with tools)
Accuracy vs. cost
BenchCAD 2.1 measures hardware engineering, specifically how closely a model’s designs match reference geometry and circuits, and is scored 0–100 with partial credit. At Max effort, Fable 5.2 scores 83.5, ahead of Opus 5.5 (65.3) and Fable 5.1 (44.4).
Humanity’s Last Exam (with tools)
Accuracy vs. cost
Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) is a test of expert-level academic knowledge and reasoning. At Low effort, Fable 5.2 matches Opus 5.5’s top score for less than one-tenth of the cost per task.
Chartography (no tools)
Accuracy vs. cost
Chartography tests how accurately a model can read charts and figures. At Medium effort, Fable 5.2 scores 66.4%, ahead of Opus 5.5 at Max effort (64.4%) for less than one-tenth of the cost per task.
Coding
Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.
As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).

Cybersecurity
Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²
CVE Rediscovery
Accuracy vs. cost
CVE Rediscovery is an internal cybersecurity evaluation that assesses how many published CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) a model can independently find when given a snapshot of the project before a CVE was fixed. Our October 2026 run against 1,829 CVEs showed Claude Mythos 5.2 outperformed Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 at every effort level.

Cyber Verification Program

, which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2.
A recent update to Claude Security
helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.

Science and engineering
Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.
Theoretical physics
Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.
Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints,
here
and
here
.
Protein folding
Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the
capsid
, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.
Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:
Dyno Therapeutics
Columbia University
Biohub
Quote
“This acceleration could save meaningful time and cost from our capsid folding pipeline, enabling us to deploy compute more efficiently across many capsid properties that are needed for a genetic medicine. We are excited to help Anthropic push the reasoning capabilities further to reduce the cost of designing capsids overall.”

Dyno Therapeutics

Sam Sinai, Cofounder and Head of AI

“Large protein assemblies, including capsids, remain an open problem for protein modeling, due to the complexity of accurately predicting and positioning the structures of dozens of individual macromolecules, not to mention the inordinately high computational costs involved. Claude’s approach cleverly tackles this problem for symmetric assemblies, making it possible for individual scientists to model systems on personal workstations that would otherwise require dedicated clusters.”

Columbia University

Mohammed AlQuraishi, Assistant Professor of Systems Biology and Computer Science

“Biohub’s goal in open-sourcing ESMFold2 was to enable the scientific community to build on the biology it has learned. We will continue to incorporate such contributions from the community that extend our tools to important application domains.”

Biohub
Author
Zeming Lin, Principal Research Scientist
Mathematics
Mathematical formalization.
Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.
Our first
formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem
, performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, and built its own ways to coordinate.⁴ It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30.
Read more about the formalization
here
.
Fermat’s Last Theorem proof formalization
Completion over time
Formalizing the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in the mathematical programming language Lean. Each line shows the proportion of the full formalization that Fable 5.2 (green line) and Opus 5.5 (orange line) had completed over 30 hours with about 1,000 agents, and a single run per model. At the dashed line (18 hours), both teams resumed from their last save with 12 more hours.
Hardware and robotics
Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of
increasing usefulness
in the
real world
, showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots.
Hardware engineering.
We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with
Diode
, a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards.
Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills
here
.
Robotics.
Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public
RoboDojo
benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots.
RoboDojo (average)

Research and analysis
Early testers using Claude Fable 5.2 for research and analysis tasks found that it can handle more ambiguous, data-heavy tasks than previous models and has better judgment on ambiguous tasks—particularly those that require abstract reasoning and design. Proprietary trading firm Jump Trading tested Fable 5.2 on proxy evaluations that resemble some of its quantitative research tasks, embedding it in a harness similar to the one the firm uses for its own research. In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses.
Other testers from research and analysis organizations sent us the following statements on their experiences with Fable 5.2:

It traced the answer to the right sources and didn’t overstate what the evidence showed. It also flagged that the question’s framing could be misleading. In investment research, that restraint makes clear what remains unknown and where the market may be mispricing risk or opportunity.”

“On one task, Claude Fable 5.2 had to pull a company’s financials out of its 10-K into a forecasting model, and the template didn’t say whether a metric should be the reported figure or calculated. It inferred the author’s intent from the cell formatting, caught that the regional numbers didn’t sum to the reported total, and got every cell right. Better judgment calls like that are the main reason it scored 91% on our eval versus 86% for the next best model.”
Company

“Before putting AI to work across workflows, you need to trust its approach and conclusions. In our testing, Claude Fable 5.2 identified inconsistencies, drew on context across entire document sets, and adjusted recommendations based on relevant evidence. For example, when reviewing files attached to a loan application, it flagged that the salary deposits and the bank statement’s balance didn’t match, so the underwriter could focus on what to check.”
Company
Box
Author
Yashodha Bhavnani, VP of AI Products
Safety and alignment
No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the
UK AI Security Institute
,
Frontier Design
, and
METR
. See the
Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card
for a summary of their reports⁵ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing.
Alignment testing
We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models).
We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁶
Automated behavioral audit
Overall misaligned behavior score
Mythos 5.1
Opus 5.5
Sonnet 5.5
Mythos 5.2
Overall score from our automated behavioral audit, a composite of many undesirable behaviors including cooperation with human misuse and autonomous actions across a range of scenarios. Lower scores are better. See Section 6.4.1 of the
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 System Card
for full details.
We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences).
We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1.
The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss.
Safeguards
Cybersecurity and biology safeguards.
Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas.
AI research and development.
The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did
not
affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the
System Card
and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators.
Anti-distillation.
Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our
September 2026 threat intelligence report
for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a
recent report
, which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%.
We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation:
preserved thinking
now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our
preserved thinking docs
to learn how to update integrations with new API features).
Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards
Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2
rely on
safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With
Enterprise Frontier Safeguards
, automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe.
Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing
this form
. Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring.
Availability
Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can
get started
with
claude-fable-5-2
on the Claude Platform.
This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion
here
.
Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the
Cyber Verification Program
. Claude Enterprise customers can also use
Claude Security
, powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also
apply
for access through the
Life Sciences Verification Program
.
Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs.
Edit 11 November: Amended a sentence and added a footnote to the “Mathematical formalization” subsection to more accurately describe the information we provided to the model.
Footnotes
1

CVE refers to
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures
, a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities.
2

The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the
system card
).
3

Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes
FoldaVirus
,
EvoDOCK
and its
symmetric extension
,
SymProFold
,
CapBuild
,
MoLPC
,
CombFold
,
Uni-Fold Symmetry
,
Apodex Discovery
, and the
“big bang” initialization
(the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for
OpenFold3-preview2
and 1.4 Å for
ESMFold2
on AAV2 (
PDB:1LP3
). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2.
4

As described in our
accompanying post
, we “gave the agents a list of 60 statements, a one-sentence sketch of the classical route, the definitions those statements use, and 47 proved lemmas from our earlier formalization, and assigned lead and helper roles. We offered no other guidance on how to prove the theorem or organize themselves.”
5

6
