Tools & Resources
Note
Starting in
November 2026
, we are gradually rolling out a requirement for every sending IP to have a valid HELO, a reverse DNS (PTR) record, and a matching A record. Use the HELO checker below to see whether the DNS meets our best practices, and follow the guidelines to avoid being listed.
Minimum requirements
Guidance for senders, mail admins, and postmasters on meeting Spamhaus's sending requirements. All senders must meet these minimum email sending requirements to avoid being listed.
1
Use confirmed opt-in (COI) for all subscribers
Each recipient should confirm their address by clicking a link in a confirmation email. If no confirmation is received, do not send email to that address. Purchased, rented and harvested lists are the most common source of spam trap hits, and hitting traps is one of the fastest routes to a listing.

See section
2
Publish forward-confirmed reverse DNS for every sending IP
Every sending IP must have a reverse DNS entry pointing to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). That hostname must, in turn, resolve back to the same sending IP address. This is known as forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS). An IP with missing or mismatched reverse DNS is treated as suspicious and is one of the most common reasons for an IP to be considered for listing.

See section
3
Use a HELO/EHLO hostname that resolves to the sending IP
The hostname the server announces in the HELO/EHLO command must resolve to the IP it is connecting from, and must stay consistent across connections from that IP. Placeholder values, hosting-provider defaults, and hostnames that vary between connections are treated as signals of misconfiguration or compromise and can result in a listing.

See section
4
Meet the IPv6 allocation and reverse DNS minimum
If sending over IPv6, the sending address must fall within an allocation of /64 or larger (a /64 is the standard block size we recommend assigning), and that space must have valid reverse DNS. IPv6 ranges without reverse DNS or with allocations smaller than /64 are often misused by spammers.

See section
5
Authenticate mail with
SPF
,
DKIM
and
DMARC
Publish SPF and DMARC records for every sending domain, sign every outbound message with a signature, and align the DKIM sending domain with the domain in the message's
RFC 5322
From address. Authentication is one of the signals that shapes reputation, so gaps here make a listing more likely when other signals are weak.

See section
Operating an Email Server Provider (ESP) or other shared sending infrastructure?
See the ESPs and Large Senders guidelines
1. Infrastructure and DNS
All sending infrastructure must have the following DNS and mailserver configuration. Failure to do so can result in IPs being listed on the Email Spam IPs (CSS) or compromised IPs (XBL) zones.
Do
Don't
Do
Required
Ensure the sending IP address has a valid
reverse DNS (rDNS)
entry resolving to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for the sending IP address. Spamhaus will treat emails originating from IP addresses without rDNS as suspicious and this will be reflected in the IP's reputation, and receivers using Spamhaus data may subject it to additional filtering.
Ensure the rDNS hostname resolves to the connecting IP address via a corresponding
forward DNS (A/AAAA) record
.
Recommended
Abusive actors often rely on the reputation of upstream DNS records to hide their identity. Instead, configure a branded reverse DNS to use the sender's own domain, to improve trust signals for the IP address.
Don't
Do not use generic or auto-generated rDNS entries for dedicated IPs that point to the hosting provider (e.g.,
static-203-0-113-25.hosting.example.net
,
203.113.0.25.broadband.example.net
,
vps-25.dedicated.hosting.example.com
etc). These can negatively impact reputation.
Do not use random dictionary words in the rDNS and make it identifiable to the sending infrastructure.
How to check
Use the
Spamhaus DNS checker
tool to check your rDNS configuration.
Do
Don't
Do
Required
Ensure the hostname used in the
HELO/EHLO
command resolves to the sending IP address.
Maintain a consistent HELO value that resolves to the sending IP address. Multiple HELO values resolving to different IP addresses may indicate residential proxy and/or malware behaviour.
Recommended
Where possible, ensure the HELO/EHLO hostname is consistent with the rDNS hostname.
Host a webpage on the domain of the HELO, that explains what the domain is for, or that redirects to the main brand domain.
Don't
Do not use placeholder values such as
localhost
or generic hostnames that point to the hosting company/ISP as the HELO value.
Do not resolve HELO hostname to infrastructure that is not used for sending — this behaviour is associated with spoofing and misconfiguration.
Do not use generic or auto-generated names provided by the hosting provider, use the sender's own domain where possible.
Do not impersonate the HELO value of well-known mailbox providers like Gmail or Hotmail.
How to check
Enter an IP address into the
Spamhaus DNS Checker at the top of this page
, to check its HELO value. An email can also be sent to
helocheck@abuseat.org
to check the HELO being used.
Do
Do
Required
IPv6 customer allocations must be at least /64 and must have valid reverse DNS. The /64 minimum is consistent with IPv6 subnet architecture and
RFC 6177
's guidance that email senders should be able to obtain at least a /64. This is further discussed in
M3AAWG best practices
for IPv6 allocation.
Recommended
Add routes for all IP space owned by the sender to reduce vulnerability to
BGP hijacking
, which can allow hackers to send email that appears to originate from the IP space.
How to check
Run
dig -x <an IPv6 address in the allocation>
to confirm reverse DNS is present. To confirm the space is actually routed, look the address up at
bgp.he.net
.
Do
Don't
Do
Required
Make sure SPF is set up correctly for the domain used in the envelope sender (
RFC 5321
MAIL FROM), and points to the sending infrastructure.
Use
SRS
(Sender Rewriting Scheme) to rewrite the envelope From (MAIL FROM) if mail is forwarded, so SPF can still be checked against the forwarding domain.
Don't
Do not allow freemail addresses such as
gmail.com
or
hotmail.com
as the 'Envelope FROM.'
Do not use the NULL envelope sender
<>
for anything other than indirect out-of-band delivery reports, DSNs and MDNs.
Do not send bounce messages after accepting unwanted mail. Reject it during the SMTP transaction instead. Bounces sent to forged senders are known as backscatter, which is indirect spam and can severely harm reputation.
How to check
Run
dig TXT <envelope sender domain>
and confirm an SPF record is returned and includes the sending IPs.
Do
Don't
Do
Recommended
Audit DNS regularly and remove records for services, hosts and IP space that are no longer used, including
CNAMEs
, NS delegations, A records and SPF
include:
entries for former providers.
Don't
Do not leave records pointing to decommissioned hosts or former providers.
Dangling records
can be claimed by others and used to send mail that appears to come from the domain.
Do not use wildcard DNS records.
This
article
explains domain, hostname terminology and domain alignment in email. Also, use
aboutmy.email
to check for email configuration setup.
How to check
Run
dig
against the subdomains and look for CNAMEs that resolve to a provider that no longer serves the domain.
2. Authentication
Authentication is how receiving mail servers verify that emails are authorized to send from the domain. Without SPF, DKIM, and DMARC properly configured, the domain is exposed to spoofing and phishing, and emails are more likely to be rejected or flagged by Spamhaus.
Do
Don't
Do
Required
Publish an
SPF TXT record
in the domain's DNS zone file that specifies exactly which IPs and hosts are authorized to send email on the domain's behalf.
Ensure the sending IP is explicitly included in the SPF record. Email sent from IPs not included in SPF will not pass SPF checks.
Make sure both the HELO domain and the envelope From domain have a valid SPF record. Publish SPF records on this domain (which might be the infrastructure domain) and not the visible header From domain.
Keep the SPF record within the
10 DNS lookup limit
(this includes all nested
include:
statements). Exceeding the limit returns a PermError, which is not a pass, so SPF cannot authenticate mail or satisfy DMARC alignment.
Recommended
Keep the SPF record as narrow as possible. Only include the sending infrastructure actually in use.
Don't
Do not use overly permissive qualifiers like
+all
or broad
include:
ranges that authorise IP space not under the sender's control.
Do not leave
include:
statements for providers no longer used for sending. Audit the SPF and remove outdated vendors. Check for typos.
Recommended
Avoid using SPF macros unless needed. They are expanded per message at evaluation time, which is costly and makes failures more likely.
Do not use
a
or
mx
mechanisms where
ip4:
or
ip6:
would work. Each one costs a DNS lookup against the limit of 10, while
ip4:
and
ip6:
cost none.
How to check
Run
dig TXT <domain>
, then count the mechanisms that trigger a DNS lookup —
include
,
a
,
mx
,
ptr
,
exists
and
redirect
— and confirm the total is 10 or fewer.
Do
Do
Required
Ensure every outbound message carries a valid
DKIM
signature, using a minimum 1024-bit key length while 2048-bit is recommended.
Ensure that the
d=
domain on the DKIM signature matches the domain on the header From.
Recommended
Rotate DKIM keys at least annually, or immediately if a key is suspected to be compromised.
Use a different
d=
domain for different mailstreams (for example, separate subdomains for transactional and marketing email), so that each mailstream builds its own reputation.
How to check
Run
dig TXT <selector>._domainkey.<domain>
(the selector is set in the ESP's DKIM setup page) and confirm a DKIM key, starting
v=DKIM1
, is returned.
Do
Don't
Do
Required
Publish a
DMARC record
with a policy defined for the sending domain.
Ensure the header From domain aligns with the DKIM signing domain (
d=
) so that DMARC alignment passes.
Recommended
Set up a DMARC aggregate report address (
rua=
) from day one as this will help audit email sent from the domain.
Don't
Do not remain at
p=none
permanently. Starting with
p=none
is acceptable, but we recommend having an enforcement policy.
How to check
Run
dig TXT _dmarc.<domain>
and confirm a DMARC record, starting
v=DMARC1
, is returned.
3. Permission and List Hygiene
Send email only to people who want to receive it. Once the technical infrastructure is in place, the next step is building a legitimate list of email addresses from people who have provided explicit permission to receive the email. Lack of permission is one of the most common reasons for being listed by Spamhaus.
Do
Don't
Do
Required
Ensure all bulk email is ONLY sent to recipients that have
Confirmed Opt-in (COI)
. Send a confirmation email requiring recipients to explicitly opt-in to verify their email address. This will prevent unwanted signups, bot signups and typo email addresses. If no opt-in is received, do not send email to that address.
Recommended
Utilise available signals like bounce data, feedback loops, postmaster tools and engagement data to ensure the mailing list is up to date and email is sent to an engaged audience.
Keep a timestamped record of when and how permission was obtained.
Don't
Do not send emails to purchased, rented, or harvested lists, as these are the most common source of spam trap hits.
Permission is NOT transferable. Do not grant or assume permission retroactively or transfer it between organisations or domains.
How to check
Look for high bounce rates, low engagement and unusual sign-up patterns in the mailing platform.
Do
Don't
Do
Recommended
Refer to the
guidelines from M3AAWG
for managing spamtraps, and follow the best practices outlined in our
resources
.
Implement a robust
email sunset policy
to help remove temporary email sign-ups and email addresses that no longer engage with email.
Don't
Do not attempt to identify or suppress a spam trap address. Audit the acquisition process to identify which list segment or collection method introduced the problem address, and remove that source entirely.
Spamhaus spamtraps do not subscribe to email or engage with them.
According to
M3AAWG spam trap best practices
, mailboxes that remain inactive for more than 12 months can be repurposed as spamtraps.
4. Sending best practices
How email is sent matters as much as what is sent. Warming the IP and domain, maintaining a consistent volume, using trusted links and domains within emails, and providing clear, legitimate ways to opt-out of emails will help improve overall deliverability.
Do
Don't
Do
Required
HELO domains which DO NOT have a sending history will be subjected to additional filtering. Please read our
best practices
around IP/Domain warm-up.
Recommended
Start sending slowly, and consistently for any IP address or domain that has not sent email in the past 90 days, before gradually increasing volume.
Domains which have been registered in the past 24 hours will be part of Spamhaus Zero Reputation Domains (ZRD) list.
Additionally, domains used for mailing within 30 days of registration will be treated suspiciously and we recommend following best practices for
newly registered domains
.
Treat any change in IP or HELO hostname as a new asset if no prior sending history is available, and apply the same
warm-up process
as used for a new IP or domain.
Begin with a few initial campaigns sent to the most engaged recipients to reduce the risk of hitting older invalid addresses. Maintaining a slow and consistent email volume will help build a strong sender reputation.
Don't
Required
Do not use warm-up services that generate artificial traffic or simulate opens, clicks and replies. Using an engagement inflation service will result in the IP or domain being listed.
Infrastructure operated to inflate engagement or otherwise trick filters will be listed as a spam-enabling service.
Recommended
Do not send inconsistent email volumes or trigger a sudden spike in sending, as this could negatively impact reputation.
Do not send to addresses which are old and unengaged while warming the IP or Domain.
Do not send the entire daily volume in a single burst at the top of the hour. Spread it across the day as spikes in mail volume can look suspicious.
Do not use more IPs than required to manage the mail volume as this can be perceived as snowshoe behaviour.
Do not begin sending on new infrastructure without carrying the suppression list across. Addresses that previously bounced or unsubscribed will otherwise be mailed again, and old inactive addresses are where recycled spam traps sit.
How to check
Plot the daily send volume for the IP or domain against the warm-up schedule and confirm it is increasing gradually, not spiking.
Do
Don't
Do
Required
Keep the overall bounce rate below 5%.
Recommended
Suppress
hard bounces
immediately.
Investigate and remove repeated soft bounces after a defined threshold; this is typically 3–5 consecutive bounces.
Don't
Avoid using
email list validation
as a source to clean spamtraps as it does not do so, and is not and never will be a replacement for permission.
Do
Don't
Do
Recommended
Use HTTPS for all links, and only use links generated by the sender's own system.
Sign or validate tracking and redirect links so they cannot be altered to point elsewhere. This prevents malicious actors from abusing them as open redirects.
Don't
Do not use free or unbranded URL shorteners in the content of an email. URLs and/or domains used in the content of an email will affect the overall reputation of the sending domain.
5. IP and Domain Reputation
The reputation of the
IP
and
domain
as seen by Spamhaus can be checked via our
reputation checker
.
Spamhaus looks at multiple signals before assigning a reputation score, and a strong negative signal can outweigh the absence of positive ones — so following all email best practices consistently is essential.
Factors that influence reputation include: the service provider, the IP neighbourhood, the infrastructure the IPs are associated with, the upstream networks that connect to internet backbones, and the IP or domain's history — when it was first seen, when it was last used, and how it was used.
Do
Don't
Do
Recommended
Check the
IP reputation
and
domain reputation
regularly and do not wait for a delivery issue or listing to discover an issue.
Associate the domain with network providers and registrars that maintain a good reputation. The reputation of the hosting provider or registrar can be checked on our
reputation statistics page
.
Ensure newly registered domains are not used for at least 30 days from registration. The domain can be used for non-email purposes during this period, and establishing a web-presence prior to sending email will help improve the credibility of the domain.
Refer to our recommendations for best practices when using
newly registered domains
.
Don't
Do not use newly registered domains in SMTP as a FROM domain or a HELO domain unless the domain is properly warmed up. Similarly, using a newly registered domain in the content of the email can also look suspicious. The age of the domains used in the email can affect the overall sending reputation.
Do not use cousin domains for additional mailstreams or geographies for the same brand. Use sub-domains.
Do not hide WHOIS information for the root sending domain. The reputation of the upstream provider may be used for evaluating domain reputation. The reputation of the upstream provider can be checked in our
Registrar reputation
page.
How to check
Run the domain through the
Reputation Checker
to get more insights.
Note: We do not accept requests for explanations of the attributes shown here or requests to reset reputation.
6. ESPs & Large Senders
ESPs and shared infrastructure hosts are responsible for the email sent via their infrastructure. Hosting abusive senders will negatively impact the reputation of shared domains and infrastructure.

title: External sandboxes for coding agents
content:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with
Prime Radiant
, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and
other projects
.

My post
on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the
external sandbox
pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

external-sandbox-v86
runs a Node.js server which then uses
v86
to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.

external-sandbox-container
is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.

external-sandbox-quicksand
is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's
Quicksand
sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU
and
Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
content:
Datasette Lite
is my port of the
Datasette
Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and
Pyodide
. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.

You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to
lite.datasette.io
:

Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script

Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI

Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository

Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette

Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools

The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.

As an example, consider the following URL:

https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this:

That's Datasette running the new
datasette-maplibre
plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.

Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing:

https://lite.datasette.io/
?install=datasette-maplibre
&url=https://.../demo.db
&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

The
?install=datasette-maplibre
installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass
&install=...
as many times as you like to load more plugins.

&url=https://.../demo.db
loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have
open CORS headers
- I host files like this in
Gists
, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.

&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
loads
this metadata.yml file
. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit
that homepage here
for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.

#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent
is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the
/demo/capitals_and_countries
SQL view, then appending
another
fragment hash to it (
%23
is a URL-encoded
#
) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the
continent
column in the data.

That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in
URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments
last year.

The full set of supported URL arguments is
described in the Datasette Lite README
.

I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's
a recent issue
describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite:

Demo of the bug:
https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score
- click next and the second page is empty.

Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43):
https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score

How this works, using service workers

Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version
back in 2022
, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value.

The problem with that initial version is that it was a
hack
. It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using
innerHTML
.

This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in
innerHTML
don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files.

The new version takes a completely different approach based on
Service Workers
. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead.

Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire
lite.datasette.io
domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this:

/app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS)

Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a
/app/aa94e6851595/
prefix. What's that about?

The
/app/<session>/
prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs.

Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the
datasette-maplibre
plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another.

The service worker for
lite.datasette.io
is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure.

Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session.

(We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!)

I had Claude Fable 5.2
generate several SVG diagrams
to help explain this. Here's my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README:

This system started life
back in May
as an
AI research spike
generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production!

Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite

I added this feature
last night
as an off-shoot of investigating
a potential bug in SQLite
.

Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then.

Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues.

In the past I've
used various tricks
to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process.

WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab.

datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels
is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for
pysqlite3
for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this:

pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl

That's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version.

Datasette Lite now takes a special
?sqlite=
URL parameter, which will accept a version number like
3.54.1
, resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it.

Once I'd built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool](
https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29)
for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here's an example showing how
select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))
differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1:

This should work for every other Python app, too

Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.

C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can
even publish them to PyPI
as of PEP 783 in April 2026.

One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden.

I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.

For Hacker News: Full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers

title: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
content:
AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings.

Maintainers are under intense pressure from this flood of reports. As Christian Grobmeier, a maintainer of Log4j, has put it, the
AI defending open source has to be better than the AI attacking it
.

AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings?

GitHub and Microsoft are using
Codename MDASH
, Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on.

The process

Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked:

Find.

Codename MDASH
, an AI system from Microsoft Security, scanned each project using Microsoft’s
MAI Cyber model
and suggested fixes for what it found.

Filter.
An
AI triage agent from the GitHub Security Lab
, built on tailored Copilot skills, removed duplicates, checked validity, and focused on high-impact bugs, so maintainers never had to review raw scan results.

Verify.

Researchers from Microsoft FORGE Lab
checked every remaining finding by hand.

Report privately.
Reports reached maintainers through GitHub private vulnerability reporting, with a proof of concept and a suggested fix.

Fix.
Maintainers decided what to fix, how to fix it, and when.

Reports and fixes stayed on GitHub, where maintainers already work.

The result: Codename MDASH, using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model, flagged thousands of possible issues across the six projects. After AI triage and hand review by seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers, maintainers received 99 private reports. As of November 15, they had fixed 55, and 14 of those fixes were already in a release.

What we learned

These lessons come from what the six projects fixed and what their maintainers chose to share. Six projects is a small sample, so read them as early lessons.

1. Fixes matter more than findings

Fixing is where maintainers spend their time. So every report arrived already checked, with a suggested fix to review, adapt, and merge. Maintainers started from a well-scoped patch, not a raw finding.

The first fixes shipped about a week after the initial scan. Caddy’s maintainers fixed all 22 of the reports they received in a week or less. Maintainers used the suggested fixes, some as written and some with changes.

AutoGPT’s maintainers had recently shipped a new check, and it was broken. The report landed three days later and pointed at the right line. They took the fix further than the suggested patch, wrote it within a day, and had it in production less than a week later.

Finding vulnerabilities is no longer our bottleneck. Fixing them is the hard part, and that depends on maintainers.

Netty maintainer

2. Codename MDASH, with researcher review, gave maintainers high-quality findings with fixes

Maintainers got a short list, not a flood. Express maintainers said the reports cut through the noise. Caddy maintainers said they surfaced obscure bugs and filled gaps that earlier reports had missed. For FastMCP, the scan went beyond what AI scanners had given them before. ImageMagick, maintained by a two-person team, received 22 reports.

AI did the finding, researchers did the checking, and maintainers stayed in charge.

One ImageMagick report looked like a kind of issue the maintainers had seen before. Its summary showed it wasn’t and pointed to the exact lines of code. They were able to push a fix in 15 minutes.

Normally, a security advisory would take us around 30 minutes to 1 hour on average to read, understand, and make a fix. It is a huge difference.

ImageMagick maintainer

Codename MDASH was able to find unknown, obscure security bugs in our project with succinct reports, and it filled in gaps from some prior reports that hadn’t been noticed.

Caddy maintainer

3. Open source still has gaps to close

The pilot worked because people did careful work at every step, and that work doesn’t scale yet. Seven researchers spent about two days per project checking findings by hand. Meanwhile, low-quality reports still reach maintainers every day.

For open source, fixes need to be delivered via private vulnerability reporting (PVR). Maintainers need to run CI/CD tests on private forks to verify those fixes. And to close the gap between defenders and attackers, maintainers need access to cyber-capable models to verify a proof of concept, before and after the fix.

The Codename MDASH scan provided unique insights into the security of our project above and beyond what AI scanners have provided us in the past

FastMCP maintainer

Why it matters

If you’re a maintainer, this approach changes what a security report costs you. A checked, private report that comes with a suggested fix takes less of your time. You shouldn’t have to triage a scanner’s output. That’s the sender’s job.

If you use AI to find vulnerabilities in open source, maintainers’ feedback points to this standard:

Check every finding before you send it, against what the project already knows and against its threat model and security policy.

Report it privately.

Include a suggested fix. Let maintainers set the pace.

Features are easier and easier to ship, but in the future maintaining software will probably come down to who cares enough to manage the security.

AutoGPT maintainer

Codename MDASH is very useful for cutting through the noise of vulnerability reports.

Express maintainer

What you can do today

If you maintain any open source project, turn on
private vulnerability reporting
so researchers can report security issues to you without making them public. If your project is on GitHub, turn on core security features in about two minutes with
gh-secure
.

If you build on open source, turn on
Dependabot alerts
so you know when a dependency you use needs a security update.

If you send AI-generated vulnerability reports to open source projects, hold them to the standard above before you send them.

Repositories using GitHub code security can use
agentic autofix
to help automatically remediate their alerts with Copilot

What happens next

Fixes, where maintainers already work.
GitHub is bringing these lessons into private vulnerability reporting and security advisories, where GitHub Security Lab is already investing to reduce the burden of low-quality reports on maintainers.

MAI Cyber 2.
Today Microsoft announced
MAI Cyber 2
. The Codename MDASH pilot ran on the earlier MAI Cyber model. GitHub and Microsoft will keep working together to help secure open source.

Closing the gaps, starting with the
GitHub Secure Open Source Fund
.
We’re working with Microsoft to scale researcher review without cutting corners. GitHub will offer every alumni project AI security scans, with findings checked before they’re reported privately. Alumni also get
GitHub Copilot Max
. We’ll bring this support to future sessions of the Fund.

Everyone downstream benefits from this system. When a maintainer publishes a security advisory on GitHub and it’s reviewed for the GitHub Advisory Database, Dependabot can alert the repositories that depend on that package. That’s the idea behind the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund: 216 projects so far, with more than 300 maintainers fixing more than 4,000 vulnerabilities in software downloaded more than 20 billion times a month.

Thank you

To the maintainers of AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick, and Netty: thank you for your time, your trust, and your feedback. Thank you also to the Codename MDASH team at Microsoft Security, the MAI Cyber team, the researchers of Microsoft FORGE Lab, and GitHub Security Lab.

Maintainers do the fixing. Our job is to make sure they never do it alone.

Hear from maintainers about their experience with Codename MDASH. 👇

About the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund

All six projects in this pilot are alumni of the
GitHub Secure Open Source Fund
, which gives each project $10,000 through GitHub Sponsors, plus security training and a supportive alumni community.

The GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, powered by
GitHub Sponsors
, funds open source projects that underpin the digital supply chain, catalyze innovation, and are critical to the AI stack. Want your company to help secure the open source it depends on? Become a funding partner through the Fund page.
Learn more about the Fund or apply
.

Through the Fund, maintainers receive security training and
Azure
credits from
Microsoft for Startups.
That support sits alongside
Microsoft’s European Security Program
and its
Secure Future Initiative
, whose principle is security above all else. Most organizations are downstream in the same way. If your software depends on open source, do the same: back the maintainers you rely on.

title: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices
content:
Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own. You don’t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are. An agent can’t live only inside one application. The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices.

In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another. This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub. Here’s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows.

Why one integration per client stopped working

GitHub Copilot was first built in VS Code as an extension that bundled its own harness. This gave you access to your agents in VS Code, but it tied their lifetime to the editor. Extensions are attached to a single VS Code window. Close that window, and the agent is gone. Update VS Code, and every agent stops as the application restarts. Connect to a remote machine, and you get an entirely new extension host commit-locked against the version of the VS Code workbench you have.

At the same time, the
Copilot app
was being developed, alongside the existing GitHub mobile apps for iOS and Android. Each product was doing its own distinct integration with
cloud-based agents
to work towards delivering session continuity.

Each of these integrations solved the problem for one product, but developers also still want to be able to pull their agents into their own workflows–whether that’s an editor, a terminal, a phone, or a tool they built themselves–and they can’t do that if every client needs its own one-off integration. That’s why developers needed a protocol: a standard, independently versioned language across versions of VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, mobile apps, and any other client that might host an agent. A shared protocol means every client sees the same agents, history, and state without bespoke integrations, and you aren’t tied to one app’s idea of what an agent session is.

Designing a protocol for agents on every client

The protocol needed to allow multiple clients to interact with the same set of agents seamlessly. Start a session in the cloud from your phone, for example, then continue it from your laptop. It should tolerate network interruptions, reconnections, and concurrent client mutations. And it needed to be full-featured enough for you to do real work from each of your clients.

At the same time, the protocol needed to stay out of agent
behavior
. Unlike the domains that produced the
Language Server Protocol
and
Debug Adapter Protocol
, the world of agents is evolving quickly. That’s why AHP avoids encoding how agents work, and instead focuses on how you want to interact with them.

You also need the protocol to be simple enough to implement on your own client or server. While the full feature set would necessarily be extensive, the core protocol needed to be minimal.

The result of these requirements is the
Agent Host Protocol
(AHP). It is oriented around URI-identified “channels”, which are the coarsest unit of functionality in the protocol. Every server must implement the root, session, and chat channels, but can also implement more channels that provide terminal support, MCP additions, or OTel reporting, for example.

Within each channel is a reducer-based state object, which drives most of the logic for clients. The server is the arbiter of the state, and each client sends a sequence of actions that either mutate the state or trigger side effects, like sending a chat message. This provides a few very nice properties. Reconnection and replay in poor network conditions are easy: a client sends all queued actions, presents the right ‘loading’ state, and waits for the server to reconcile and acknowledge the actions before confirming them. Clients and servers are straightforward to debug. And reducer-based state also plays nicely with popular UI frameworks like React.

Shipping five clients and two hosts

Adopting the Agent Host Protocol in VS Code required building a new harness and agentic stack underneath it. The Copilot Chat extension, which used to provide all of VS Code’s AI and agentic capabilities, had been growing for over three years, reaching over 400,000 lines of TypeScript, not counting tests. But, as a VS Code extension, it was structured around the lifecycle of a VS Code window and depended entirely on the VS Code extension API. Neither that lifetime nor those APIs would be available in a standalone agent host process.

As we started building the Agent Host Protocol in early 2026, the
Copilot SDK
was also being developed, and it made sense to leverage it as the foundation for the new agentic stack. This was a big transition. It’s easy to build a harness implementation that says hello and can edit files—we were using the agent host to develop the agent host after the first couple weeks—but it’s another thing to build one that covers the long tail of features developers had come to expect from Copilot Chat.

GitHub has had
Copilot cloud agents
for a couple of years, allowing developers to run tasks in the cloud from any device. While VS Code was quietly developing the Agent Host Protocol, GitHub was looking to expand that capability to coordinate sessions running on your own devices via the Copilot app, or in cloud sandboxes. This was exactly the
N:M
problem that AHP was built to solve, so adopting the same technology made perfect sense.

From the outset, the GitHub Agent Host had different requirements than VS Code’s implementation. VS Code runs the host locally and can drop its host on other compute over SSH, containers, WSL, or Dev Tunnels, and it is actually included as part of the
VS Code Server
bundle. The GitHub Agent Host needed to run in the cloud and across a much wider variety of infrastructure, environments, and security constraints.

Those differing requirements are why they’re separate implementations written in different languages: VS Code’s in TypeScript and GitHub’s in Rust. For now, having two agent hosts has been a good acid-test for the protocol itself. How well does it work when two entirely different teams and sets of agents implement the same protocol independently?

Pretty well, it turns out. Like MCP, the Agent Host Protocol provides escape hatches via custom methods and
_meta
data on objects that consumers can use for out-of-band signaling. After several months heads-down on our respective implementations, our first task as we worked toward unification was inventorying the ways each implementation had extended the protocol. Many of these extensions reasonably stay GitHub-specific, such as the GitHub Agent Host using metadata to link to project boards. In other cases, variance was a sign of a gap in the protocol; early versions, for example, could not accurately represent shell-type tool output that wasn’t backed by a PTY. And some were bad assumptions, like VS Code’s client assuming a particular structure for the session URIs it received from the agent host. A protocol with only one implementation isn’t truly portable; as we taught our clients and servers to talk to each other, AHP became portable in practice, not just in theory.

Today, the Agent Host Protocol provides that same continuity across all VS Code and GitHub surfaces. Agent sessions running locally in the GitHub Copilot app, in cloud sandboxes, and in VS Code all share the same underlying protocol. To see how it’s used, read about how you can
work from anywhere with the new connected Copilot cloud experience
.

Using the Agent Host Protocol

AHP was designed to be easy to use in clients and servers.
Agent Host Protocol
libraries are available in Rust, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift, .NET, and Go, and agents are able to build clients and servers with little prompting. I have a macropad sitting on my desk that reflects my agent’s state in real time, and others have built everything from smart watch apps to Kanban-style task management tools against the protocol. Whether you want a companion app for your own agents, a way to bring agent sessions into your team’s tools, or AHP support in your own editor or agent, the protocol is open for you to build on.

You can connect to an agent host you implement in the Copilot app (enable
Experimental > Direct Connections
, then go to
Environments > Add Agent Host Protocol Host
) and in VS Code (via
Add Remote Agent Host
in the Agents window). You can spawn a standalone version of VS Code’s agent host by running
code agent host
in your terminal, or see the endpoints for the one in your editor by running
code agent endpoints
, and
samples
can help you and your agent get started.

The Agent Host Protocol is an open standard, and questions and suggestions are welcome
on GitHub
.

Happy coding!

Explore the Agent Host Protocol on GitHub >

title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
content:
The Tail of Base64

By Quang Luong

On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution.

Discovery

A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode.

After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway.

Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues.

Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder...

Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold?

The vulnerability

The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write.

The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses
evmovdqub
, the intrinsic for the
VMOVDQU8
instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes (
'='
) in the Base64-encoded string. This is shown in the following (pseudocode):

// Zero High Bits Starting with Specified Bit Position
input_mask := bzhiq(-1, input_length)
output_len := (input_length / 4) * 3

// handle padding
if input[input_length - 1] == '=':
output_len -= 1
input_mask >>= 1
if input[input_length - 2] == '=':
output_len -= 1
input_mask >>= 1

output_mask := bzhiq(-1, output_len)

In the above code, if the remaining
input
is of the form
=, ==, X=, X==, XY=
, or
===
, then
output_len
will be computed as zero. However, since there is padding,
output_len
is decremented, resulting in an underflowed value of
-1
or
-2
. Since
bzhiq(-1, output_len)
doesn’t change any bits if
output_len >= 64
, this results in
output_mask == -1u64
.

Later the code uses
evmovdqub
to read and write multiple bytes at a time. For a write, if the mask bit is
1
, the byte at that index in the vector register is written to memory. So when
output_mask == -1u64
, all
64
bytes are written during the following operation:

evmovdqub(
Address(dest, dp) /* Address: destination address addr */,
k1 /* k1 == output_mask */,
tmp /* XMMRegister src register/value to write */,
true,
Assembler::AVX_512bit /* vector length */
);

The generated stub returns the number of bytes it successfully decoded, and returns early when it detects invalid input. The remaining bytes are handled by the Java code, which throws
IllegalArgumentException
if the input is invalid.

At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as
(ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding
. When the bug is triggered, with
65
bytes (
[64 bytes] + '='
) as input, that calculation allocates a
50
-byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes
output_mask == -1
for
evmovdqub
, so
64
bytes are written starting at offset
48
, an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer.

On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is
'A' * 128 + '='
instead of
'A' * 64 + '='
, because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher.

Exploitation strategy

The Base64 bug was gold, but not the type that sits on the riverbed waiting to be panned out. It was the type that was deep, dark, and hard to access. While we had memory corruption, exploiting it looked difficult, perhaps even borderline unexploitable, since it only wrote fixed bytes to the heap. Only the landing position of the out-of-bounds write is controllable.

We get the following 64 bytes write starting from the position in buffer where the remaining sets of Base64 decoded bytes would have been written to:

Full controlled write to byte 0 (in bound)

4-bit controlled write to byte 1 (in bound)

Uncontrolled write to bytes [2, 63]. For bytes
48..63
, the value will always be
0x9a
.

The uncontrolled out-of-bounds write turned out not to be a big problem. We reused a common JavaScript engine exploitation primitive, the classic technique of overwriting a buffer length.

We call the buffer whose length we overwrite the
writer
. Once its length is corrupted, it keeps accepting our chosen bytes, so if we place another array or object after it, we can corrupt that neighbor with all of our chosen values. That upgrades the fixed write into a bounded, chosen-value linear write.

If we then corrupt another array's length and its data is copied back into the response, we have built a heap disclosure primitive, the
reader
, from the out-of-bounds read. At this point, before any code execution, we already had JavaBleed, the ability to leak contents from the Java heap, which may hold PII, private keys, other secret keys, and tokens.

From the
writer
and
reader
, the rest of this write-up builds the full attack. We repair the objects the linear write damaged to keep the JVM running, mount data-only attacks on application logic, and escalate the bounded write into arbitrary writes that reach the Code Cache and JVM hooks for code execution.

But first things first, we need to align the heap to our advantage.

Heap Feng Shui (Grooming)

G1 divides the heap into fixed-size regions
. Before the region arithmetic matters, the critical arrays have to leave their threads' private allocation ranges.

HotSpot normally gives each Java thread a
thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB)
, a private slice of Eden. Objects created by different request threads advance different cursors, which gives us no useful order between a Base64 decoder in one TLAB and a writer in another.

The first grooming layer controls the allocation route. The critical array's size and the space left in the worker's TLAB decide whether HotSpot refills that TLAB or takes the attacker-preferred
outside-TLAB allocation path
.

The second layer controls the layout. However, we do not choose how G1 allocates memory, and we don't know the current heap state. To approach this limitation, Calif used the tried and tested method of Spray and Pray.

Object sizes and padding fix offsets inside region-sized spans. We spray several live writer and reader pairs to give the decoder output several possible neighbors. When its region lands immediately below a writer region, the widened reader produces a larger application response. We discard misses and retry until successful.

One early challenge during exploit development was that the AI would get stuck during heap grooming primitive development. In order to save tokens and time, Calif wrote a small heap tracer and visualizer to give the agent information about the heap state, combined with our expertise on specific cases.

Remote Heap Feng Shui

In order to perform remote grooming, each request data would be sent up until the critical heap allocation would occur. By ensuring the data that was previously sent had a TCP acknowledgement, the exploit would have control over the allocations up to date. Once we were confident our data so far is buffered on the target, we then sent the rest, completing the http request. This allows both heap allocation control and more precise schedule as delivering small network packets is more stable than big ones.

The exact allocation and free order schedule belongs to the targeted application profile, while we are able to control the adding, writer, reader, and decoder pieces.

The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.

Warm-up, rehearsal, and retries

To summarize the chain so far, we will warm up the Base64 decoder to C2 tier. We can rehearse the exploit run to calibrate timing and responses against the target before causing corruption to occur. Once the required information has been obtained, we can trigger the vulnerability. Incorrect placement could cause the JVM to crash, but in many instances, we can simply try again.

WARM
Run valid decodes until the JIT selects the affected fast path. No memory is corrupted.
REHEARSE
Optional safe round for calibration.
TRIGGER
Send the malformed tail. If the objects line up, the fixed spill enlarges the writer.
DISCLOSE
Continue the writer so chosen bytes enlarge the reader, then collect the response-derived heap bytes.
REPAIR
Use the disclosed originals to restore temporary headers and untouched neighbors when the chain has a repair path.
FINISH
Make the application-specific change and verify it through a live request.

Limitations

Request streaming.
Some current grooming profiles need partial request bodies to reach the application. A proxy that waits for the complete body removes their release timing.
nginx buffers request bodies by default
.

Request buffering is not a general mitigation. Elasticsearch runs from one complete request, so this setting does not stop that chain. After a configured
WebSocket upgrade
, later frames pass through a tunnel and request-body buffering no longer applies to them.

Application profiles.
There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.

PoC

Here is a self-contained proof of concept. It warms the Base64 decoder until the vulnerable intrinsic is used, then decodes the malformed
64 × "A" + "="
input into a 4096-byte array. On an affected JDK it prints
REPRODUCED
: the decoder rejects the input, but 62 bytes (offsets 50 to 111) past the decoded output have already been overwritten. Every write lands inside a real array, so the trigger is safe to run.

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Base64;

/** Bounded standalone trigger: every write stays inside a real 4096-byte array. */
public final class Base64Trigger {
private static volatile int sink;

public static void main(String[] args) {
Base64.Decoder decoder = Base64.getDecoder();
byte[] valid = "A".repeat(64).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII);
byte[] malformed = ("A".repeat(64) + "=").getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII);
byte[] target = new byte[4096];

for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) {
sink += decoder.decode(valid, target);
}

Arrays.fill(target, (byte) 0x5a);
boolean rejected = false;
try {
decoder.decode(malformed, target);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) {
rejected = true;
}

int changed = 0;
int first = -1;
int last = -1;
for (int i = 50; i < target.length; i++) {
if (target[i] != (byte) 0x5a) {
changed++;
if (first < 0) first = i;
last = i;
}
}

System.out.println("runtime=" + System.getProperty("java.runtime.version"));
System.out.println("vm=" + System.getProperty("java.vm.name"));
System.out.printf("rejected=%s changed=%d first=%d last=%d%n",
rejected, changed, first, last);

if (!rejected || changed != 62 || first != 50 || last != 111) {
System.err.println("NOT REPRODUCED");
System.exit(1);
}
System.out.println("REPRODUCED");
}
}

We are holding back the application-specific exploits for now. This write-up covers the vulnerability and the general exploitation technique. The weaponized chains for individual products stay private until everyone has had a chance to upgrade. We will publish them later.

Affected products

Java4Shell affects OpenJDK from version 17.0.6 or newer.

Because they are built from OpenJDK, the following Java distributions are also vulnerable:

Amazon Corretto

Eclipse Temurin

Microsoft Build of OpenJDK

Azul Zulu

BellSoft Liberica

SAP SapMachine

Red Hat OpenJDK

Oracle OpenJDK

Oracle Java SE

Oracle GraalVM for JDK

According to Oracle, the following Oracle Java SE versions are vulnerable: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3. We thank Oracle for providing this information ahead of publication time.

Because the vulnerable code is hardware-specific, Java4Shell also requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. ARM64 CPUs are not affected.

These mainstream CPU families meet the hardware requirements:

Intel Xeon: Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids

AMD EPYC and Ryzen: Zen 4 or newer

On Linux, you can check whether your CPU is vulnerable with this command:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

The output must include all four flags.

Recommendations

OpenJDK released
a security advisory
and Oracle released
a patch
at 1:00pm PT on Nov 17, 2026.

All Java users should update immediately.

You can also mitigate Java4Shell by starting OpenJDK with either:

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics
to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding, or

-XX:UseAVX=2
to disable AVX-512. Apply this flag only on x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM doesn't recognize it and will fail to start.

Credits

Research, write-up and exploits by Quang Luong.

Exploit improvement by Jenish Rakholiya.

Artwork by Michal Zalewski.

title: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
content:
Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9
announced
that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement.
Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead.
The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation.
Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an
order
that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done.
Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet.
A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name System
To understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory.
DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blog post at home and have never thought about DNS before, chances are that you’re using your ISP’s default resolver. Because you use your DNS resolver every time that you visit a website, it’s important for it to be reliable and trustworthy.
And because the DNS resolver has access to all of your browsing activity, which resolver you use has real privacy implications.
In addition to DNS resolvers that are provided by your local ISP, there are a variety of public DNS resolvers available. Cloudflare launched our public DNS resolver
1.1.1.1
in April 2018 to give back to the Internet.
Our goal
was to make a fast, reliable, privacy-first consumer DNS service available for free to everyone. We succeeded. 1.1.1.1 is among the fastest DNS resolvers
in the world
, including in Europe. Cloudflare's resolver doesn’t collect any user data, let alone sell it to advertisers. 1.1.1.1 has always been one of our favorite examples of Cloudflare fulfilling its mission to help build a better Internet.
1.1.1.1 is one of many public resolvers that anyone can use. In addition to 1.1.1.1 and Quad9’s 9.9.9.9, some of the other best-known public resolvers include Google’s 8.8.8.8 and Cisco’s OpenDNS. Just because these services are offered for free doesn’t mean they’re easy to provide. A well-run global public DNS resolver is an extraordinary engineering feat, built to securely and privately resolve hundreds of billions or even trillions of queries a day across a globally distributed network of hundreds of server locations.
As Quad9 notes, there are many other DNS resolvers available to users, many of them offered by essentially anonymous services whose practices are unknown or undocumented. It’s easy to change your DNS resolver, and people do so for a variety of reasons including performance, reliability, or to access specific security features.
Why public DNS resolvers should not be required to block
Rightsholders have a legitimate interest in preventing online piracy. But trying to address online infringement through public DNS resolvers is fundamentally the wrong approach.
Among other things, such blocking is ineffective. Think back to the analogy of an operator finding a phone number in a directory. If a court wants to shut down an illegal business, forcing the directory operator to cross the business's name out of the phone book doesn't actually close the business. The storefront is still open, the products are still there, and anyone who already knows the address, or uses a different phone book, can walk in.
The same is true for the Internet. DNS resolvers are just one link in the transmission chain. The only way a DNS resolver can “block” content is by declining to return the IP address for a particular website. But a public DNS resolver cannot remove the actual infringing content from the Internet, nor can it take down the servers hosting it.
Because of this, blocking by public DNS resolvers is remarkably easy to bypass. Any Internet user who wants to reach a blocked site can circumvent the block in less than a minute simply by switching to one of the thousands of other DNS resolvers available online. In fact, users don’t even need a resolver at all to reach infringing content if they already know the underlying IP address. Unsurprisingly, while blocking via public resolvers may inject some friction for some users when accessing content, there is no evidence that it actually reduces the total amount of online infringement that occurs.
In addition to being ineffective, as we’ve
written previously
, DNS blocking is a blunt instrument that causes collateral damage. Because DNS operates at the domain level, a resolver cannot block a specific infringing video or file; it must block the entire domain. This affects all content on that domain, whether legal or illegal. It is also entirely opaque to the user: when a resolver is forced to block a domain, the website simply fails to load. The user receives no explanation or legal notice, making it impossible to know if the site is down for maintenance, if their network is broken, or if the site was blocked by a court order.
The problem is substantially worse with respect to public DNS resolvers. Because public resolvers operate globally, any blocking will naturally cross borders, meaning that a single country could dictate what content is accessible around the world. For example, while the EU-dedicated DNS resolver DNS4EU operated by Whalebone blocks in response to country-specific orders, it does so across the entire EU. Efforts to reengineer public DNS resolvers to allow for more localized blocking would fundamentally alter the service, harming performance and resilience, undermining user privacy, and fragmenting the open Internet.
For these reasons, Cloudflare, Google, Cisco, and Quad9 have all opposed efforts to mandate blocking by public DNS resolvers, with some success. Several years ago, courts in Germany ruled in favor of
Cloudflare
and
Quad9
, rejecting requests to require DNS blocking. More recently, a French court
rejected
penalties against Cloudflare for failing to block through 1.1.1.1, finding that other actions we had taken through our CDN and reverse-proxy service were sufficient to comply with the underlying order.
Undeterred, rightsholders have continued to press for blocking by public resolvers with a level of determination that is hard to explain. A recent study
found
that the majority of online piracy in Europe is hosted in Europe. If rightsholders want to genuinely address online infringement, there are far better places to focus their efforts — most notably by requiring the hosting providers who actually store the pirated files to take them down.
Forcing public DNS resolvers out of markets hurts the Internet
The French court’s penalty order against Quad9 represents the culmination of these rightsholder efforts. As a small non-profit that only offers a public DNS resolver, Quad9 had no alternative methods for demonstrating compliance with the order. The French court therefore granted rightsholders’ request to issue penalties for non-compliance, forcing Quad9 to undermine its own service or leave the country.
Quad9’s withdrawal from France represents a genuine loss for the Internet. In the short term, removal of Quad9’s resolver is likely to cause immediate and potentially severe disruptions to Internet access. Because of the way their service is set up to preserve privacy, Quad9 has no way to know who exactly is using its resolver, let alone to directly communicate to them about the upcoming withdrawal of services. That means that individuals, hospitals, universities, and government offices all may be caught unaware when the resolver stops working. Again, because of how DNS resolvers work, those users will not receive a detailed error message explaining what happened — their Internet will simply stop working. The problem will be even worse when devices like security systems or thermostats are hardwired to use Quad9’s resolver. Fixing these issues may be slow or even impossible.
More generally, driving Quad9 out of France does absolutely nothing to prevent online infringement, but it does leave everyday Internet users with fewer safe, reliable options, particularly ones like Quad9 that also protect users from phishing and malware. Taking established public DNS resolvers away forces Internet users to fall back on the default resolvers offered by their ISPs (which may monetize their browsing data), try lesser-known resolvers operated by anonymous or less trustworthy organizations, or run their own resolver. The irony is that Quad9 and Cloudflare are being pulled into court precisely because we are transparent, reputable organizations. Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web.
The way forward
If nothing else, we hope that Quad9’s announcement may serve as a wake-up call to rightsholders and policymakers that seeking to block infringement at every layer of the Internet has real costs.
We believe there are far better ways to work together to fight piracy without compromising the integrity of the Internet, and Cloudflare continues to pursue
innovative collaborations
to that end. Our collective efforts in addressing online infringement would be put to better use in seeking to have such content removed at the hosting provider, which would both achieve a more durable solution and avoid collateral damage to the Internet.
In the meantime, we will keep resisting misguided efforts to require blocking by public DNS resolvers. Along with Google and Cisco, we have appealed the Belgian order that would impose penalties on us if we do not start DNS blocking by January 2027. We hope to get a resolution before the end of the year that would avoid another situation like the one Quad9 faces now in France.
We have grave concerns about the disruption that would be caused if additional resolvers are forced to withdraw from markets, and we will continue to advocate against that possible result.
