title: Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
content:
Google's AI Overviews cut clicks to websites by 40%

November 9, 2026

Google's AI answers are taking clicks from websites in the search results. In a randomized experiment, researchers hid AI Overviews from some US desktop users. Comparing them with users who still saw Overviews shows that an Overview cuts clicks to outside websites by about 40%. Those Overviews now appear on more than half the US keywords DataForSEO tracks, up from 6% two years ago. The industry's answer, GEO (generative engine optimization), has yet to show a way to compensate for the loss. While AI citations correlate with the same kind of link profile that goes with higher Google rankings, in March AI assistants sent websites just 0.3% of their traffic.

Search engine optimization (SEO) still decides whether you can be found, but where an AI answer appears, a ranking
brings 40% fewer visits than it used to. Generative engine optimization (GEO), the
practice of getting your content cited in AI-written answers, looks mostly like SEO plus two additions: being present
on the third-party sites AI answers draw from, and writing pages that are easy to quote. We found little
evidence for any other tactic.

Google answers first

An AI Overview is a generated summary that Google places above the ordinary results, with links to the pages it drew
on. In DataForSEO's monthly panel of 20 million keywords, the share of results showing one climbed from 5.93% in
September 2024 to 61.43% in August 2026. The chart at the top of this post shows that climb. Over the same period the
featured snippet, the quoted passage Google used to show at the top of a page, fell from 8.96% to 0.44%, and the
discussions and forums block fell from 21.13% to 7.42%. Video results rose from 9.67% to 19.98%, though that is
down from a peak of 31.05% in October 2025, and local map listings rose from 19.98% to 25.99%. DataForSEO's dataset
covers 190 million keywords, 165 million AI answers, and 1.1 billion backlinks, mostly for US English searches.
Pew Research Center's data gives an independent check. Pew logged the searches of 900
US adults in March 2025, re-ran them in April, and found summaries on 18% of them. DataForSEO's figures for
those months are 14.67% and 17.63%, close to Pew's.

You can't reliably avoid Overviews by choosing different keywords. Between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the third
quarter of 2026, the rate rose for every type of search intent:

Search intent
Q4 2025
Q3 2026

Informational (looking something up)
48.42%
70.44%

Commercial (comparing options)
26.30%
51.35%

Navigational (looking for a site)
17.04%
34.03%

Transactional (ready to buy)
10.82%
28.64%

Low-volume keywords aren't safer either. In the third quarter of 2026,
keywords with 201 to 300 monthly searches showed Overviews 58.59% of the time, against 48.62% for those above 600.
A separate dataset, from June to September 2026, covers
difficulty and price. The easiest keywords showed Overviews 60.64% of the time and the hardest 53.76%. Keywords costing
advertisers more than $5 a click were at 49.55% and those under 25 cents at 50.54%, with a low of 42.63% between $0.51
and $1.00. More than half the result pages have no price data and show Overviews 60.06% of the time.
The rate does vary by industry. Health is at 69.68% and finance at 68.80%, while apparel is at 37.48%, dining
at 29.37%, and real estate at 22.27%.

Queries are also getting longer, especially on desktop. Over a year, queries of five or more words grew from 29.3% to
34.8% of unique desktop queries and from 29.6% to 31.9% on mobile. Three and four word searches are still the most
common.

What happens to the clicks

The strongest evidence is an experiment. Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen gave US desktop Chrome users an extension that
put each of them at random into a group. One group saw Google as usual, and another had AI Overviews hidden. The
researchers then watched two weeks of real searches in January and February 2026. On searches that would show an Overview, the group that could see them averaged 0.37 clicks
to outside websites per search, against 0.62 for the group that couldn't, which the authors report as a 39.8% reduction.
Searches ending with no outbound click went from 54% to 73%. Clicks on ads didn't change, which suggests Google takes
care not to cannibalize its own revenue. Across all searches, with and without an Overview, the authors put the loss
at roughly 18.5% of the organic clicks a site gets from Google. The authors expect the loss to grow as Overviews appear on more
searches. This is a randomized controlled trial, the most reliable kind of study for separating cause
from correlation or coincidence. The effect was statistically significant for informational searches.
The navigational and transactional samples were too small to settle anything.
This is a working paper, not yet peer reviewed, and it covers desktop only. A separate preregistered experiment by Wang and colleagues, with 1,100
people, also found that removing AI Overviews and AI Mode raised clicks to publishers.

Observational data points the same way. Pew found people clicked an ordinary result on 8% of visits to a results page
with a summary and on 15% without one, and ended their browsing session on 26% against 16%. Pew's comparison isn't a
controlled experiment, because the searches that draw a summary tend to be longer and phrased as questions.

Click-through rate (CTR) is the share of people shown a result who click it. Across more
than 2,000 websites in DataForSEO's panel, the desktop CTR of the first organic result fell from 17.83% in September
2025 to 7.43% in August 2026, a drop of 58%. Mobile fell from 25.17% to 20.80%, a drop of 17%.

Desktop lost nearly half its click-through rate in one month, March 2026, and stayed down. Mobile fell about as far
over five months, then recovered most of it. These figures come from Table A2 of the report.

Desktop plunged from 15.18% to 7.94% between February and March 2026. AI Overviews can't easily explain that step
since the report has them almost flat that month, at 42.79% and then 43.38%. A change in the format or quality of the
Overviews might explain part of it, though that is speculation on our part.
Mobile, meanwhile, sank to 12.96% and then rebounded to 22.49% by
May. The report itself says its data "does not establish" whether AI answers, layout changes, or changes in behavior
are the cause. Its sample may also be shifting underneath it, since the unique desktop queries it counts fell by a
third over the year, from 1.97 million to 1.32 million. Whatever the cause, a top ranking on desktop now earns less
than half the clicks it did a year earlier.

DataForSEO also estimates where clicks go on pages with and without an Overview. By its model, the first organic result
holds 9 to 16 points less click share on pages with one, though these are different searches on a single day's snapshot:

Search intent

Position 1, no Overview

Position 1, with Overview

Overview's cited links

Informational
37.1%
20.7%
42.4%

Navigational
33.4%
24.1%
44.8%

Transactional
37.6%
21.4%
43.0%

Commercial
33.8%
21.1%
42.2%

The click share for the Overview's cited links looks promising, but it comes from a model. Pew, which logged real
browsing, saw people click a link inside a summary on just 1% of visits, against 8% for ordinary results. Eighteen months and a large change in the product
separate the two measurements, so it is difficult to say which is closer to the truth.

Google disputes that search traffic to websites is declining. In August 2025 its head of Search, Liz Reid, wrote that total organic clicks were
"relatively stable year-over-year" and that Google was sending "slightly more quality clicks", meaning clicks where
people don't quickly come back. She gave no figures to back that up.

Your site can't see whether someone goes back to Google, so you can't check Google's quality-clicks claim yourself, but
you can check what your Google clicks are worth.
RevScope
, our product, shows your revenue per visitor
from Google, AI Overviews included, and which landing pages earn the most.

Who the answers cite

If people read the summary and stop there, it matters which sites the summary cites. The report compares Google's AI
Overviews with ChatGPT. Their most-cited lists overlap, but a different kind of site leads each one.

Rank
Google AI Overviews
Citations
ChatGPT
Answers citing it

1
youtube.com
51.9M
wikipedia.org
4.88M

2
reddit.com
25.1M
reddit.com
3.25M

3
facebook.com
20.4M
fandom.com
670K

4
wikipedia.org
19.9M
britannica.com
486K

5
google.com
15.9M
nih.gov
476K

The report warns that the two platforms' counts aren't comparable, so compare where a site ranks within each list. Reddit and
Wikipedia rank near the top of both, and by our count 16 of the 30 domains in each top 30 appear on both lists. The
differences are still large. YouTube is first in AI Overviews and nineteenth in ChatGPT. Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok
make Google's top ten and miss ChatGPT's top 30, while Reuters, The Guardian, AP News, and The Washington Post make
ChatGPT's top 30 and miss Google's. ChatGPT also often cites nobody: 27.3% of its answers had no source, against 0.7% for
AI Overviews. So, as the report puts it, strength on one platform "doesn't automatically guarantee" the same on another.

Reddit also appears in Google's ordinary top ten for 32.15% of the report's tracked results, nearly eight times Quora's
4.11%. Two limits apply to all of this. The first is that the answers come from prompts DataForSEO collected, and the report
doesn't explain how they were chosen or whether they match what people really ask. The second is that big platforms do
about as well in ordinary results: Pew found Wikipedia, YouTube, and Reddit made up 15% of the sources in AI summaries
and 17% of those in standard results. Still, the common belief that AI favors Reddit holds up in this data.

GEO looks mostly like SEO

Google's position is that there are "no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI
Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary", beyond a page being indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. Since
that is a company describing its own product, we looked at outside data on two questions. The first is
which sites get considered, and the second is which page on a site gets picked.

Which sites: link profiles correlate with citations

A referring domain is another website that links to yours. DataForSEO measured
how closely referring domains track AI citations using Spearman's correlation, a score where 0 means no relationship
between two rankings and 1 means they match exactly. The score was 0.406 for AI Overviews and 0.377 for ChatGPT. Links
marked as coming from user-generated content, such as forum posts, scored lower, at 0.342 and 0.314.

These are moderate relationships, and they don't show that links cause citations, since large, well-known sites tend
to have more of everything. The samples also contain only domains cited at least once, so they can't tell you what it
takes to get cited for the first time. A similar pattern shows up in ordinary rankings: domains ranking first had a
median of 111 referring domains against 85 for positions 4 to 10, with heavy overlap between the groups. For AI
Overviews, the median cited domain had 282 referring domains on the easiest keywords and 1,571 on the hardest, after the
report excluded giant platforms like YouTube and Amazon and any domain with fewer than 50 referring domains. Small sites
weren't measured at all. The ranges are also wide, at 518 to 5,765 for the middle half
of domains on the hardest keywords, so sites with very different link profiles get cited.

Which page: cited pages often don't rank for the query

Ranking for a query and being cited for it are drifting apart. Ahrefs found 76% of pages cited in AI Overviews ranked in
the top 10 for that query in

July 2025
, and about 38% in

March 2026
. The two studies differ in sample,
parsing, and the Gemini model behind the Overviews, so the size of that fall isn't a clean measurement. One possible
mechanism is what Google calls query fan-out: its documentation says these features may issue "multiple related searches
across subtopics and data sources". A page could then be cited because it ranks for a related question the reader never
typed. Ahrefs offers this only as a possibility, and its earlier study tested the idea and found that the data didn't
support it.

The most careful test of page-level tactics we found is a study by the SEO software company SISTRIX, published in October
2026. It paired 48,527 pages cited by ChatGPT, AI Mode, or AI Overviews with uncited pages from the same site, which
removes the site's overall strength from the comparison. In the table, a factor of 2.7 means pages with the
feature were cited 2.7 times as often as pages without it.

Page feature
Factor
What SISTRIX says about it

Current year in the title
2.7
A rough stand-in for maintained content, not a title trick; an initial indication

Table of contents with jump links
1.7
Only 14% of pages had one; 2.5 on editorial sites

FAQ structured data
1.5
At 833 URLs it pointed the opposite way, a warning about small GEO studies

Visible last-updated date
1.3
1.9 on editorial sites, but 0.7 on shops; only 5% of pages showed one

Ten or more external links
1.3
Linking out to sources

0.8
0.5 in AI Overviews, but "not a lever, but no cause for concern either"; it should stay

Many features combined
2.1
Against barely optimized pages

An experiment in the paper that gave GEO its name points the same way as SISTRIX's correlations. Aggarwal and colleagues rewrote web pages
and measured how much of a generated answer drew on them. On their 10,000-query benchmark, adding quotations raised a
page's visibility by about 41%, adding statistics by about 31%, and citing sources by about 27%, while keyword stuffing
lowered it by about 8%, all on their main measure, the position-weighted share of the answer's words. Lower-ranked pages
gained the most: citing sources lifted a page ranked fifth by 115% and cut the top-ranked page by 30%.
They also tried Perplexity, an AI search product, on
200 samples, uploading the source text as files rather than letting it search. The gains on that measure were smaller, at
about 21% for quotations and 9% for statistics. The main test used GPT-3.5 reading the top five search results, which is
well behind today's products, so the percentages are dated even if the direction still holds.

The most debated shortcut has nothing behind it so far. llms.txt is a proposed file that tells AI systems what a site
contains. SE Ranking analyzed nearly 300,000 domains and found no correlation with citations. SISTRIX also concluded there
is "no measurable effect", though it cautions that domains with the file differ from others in many ways, so this part of
its data doesn't have the same-site pairing. Google says "you don't need to create new machine readable
files, AI text files, or markup" for its AI features. The data agrees about the files, though SISTRIX's FAQ structured
data result suggests some markup may help.

AI sends little traffic, but it is growing and may convert well

AI assistants sent 0.28% of total traffic across 74,752 websites in March 2026, according to Ahrefs. That was about 3.5
million visitors, against 345 million from Google, or roughly a hundred to one. Ahrefs describes it as small but growing fast.
The true figure is somewhat higher because some visits, especially from mobile apps, get counted as direct traffic.
The same Ahrefs article reports that on its own site, AI search visitors were 0.5% of visitors and 12.1% of signups.
Ahrefs sells SEO software, so its audience may be unusually likely to use AI tools, and one site proves little. Still,
on that site an AI visitor was about 24 times as likely to sign up as the average visitor.
Some of the value never shows up as traffic. People read an AI answer, form an opinion, and never click.

To count what AI visits are worth on your own site,
RevScope
reports when ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and
other assistants send visitors and whether they buy. It also tracks when AI and search engine bots crawl your pages.

Google's own reporting has a gap too. It counts traffic from its AI features inside the overall "Web" numbers in Search
Console. Since 2026 Search Console also has generative AI reports, which Google says show how often your URLs appeared in
those features, along with pages, countries, and devices. The announcement describes impressions and doesn't mention
clicks, so you learn how often you appear, not how many visits or sales that brings. Rank tracking can't fill the gap,
since a page can hold position 1 and earn fewer clicks than it used to.

What to do about it

Keep the fundamentals.
Pages must be indexable and eligible for a snippet. Referring domains correlated
with citations more strongly than user-generated links did, and higher-ranking domains had moderately more of them, so
links from other sites remain a reasonable investment, even though neither relationship proves cause.

Find out who gets cited on your topics, per platform.
Check your important queries in AI Overviews and
ChatGPT and note the sources. Being described accurately there may matter as much as your own page.
Take part in the communities those answers cite, such as Reddit, so that you are mentioned there.

Write pages worth quoting.
Answer related questions directly, add original data and named sources, and
use clear headings. If you run an editorial site, show when the page was last updated.

Skip the shortcuts.
An llms.txt does no harm but has shown no benefit, AI-specific markup isn't
needed, and keyword stuffing lowered visibility in the GEO paper's test.

Judge the work by revenue.
With fewer clicks to go around, it matters more which ones pay. Tie each
channel to the sales it produces rather than to its rank or its visit count.

The numbers above are mainly US English, and the
products change quickly, so the 2025 figures may already be out of date. Nearly all the large datasets come from
companies that sell SEO data or software, including DataForSEO, Ahrefs, SISTRIX, and SE Ranking, and we sell analytics.
Almost everything about what earns a citation is correlation. Three findings hold up. Controlled experiments show fewer clicks to outside websites when Google's AI
features are present, domains with more referring domains tend to be cited more often among those already cited, and we
found no proven shortcut to being cited.

Sources

Search Insider: 2026 Edition

DataForSEO · Annual research report · October 2026

DataForSEO collects search and AI answer data for a living and publishes its tables and methods, which allowed us to
check the monthly figures behind its headlines. It sells this data, its answer prompts aren't explained, and its click
shares are modeled. We rely on it for what appears where, and treat its click estimates and correlations as indications.
Our charts are redrawn from its published values.

The Impact of Google AI Overviews on Publisher Traffic and User Experience: Evidence from a Field Experiment

Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen · Working paper · SSRN · draft of June 2026

University researchers ran a preregistered randomized experiment on 1,065 US participants, 770 of them in the two groups
compared here. Random assignment makes it the best evidence that Overviews themselves reduce clicks. It isn't yet peer
reviewed, and it covers desktop Chrome for two weeks. We read a copy of the June draft hosted outside SSRN.

AI in Search Reduces Publisher Referrals Without Improving User Experience: Experimental Evidence

Stephanie T. Wang, Jeffrey Gleason, and colleagues · Preprint · arXiv · August 2026

A second preregistered experiment, with 1,100 people, which independently supports the direction of the result. We read
its abstract only, so we use it for that direction and not for any figure.

Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears in the results

Athena Chapekis and Anna Lieb · Short read · Pew Research Center · July 2025

A nonprofit research organization with no search product to sell, logging the real browsing of 900 consenting US adults.
It covers one month, March 2025, re-collected the summaries in April, and doesn't control for which searches draw a
summary.

AI Features and Your Website
and

the Search Console reports announcement

Google Search Central · Documentation, last updated December 2025, and blog post, June 2026

title: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
content:
The National Security Agency (NSA) headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, in 2010.

Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images

See all topics

The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter.

The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said.

As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. The agency reverted to its typical work schedule Tuesday evening.

“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”

A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were
discovered
last month.

“The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.”

The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. AI tools helped researchers exploit them, setting off a scramble by government agencies and corporations around the world to address the issue in recent weeks. The NSA itself
urged
organizations to apply software patches.

The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords.

Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack.

A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is
traveling in Asia
on Air Force One.

Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. “It could impact analysis and reporting, but for highest priority requirements they would find a way to work those. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.”

A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail.

Sometime Tuesday evening, the inbox reverted to “code green,” instructing employees to report to work as scheduled. It was not immediately clear whether the outage was resolved.

The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country.

All
flights nationwide were grounded
for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas.

Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings.

And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of
Chase Bank customers
reported they had trouble using their online accounts.

There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security.

The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official.

Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson
said
at the time.

This story has been updated with additional information.

Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between
Outrider Foundation
and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting.

CNN’s Kylie Atwood and Haley Britzky contributed reporting.

--[ Past ]
Last year marked the 40th anniversary of Phrack so we went big. We published
our anniversary launch release in print at Defcon 33, HOPE, WHY25 and some
additional variations at several conferences around the world including
AlligatorCon, B-Sides Canberra, Out of the Box, Datenspuren, DistrictCon,
OffensiveCon, Recon, and Toorcamp. We included a CTF with exploit challenges
and had puzzles and easter eggs included in the zine. We threw parties and
had talks at Defcon and WHY25 to celebrate this milestone.
More importantly, we got new research into people's hands. The point of the
relaunch was to get people reading, researching, writing, and contributing
again. We wanted the next person picking up Phrack to find something that
made them sit down at a computer and start pulling a system apart.
We owe a huge thanks to the authors, editors, artists, publishing partners,
donors, and staff who made it happen. Writing the paper, working through
revisions, putting the print editions together, paying the bills, and
getting boxes of zines to the right places all take time and effort. Most of
that work is invisible when you are holding the finished issue. We
appreciate everyone who did it.
And to the readers: thank you for giving a shit. Seeing someone get excited
about an article, connect it to something they are working on, or realize
that they could contribute something themselves makes the effort worthwhile.
That exchange is how this thing keeps going. The relaunch worked, and this
issue is the follow-through.
--[ Present ]
This is the third release curated by the new staff, and we are not slowing
down. This issue is larger than last year's, with 23 main papers and eight
additional articles in Line Noise. The subjects range from exploitation and
reverse engineering to machine learning, hardware, and the history and
culture that grew around this work.
We have container escapes through the vDSO, use-after-free exploitation, QNX
userland shellcode, Linux kernel research, and a Chromium renderer sandbox
escape through Skia. Elsewhere, the issue takes on Windows smart card
architecture, static taint analysis in Binary Ninja, and autonomous
underwater vehicles.  There is also work examining backdoors in machine
learning and what it means to trust an AI system. One paper takes us from
PhrackCTF to two WinFSP zero-days, which is a pretty good argument for
continuing to put challenges in a zine.
We also have four more articles in Phrack World History, including the story
of the infamous SSH1 CRC32 vulnerability featured in The Matrix Reloaded as
well as stories about blue boxing free phone calls, a confession of a hacker
who tried to backdoor Linux kernel in 2003, and an early discovery of
botnets for hire. Our Prophile features Halvar Flake, whose contributions to
reverse engineering and security research are legendary.
--[ Future ]
In 2026, we find ourselves in a time of rapid technological change. It is
hard to say what vulnerability research or red teaming will look like in
another five years. AI has moved well beyond completing a line of code into
agentic systems capable of analyzing source code and reverse engineering
binaries to find and exploit vulnerabilities.
We can be sure that the future will require us to continue to explore new
ideas, create new tools, and push the boundaries of what is possible in the
face of new challenges and opportunities created by the advancement of AI
and automation systems. As the effort required to put ideas into practice
falls, creativity and human intuition forged through experience is valued
even higher.
We hope that this release of Phrack will inspire new ideas, discussions, and
collaborations that will keep the human side of hacking a critical element
in shaping the future of technology and society. We will continue to do our
part to support the community and provide a platform for sharing knowledge
and ideas. We look forward to seeing what the future holds and we are
excited to be a part of it.
Read the papers, try the ideas, and challenge the conclusions. When you find
something worth sharing, write it up and send it in. We have another issue
to put together, and some of you should be in it!
--[ Greetz ]
To those who have supported us the past three years helping to restore
vitality to Phrack, we thank you.
Conferences who funded prints: Defcon, OffensiveCon, Recon, Unprompted[AU],
Unprompted[US], BSides Canberra, Alligatorcon, TenguCon
Sponsors & Major Donors - WatchTowr, Elltam, Verichains, BShield,
TrustedSec, Binarly, Trenchant, Praetorian (WWSUL), EFF, Blaze, EMX,
Mullvad, ToorCon, Hacker Initiative, Endrazine, Dug Song, Napster, halvar,
Horizon, Huku, Julio Auto, Gadi, and the rest of the people who stepped up with
smaller donations.
Artists - Ian Dash, pinguino, tainted, pepper, mar, xer0, abstrakt, ToscaKaiser,
h7, zir, Mick, p0rtL, netspooky, ackmage, digitalis, Tedsig42, and the many
others who submitted their work for consideration.
Reviewers - barbie, bsdaemon, C, chompie, danielcuthbert, devinc, grugq, joern,
jordan9001, K3, richinseattle, roddux, saber, skyper, SSHad0w, TMZ, zh4ck
All the authors past and present who are now bound to the history of phrack.
The unnamed ones who have helped us with logistics and carrying literal tons
of paper around conferences to deliver them into the hands of the next
generation.
--[ Disclaimer ]
All information in Phrack Magazine is, to the best of the ability of
the editors and contributors, truthful and accurate. When possible,
all facts are checked, all code is compiled. However, we are not
omniscient (hell, we don’t even get paid). It is entirely possible
something contained within this publication is incorrect in some way.
If this is the case, please drop us some email so that we can correct
it in a future issue.
Also, keep in mind that Phrack Magazine accepts no responsibility for
the entirely stupid (or illegal) things people may do with the
information contained herein. Phrack is a compendium of knowledge,
wisdom, wit, and sass. We neither advocate, condone nor participate
in any sort of illicit behavior. But we will sit back and watch.
Lastly, it bears mentioning that the opinions that may be expressed in

title: 350 years ago, Ole Rømer discovered that light has a finite speed
content:
350 years ago, this man discovered that light has a finite speed

Ole Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light takes time to travel.

The Danish astronomer Ole Rømer was responsible for an important discovery in the history of science.

(Image: Wikimedia Commons)

Elise Kjørstad

Elise

Kjørstad

Journalist

Published

16 November 2026 - 00:01

In September 1676, Ole Rømer made a prediction to the members of the
Académie des Sciences
in Paris.
He said that on November 9, Io, one of Jupiter's moons, would emerge from the planet's shadow ten minutes later than expected.
Rømer was right.
In doing so, he proved that light travels at a finite speed. This knowledge became crucial to how we understand the universe today.
Until then, people had believed that light travelled instantaneously from one place to another.

Annonse

People with this personality trait are more prone to anxiety and depression

Regularly disappears behind Jupiter
Ole Rømer was a Danish astronomer and physicist. In 1671, he travelled to Paris, where he spent ten years as a member of the scientific academy and an astronomer at the Paris Observatory,
according to the Great Norwegian Encyclopedia
.
In the years leading up to the discovery, Rømer and other astronomers had been closely observing Io, Jupiter's third-largest moon.
"Io regularly disappears behind Jupiter, and this regularity made it possible to use the moon as a clock," Jacob Wüsthoff Linder tells Science Norway.
He is a professor at NTNU's Department of Physics.
Such a precise ‘clock’ could be useful for navigation, among other things. Ole Eggers Bjælde, a curator at the Science Museums at Aarhus University, writes this in
an article on the popular-science media outlet Videnskab.dk
.
Rømer studied and recorded the exact times when Io disappeared into Jupiter’s shadow and when it emerged on the other side.
Discovered a pattern
Bjælde explains that because Io orbits so close to Jupiter, only one of these events could be observed on any given night.
In the days and months before Jupiter and Earth reached their closest point to each other, astronomers could observe the moon disappearing into Jupiter’s shadow.
In the period after Jupiter and Earth were closest to each other, they could see Io emerging from the shadow.
Rømer compiled detailed measurements of these events and eventually noticed a pattern.

Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Professor Jacob Wüsthoff Linder.

(Photo: Geir Mogen)

"Rømer noticed that the eclipses occurred slightly later than expected when Earth was moving away from Jupiter, and slightly earlier when Earth was moving towards Jupiter," says Linder. "He realised that this was because the light had to travel a longer or shorter distance."
"Impressive"

Annonse

In 1676, he therefore predicted that on November 9, Io would emerge from Jupiter's shadow ten minutes later than expected.
He was correct. If light travelled instantaneously, Io should have appeared ten minutes earlier.
Rømer demonstrated that light does not travel infinitely fast, says Linder. The finding was published shortly afterwards, on December 7, in
Journal des sçavans
.
Rømer was not the first to suggest that light has a finite speed, but he is regarded as the first to demonstrate it with evidence.
Other philosophers and scientists had previously theorised that light has a finite speed, including the Greek philosopher Empedocles, the Muslim scientists Ibn al-Haytham and Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, and the English philosopher and natural scientist Roger Bacon,
according to Wikipedia
.
"How accurate was Rømer's estimate of the speed of light compared with what we know today?"
"Not very accurate by modern standards, but impressive for 1676," says Linder.
Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Linder. That corresponds to roughly 225,000 kilometres per second, whereas the correct value is around 300,000 kilometres per second.
"So his estimate was about 25 per cent too low. What really mattered, however, was not the exact figure, but that he demonstrated that the speed of light was finite and could be measured," he says.

An illustration from Ole Rømer's article from 1676. B represents Jupiter, with its shadow shown by shading. K, F, L, and G indicate different observation points along Earth's orbit as Io enters and emerges from the shadow.

(Illustration: Ole Rømer)

Gained support
Was Rømer's finding quickly accepted by other scientists?
"It was probably a gradual process, and there were critical voices at first. The head of the observatory where Rømer worked, for example, never fully accepted his explanation. Nevertheless, his findings received support fairly quickly from prominent scientific figures such as Huygens, and later Newton," says Linder.
Christiaan Huygens was a Dutch mathematician and astronomer. He is known for developing the wave theory of light, among other things.
"The decisive blow came with James Bradley's discovery of stellar aberration about 50 years later, which provided a completely independent and strong confirmation that light has a finite speed," says Linder.
Stellar aberration is the phenomenon in which stars appear to shift slightly in the sky throughout the year because Earth moves around the Sun while light travels at a finite speed, the researcher explains.
Looking into the past
"Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light actually takes time to travel. It was also the first time anyone had produced a reasonably realistic estimate of the speed of light," says Linder.
This became very important for astronomy.
"Because when we look out into space, we are actually seeing things as they were when the light began its journey towards us. The farther away something is, the farther back in time we are looking," he says.
This has been important for understanding how the universe has evolved.
———
Translated by Alette Bjordal Gjellesvik

title: Solid 2.0
content:
5 years is a long time to work on anything. It took 5 years from my first commit of Solid to 1.0, and it's been another 5 since then. A lot changes in 5 years. Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces. Back then it was an unusual position. Today signals are everywhere. In Angular, in Svelte's runes, in Vue Vapor, and in a proposal before TC39 to put them in the language itself. It even pushed the conversation into React's compiler. More recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build. But Solid has always been about building the right things; the performant things. So for us the mission hasn't really changed all that much. The things that we identified as standout about our approach still stand out now. But instead of living in the shadow of more popular solutions Solid 2.0 carves out a path that others can follow. Deliberately this time. Today that solution reaches stable. Async Graph If fine-grained reactivity's greatest strength is knowing the shape of our application, that knowledge shouldn't end with the process, or the machine the code is running on. Real applications are distributed. Real applications are born from data that lives on a server. The coordination of these pieces should be intentional and by design. This starts with bringing async into the graph. A computation can return a Promise or an async iterator, and everything downstream just understands: function Profile ( props ) { const user = createMemo (() => fetchUser (props.id)); return ( < Loading fallback = {} > < h1 class = {{ stale : isPending (user) }} > { user ().name} ); } This allows authoring by affordance while automating the handling of race conditions. The introduction of async doesn't cause an app refactor. Speculative state is automatically rolled back without manually written processes ensuring the server remains the authority on truth. SolidStart introduce the world to server functions in early 2022, and now they have found their way home to Solid's core, better than ever. Not only do they support highly capable RPC calls over Request/Response but persistent connections over Server Sent Events. And consuming it remains as simple as the code below. import { live } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions" ; const stockPrice = live ( async function* ( symbol : string ) { "use server" ; for await ( const tick of subscribe (symbol)) yield tick.price; }); // in your component const price = createMemo (() => stockPrice ()) This is only the beginning of what can be done with Server Functions and we will be announcing some new features (like reactive Server Components) in coming weeks that leverage this capability. Built to Be Written by Agents "But, we aren't writing the code anymore!" We hear you. A system built on constraints by construction ends up with less code to maintain and less edge cases. What used to be considered a DX shortcoming of reactive frameworks are now their greatest strength. And Solid 2.0 goes all in. Every framework now says it "works great with AI", and usually that means models have seen a lot of it. That's a statement about training data, not about the framework. The question that matters is what happens when the agent gets it wrong. In most frameworks a reactive mistake is silent. The app runs, it's just wrong, and the framework can't tell you, because it can't see it either. Solid can. A fine-grained graph knows exactly what was read, where, and what will update. So Solid 2.0's development builds report mistakes as they happen, with a stable code, the location in your source, and the fix: [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] Reactive value read directly in an effect callback will not update. Move it into a tracking scope (JSX, a memo, or an effect's compute function). in › › effect at http://localhost:5173/src/Item.tsx:12:19 [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] what it means and how to fix it: https://docs.solidjs.com/reference/solid-js/diagnostics/strict-read-untracked [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] agent repair guide: node_modules/solid-js/skills/reactivity-diagnostics/SKILL.md#strict_read_untracked These handle everything from strict errors to helpful heuristics. Thanks to async in the graph we can detect waterfalls, poorly constructed effect loops, poorly scaling graph shapes like wide graph fanouts and fan-ins. Today along with linting rules we can provide the best in class direction for agents at compile and at runtime. This area is still evolving as we learn more about how agents build applications with Solid. The hard part, defining the primitives and semantics, is done. We've integrated with new dev tooling, and Chrome's Performance Tracks. And this capability goes beyond development as this observability powers things like our updated Sentry plugin so you can get the same information on your production builds. We've also been looking at alternative syntax. Solid 2.0 adds experimental support for ReactiveScript and TSRX , both aiming to use compilation to further improve agent authoring. One Framework for All I've always been a big believer that React's super power is its composability. That it allowed the ecosystem to build on its humble pieces. However, we've learned a lot since 2013. At that point composable state, async patterns, and server rendering lacked the primitives to build upon and the ecosystem came up with their own solutions. This was fine for a while but tied React's hands and fractured their ecosystem. Something only a framework as popular as React could survive. Newer frameworks have taken more on themselves and tend to only have one metaframework, or one router. We respect React's original positioning but have updated it for 2026. It isn't about restricting the solution but giving developers the primitives to build upon in the way React originally did. Server functions are example of this. Supporting any router, and cache solution for Single-Flight Mutation is another. We retired our metaframework SolidStart, since every primitive needed to build a Solid Metaframework is now provided by the core or by framework agnostic Vite plugins. We believe that building an opinionated layer like a metaframework shouldn't have you needing to re-implement everything again. We've taken care of the hard parts so you can focus on what you care about. And these days a lot of that work is going to be taken on by your agent. This means less to maintain but no loss in capability. And this makes it easier for the ecosystem. Solid 2.0 only requires one Clerk or Sentry plugin since we provide the primitives for Request/Response (built on web standards) and the hooks for observability that work across any library. We've already seen success with TanStack Query and Router being as capable as anything we've built first party, bringing in Tanner's impeccable attention to detail for the APIs people love to use. Less is More Somehow even though Solid 2.0 brings more capability to Solid, we've collapsed the surface area at almost every point. There are less primitives needed to be learnt, less ceremony around handling async. createResource , batch , startTransition , on , produce , createComputed , createMutable are all gone, because we no longer need them. The equivalent code written for Solid 2.0 is shorter and clearer on intent. It informs our ability observe the runtime, provide better compiler errors, and removes the need for as many escape hatches (like createEffect ) that can get us in trouble. This is something we believe important in an age of AI. Safe by construction rather than by exhaustion. Reduce complexity by deriving(reducing) state rather than putting it in a reducer. // async cascading dropdown function App () { const states = createMemo (() => getStates ( "US" )); const [ selectedState , setState ] = createSignal (() => states ()[ 0 ]); const cities = createMemo (() => getCities ( selectedState ())); const [ selectedCity , setCity ] = createSignal (() => cities ()[ 0 ]); return ( < Loading fallback = {

Loading ... } > < select onChange = {(e) => setState (e.target.value)} > < For each = { states ()} > {(state) => } { ' ' } < select disabled = { isPending ( cities )} onChange = {(e) => setCity (e.target.value)} > < For each = { cities ()} > {(city) => } < p > Selection : { selectedCity ()}, { selectedState ()} ); } When the framework carries the guarantees, all loading state, race conditions, and cancellation logic disappears and what you are left with is the UI. The Road Here The first discussions of what a Solid 2.0 would look like started at the moment 1.0 was released. We saught feedback from the community on new reactivity ideas . The real effort started in late 2024. We announced the road to 2.0 in February 2025. Over a year of experiments followed, rewriting the reactive core from scratch until the async model held up to everything we threw at it. The beta landed in March, and the Release Candidate in August, with the API frozen. Then 23 release candidates in 14 weeks. In that time alone, 971 pull requests were merged and 753 issues closed. We set one bar for stable. A full week with no regression in ordinary app code, and no crash or hang anywhere. It took a while to get there. By the end, the bug reports coming in were from people(agents) deliberately hunting edge cases in the deepest corners of the scheduler, and finding them. So many people have touched the project over the past 5 years, from working on the initial reactivity prototypes, to testing the latest RC builds on their production apps. I've tried to thank as many of you as I can and attached hundreds of handles in the RC announcement. There are so many. There are also the many great organizations that have sponsored our development over the years: Sentry, Netlify, Google Chrome, JetBrains, Anomaly, Cursor, Code Rabbit, Anthropic, Tembo and so many more. But mostly I want to thank everyone who has believed in the project. We've accomplished great things and there is much more to come. That isn't possible without all of you. Personally, the past 2 and half years have been some of the most difficult of my life, but knowing what we are building that impacts so many people leaves me with a sense of fulfillment. Solid has always been bigger than its core team, and 2.0 is the clearest proof of that yet. Terminal window npm create solid@latest Solid 2.0 is here. Let's build. The Long Hold refers to a diagnostic warning in Solid 2.0. It fires when a hold has been shown( isPending ) but sufficient time has passed since the last input. Holds were at the heart of our async work for 2.0, and we acknowledge it took a while for this all to land. All posts

title: What is the best harness for each model?
content:
TL;DR

We partnered with
Baseten
to build the largest-scale harness leaderboard using 83B tokens across 27,280 agent runs. We wanted to answer two questions:
when you switch your model, should you consider switching the harness too? What is the best harness for each model?

Previously, our
v1.0 FrontierHarness leaderboard
ranked harnesses on a single model, Kimi K3.

V1.1 expands the benchmark to 22 harnesses × 5 models × 62 tasks × 4 attempts, 76× the size of v1.0.

Through our experiments, we found that you should consider switching harnesses when switching models to maximize your experience.

Each model had a different best-value (pass rate vs. cost) harness: Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Oh My Pi with Muse and Alma with Kimi-K3.
Cost ranks moved far between models.

By cost per task, the median harness moved 11 of 22 places, and Codex CLI went from 1st with GLM-5.3 to 16th with Kimi-K3.

Result

Figure 1. Cost per task and pass rate of each harness

Each point is one harness: further left is a lower average cost per task, and higher is a higher pass rate. The orange line joins the harnesses that no other harness beats in both cost and pass rate. Select a model to filter all figures of this post.

Over all models, four harnesses are on the line: OpenCode v2 (lowest cost per task, $0.561), Pi, Codex CLI and ZCode (highest pass rate, 61.9%). The others cost up to 1.6 times as much and passed 50.6% to 60.2%.

Each card names the best-value harness for one model: the lowest cost per pass, unless another harness costs at most 30% more per pass and passes at least 5 points more often. This rule picked ZCode over OpenCode v1 with DeepSeek (25% more cost, 7.7 more points) and Alma over Oh My Pi with Kimi-K3 (9% more cost, 6.5 more points).

Why We Built
FrontierHarness
Eval v1.1

V1.0
ran nine harnesses with one model. Their pass rates were within 17 points of each other, but the median cost per pass differed by 17 times. We thought that this came mostly from the pair of harness and model: a harness that is cheap with one model can be expensive with another.

V1.1 runs each harness with five models.

What We Tested

Harnesses.
18 harnesses. The four DeepSeek Harness profiles have different tool sets, and OpenCode ran at two versions. Each counts separately: 22 configurations. Table 2 in the
appendix
gives their versions.

Models.
Baseten served all five: GLM-5.3 (
zai-org/GLM-5.3
), GLM Flash (
zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash
), DeepSeek (
deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017
), Muse (
meta-models/muse-spark-open
) and Kimi-K3 (
moonshotai/Kimi-K3
).

Tasks.
62 terminal tasks. The time limits are those of the tasks, from 15 minutes to 8 hours.

Setup and Scoring

Configuration and Runtime

We ran the Harbor evaluation with each harness’s default settings, because we think this is closest to how people use a harness every day. Each harness used the same version and settings with all models, at the maximum reasoning effort.

Figure 2. How Harbor and Runta divide the work in each trial

Each trial gets a new Runta runtime, which is deleted at the end. Thus no trial can see the files of an earlier trial.

Scoring Method

Table 1. Methodology

A cell is one harness and model pair. We use the two cost metrics of
our dashboard
:

Average cost per task:
the mean cost of the priced trials of each task, then the mean over the tasks. Figure 1 and the cost ranks use it (Figures 4 and 5).

Cost per pass:
the average cost per task divided by the pass rate. The best-value harness uses it (Figures 3, 6 and 7).

We pick the best value by cost per pass because we want harnesses at the top left of a chart of pass rate against cost per task: a high pass rate at a low cost. Draw a line from the origin to the point of a harness. Its slope, pass rate ÷ cost, is the passes per dollar. Cost per pass is the inverse of this slope, so the lowest cost per pass has the steepest line.

Audits of the trial logs flagged 216 trials for reward hacking, and 163 of them were online lookups. These trials score 0. Table 3 in the appendix gives the count for each harness and model.

Results by Model

Figure 3. Cost and pass rate of each harness with each model

A deeper cell costs less than the others in its column. Codex CLI was the cheapest per pass with GLM-5.3, $0.803, but 12th with Muse and 10th with Kimi-K3. Over all models, it cost the least per pass, $0.937, and Antigravity CLI the most, $1.63.

How Sure Are These Results?

We drew the 62 tasks again 4,000 times and chose the best-value harness each time. Codex CLI stayed first with GLM-5.3 in 99.6% of the draws. The other four winners are the most likely of several close harnesses: Oh My Pi with Muse (53%), ZCode with DeepSeek (47%), Pi with GLM Flash (42%) and Alma with Kimi-K3 (25%).

The Harness Changes the Cost

The model sets the general level of the cost, because the list prices of the models differ by 20 times or more (Figure 9). We took the average cost per task of the 110 cells on a log scale, so that a doubling counts the same with each model. A two-way analysis of variance divides the spread of these costs into three parts:

Model, 92.8%:
the differences between the five models.

Harness, 2.3%:
the part of the effect of a harness that is the same with every model.

Pair, 4.9%:
the rest. It also contains noise, because each cell has one value.

So with the model fixed, 68% of the variation between harnesses (4.9 of 7.2 points) depends on the pair, or is noise.

With the Model Fixed, the Harness Changes the Cost by 1.8 to 5.0 Times

Figure 4. Lowest-cost and highest-cost harness for each model

Each row is a model, on a log scale of average cost per task. The ratio divides the highest cost by the lowest.

To test for chance, we shuffled the trials between the harnesses of each model 300 times and calculated the ratio again. “Chance” is the median of these ratios, 1.2 to 1.8 times. All five real ratios are larger than every shuffle (p = 0.003), so the spread comes from the harnesses, not from the noise of reruns. The largest is with DeepSeek: Cline CLI cost 5.0 times as much as OpenCode v1, for 2.0 more points. With the other models, the cheapest harness per task was at most 0.4 points behind the most expensive one.

The Cheapest Harness per Task Changes With the Model

Figure 5. Cost rank of each harness with each model (1 = lowest cost per task)

Each line is a harness, with the cheapest at the top. The five highlighted lines are the cheapest harnesses per task with GLM-5.3, GLM Flash, DeepSeek, Muse and Kimi-K3.

Codex CLI was 1st with GLM-5.3 and 16th with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness: Creator moved the most, from 1st with Muse to 21st with GLM Flash. OpenCode v1 was 1st with DeepSeek and 13th with Muse.

Reruns do not explain these moves. We divided the attempts into two halves and ranked the harnesses by cost in each half. With the same model, the two rankings had a mean rank correlation of 0.71. With two different models, it was 0.26.

A Higher Cost Does Not Give a Higher Score

Figure 6. Lowest and highest cost per pass for each model

This is Figure 4 for cost per pass. After each ratio is the rank correlation of the cost per task and the pass rate of the harnesses, from −0.39 to +0.22. A positive value means that the more expensive harnesses passed more often.

The harness with the highest pass rate was 5th to 20th of 22 in cost per task. With four of the five models, the most expensive harness per pass passed less often than the cheapest one.

Does a Simpler Harness Cost Less?

No. We compared four factors with the cost per pass.
Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate are not the main cost factors. Steps are.

Start tokens:
the input tokens of the first agent-loop request: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the task.

Tools:
the tools that the first request offers.

Cache hit rate and steps:
the mean over the passed trials. A step is one entry of the agent trajectory.

Figure 7. Four factors of each harness and the cost per pass

Over the 22 harnesses, the rank correlation of the steps per pass and the cost per pass was +0.51 (p = 0.015). For the other three factors, it was −0.03 to +0.02 (p ≥ 0.88). Within each model, tool calls tracked cost as well as steps. Table 4 below and Table 5 in the
appendix
give the values.

Each step sends the context again, so a trial used 2.0 to 4.8 million input tokens on average, by harness, and the largest first request, 21,365 tokens, is less than 1% of that. mini-SWE-agent has the smallest first request, 882 tokens, but took 38 steps per pass and was 17th of 22 in cost per pass.

Table 4. Start tokens, tools, cache hit rate, steps and cost per pass of each harness

Where the Cost Comes From

Figure 8. Inference cost of each harness, by token type or by trial outcome

All costs are inference estimates at list prices. The pass rate of the harness on the model card has an outline.

Over all trials, input from the cache was 42% of the cost, output 33% and other input 25%.

Tokens and the Cache

The cache makes repeated input much cheaper. Cached input costs 2% (DeepSeek) to 20% (GLM Flash) of the price of other input (Figure 9).

Figure 9. List prices of each model (USD for one million tokens)

One pair shows the effect of the cache.
Cline CLI with DeepSeek (highest cost per task)
read 86% of its input from the cache, and OpenCode v1 read 97%. It also sent twice as much input. Input that did not come from the cache was 57% of its cost.

Most of the Cost Goes to Trials That Do Not Pass

64.5% of the list-price cost of the scored runs went to trials that did not pass
: 52.7% to failures and 11.8% to timeouts.

The traces of the five best-value harnesses show three common design choices. These are observations, not tests.

One shell tool does most of the work.
By harness, it got 61% to 93% of the tool calls. Pi’s
default prompt
has four tools and sends file searches to
bash
:

selectedTools: [...(input.selectedTools ?? ["read", "bash", "edit", "write"])],
addRule("Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find");

Each request only adds to the one before it.
The start of the context does not change, so the provider reads it from the cache: 91.1% to 94.0% of input in passed trials (Table 4). But 18 of the 22 harnesses read 91% or more, so this does not separate the five. Each step pays the full input price for only about 500 new tokens:

# Pi, GLM-5.3, merge-diff-arc-agi-task (trial cd2f6dfd)
request  prompt tokens  cached tokens
8        15,954         15,616
9        16,351         15,936
10        16,999         16,320

No subagents and almost no summaries.
Each of the five used a subagent in at most 6 trials, too few to tell if subagents help. Of the five, only Codex CLI summarized, in 8 trials (the 11 Alma trials in Table 6 only drop old images and reminders). Codex CLI summarizes at 90% of the window (Table 6):

.map(|context_window| (context_window * 9) / 10);

The five also share a weakness.
Failed runs end with a confident answer.
About three in four failed trials ended with a final answer, not at the time limit: from 68% with Pi to 82% with Codex CLI. Few said that the work was incomplete:

# Codex CLI, GLM-5.3, cancel-async-tasks (trial 37182b0e)
Agent:    - Validated with system Python, including concurrency and
cancellation-cleanup tests.
Verifier: FAILED test_tasks_cancel_above_max_concurrent
assert stdout.count("Cleaned up.") == 2
AssertionError: assert 0 == 2

Trials that did not pass took 60% (Codex CLI) to 69% (Alma) of the cost of each harness. A check before the harness stops could save part of it, but we did not test this.

Limitations and Future Work

Open models, one provider.
Closed models can give different results. The cache and the prices are those of Baseten, and another provider can change the cost ranks.

We plan two next steps:

Closed models.
We will add closed models, such as Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Carbon.

Long-horizon work.
We will study how a harness that runs continuously in the cloud improves itself during long work.

Conclusion

When you change the model, think about changing the harness too.
Test the candidate harnesses with your model on a private dataset of your own tasks, large enough to see past the noise.

The model sets most of the cost, and the harness is second.
The model explains 92.8% of the variance of cost per task. With the model fixed, the most expensive harness cost 1.9 to 4.9 times as much per pass as the cheapest (1.8 to 5.0 times per task), so compare the cost when you pick a harness.

A higher cost does not buy a higher pass rate.
For each model, the rank correlation of cost per task and pass rate was −0.39 to +0.22.

Size does not predict cost.
mini-SWE-agent, the smallest harness, was 19th of 22 by cost per task over all models.

Most of the cost, 64.5%, went to runs that did not pass.
With the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of the failed runs ended with a confident final answer, not at the time limit.

With a cheap model that has a wide range of pass rates, pick a harness with a high pass rate.
Pass rates varied by harness, from 54.0% to 69.0% with DeepSeek. But each pass rate has a 95% interval of about ±10 points, so a gap of a few points is a tie.

For harness developers: cut steps, not just prompt tokens.
Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate did not predict cost per pass. Steps did, because every step sends the whole context again.

Appendix: Reference Tables

Table 2. Harness configurations

Table 3. Reward-hacked trials of each harness

Table 5. Prompt and tools of each harness

References

FrontierHarness dashboard

Harbor
and
Harbor Hub
, where the ten jobs are stored

Introducing FrontierHarness Eval
, our v1.0 results

Baseten
,
Model APIs
, the inference provider for performant open models

Runta Harbor guide
and
Runta pricing

title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
content:
Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage.

For eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work.

Content Assessment: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review

Information - 92%

Insight - 90%

Relevance - 88%

Objectivity - 90%

Authority - 92%

90
%

Excellent

A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review."

News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat

Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found.

In the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Two legal AI announcements this month, Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and a court-filing redaction agent Cooley is developing with Google Cloud, place a lawyer at a comparable review step, and neither reports a measure of it.

What the Harvard data measured

How much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira issues, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data.

The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months.

The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI.

The current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. Her website lists coverage links to The Wall Street Journal and The Economist, and legal trade press picked it up this month, including an Oct. 12 eDiscovery Today post by Doug Austin that relayed an Ars Technica report.

Drafts went up and finished issues did not

With that provenance in view, the coding results are large. Lines of code added rose by 1,494 per worker-month against a baseline of 5,017, about 30 percent. Commits rose 20 percent, and pull requests, the bundles of code submitted for review, rose 23 percent. The authors note that these estimates capture the added effect of agents at firms that already had AI coding assistants, not the effect of AI from a standing start.

Output is where the gain stops. The paper counts finished work as Jira issues resolved, and an issue counts as complete when its code is deployed to production. Agents moved that measure by 0.12 issues per worker-month on a 3.67 baseline, with a standard error of 0.17. That result is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the 95 percent confidence interval rules out an increase above about 12 percent of the baseline, well short of the 30 percent rise in code written.

The authors tested the obvious escape route. If engineers had shifted to larger tasks, a flat issue count would understate real output. So the researchers labeled a 0.5 percent sample of issues by size with GPT-4o and extended those labels to every issue with a text-embedding model. They found no shift in average issue size, and pull requests did not grow larger either, which the authors use to set aside the simplest explanation for what happened in review.

Where the shortfall shows up: the review queue

The paper locates the shortfall in code review. The time from pull request submission to merge rose 3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline, a 49 percent increase. The share of pull requests receiving a formal change request increased by about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 13 percent, nearly doubling, and review comments per pull request rose 35 percent. The share of workers doing any code review rose 14 percent from a base of about 29 percent, while the share writing code showed no measurable change.

AI review tools did not remove the bottleneck. By March 2026, nearly 80 percent of the firms had used one, yet AI generated only 23.3 percent of review comments, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests received even one AI comment. The authors write that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt such tools. The paper’s interviews show what that looks like on a team: a junior software engineer described a project where only one senior engineer could approve changes and could review the interviewee’s code only once a week. “After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks,” the engineer said, in a quote the authors say they lightly edited for clarity.

That account fits the model the authors use to explain their numbers, which has two channels. In the first, faster drafting sends more code to a fixed pool of reviewers, a problem that moving labor into review can largely relieve. In the second, the rise in change requests and comments, which faster drafting alone does not explain, reads through the model as a sign of lower-quality drafts. That problem, the authors say, would require better technology. Anyone buying an agent should care which channel dominates, because the two call for different spending.

Employment did not move either

Nor did the coding gains show up as job cuts. The estimates rule out a decline in overall employment larger than 2.9 percent. A noisier estimate rules out a decline in engineering employment larger than 13.8 percent. The authors caution that these are short-run effects measured in partial equilibrium, which could mask job losses at competing firms, and that the assistant estimate for engineering employment shows upward pre-trends that make it hard to read causally.

Legal AI tools are designed around a similar checkpoint

Those software results arrive as legal AI tools adopt a related design, and the Harvey and Cooley announcements both follow it: automate a first pass, then keep a lawyer at the checkpoint. Harvey’s workflow, co-developed with LexisNexis and announced Oct. 7, is the drafting case. Harvey says the multi-step process of reading the complaint, researching and drafting a motion to dismiss “commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work” and that its tool produces the research and a first draft “in a matter of hours.” The announcement describes “human checkpoints at the moments where a lawyer’s judgment matters most,” but it does not state how long lawyers spend at those checkpoints or how long it takes to reach a motion ready to file.

Cooley’s Oct. 8 announcement applies the same posture to a different task, since its agent recommends redactions rather than drafting arguments. Cooley says the agent is still being developed and that attorneys make all redaction determinations before a filing goes to the court, which puts the human checkpoint at the last step before submission. As ComplexDiscovery reported Oct. 10, the announcement carries no error rate.

For a motion filed in federal court, the checkpoint is a legal duty rather than a design choice. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b), an attorney presenting a motion certifies several things about it to the best of the attorney’s knowledge, information and belief, “formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.” Its legal contentions must be “warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing new law.” Its factual contentions must have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, be likely to have it after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery. A first draft can arrive in hours, but that inquiry stays with the attorney, and the software evidence raises the possibility that review could absorb some of the drafting savings.

The paper’s method carries a second lesson, this one for information governance teams. The researchers identified agent use partly from traces inside the firms’ own systems, including bot accounts tied to AI tools and signatures such as “Co-authored-by” lines in commit messages and pull request descriptions. AI authorship can leave its own metadata trail in collaboration systems. That trail is a record that a retention schedule and a legal hold may need to reach.

None of this means legal work will behave like software, and the limits of the comparison matter. Document review is not code review, a production is not a pull request, and Chen and Stratton studied no legal work. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, revised in September 2026, reports a similar falloff using data on over 500,000 GitHub developers. Its authors, Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, found a 240 percent cumulative rise in commits from autonomous agents shrinking to 30 percent for actual releases. That paper carries its own disclosure: Demirer and Musolff each previously held a postdoctoral research position at Microsoft, which owns GitHub, and each now works as a paid research consultant for the company. Two software studies point to a pattern in software, not a finding about law firms.

Document review offers a partial precedent

Discovery practitioners have argued a version of this question before, and Austin’s post draws that comparison. He wrote that discovery has seen a similar debate over generative AI review, with some practitioners saying manual validation offsets the gains and others, including him, saying statistical sampling of the kind used in predictive coding is enough. For coding agents, though, he wrote that the extra review time may be warranted, since code that is 90 percent correct can still fail to run.

His comparison suggests a useful split between two kinds of legal output. Population-level work such as first-pass relevance review can be validated by sampling. A single filing is different, because its citations, factual assertions and sensitive data generally need direct examination when one fabricated citation or one missed Social Security number is the failure. Buyers can turn that split into a test. Ask a vendor which kind of output its agent produces, then ask for the downstream measure rather than the drafting one: hours from upload to an approved work product, the share of drafts a reviewing attorney sent back and reviewer time per matter. Budget review capacity before scaling drafting volume, and log what reviewers change, because that log shows whether the bottleneck is volume or quality.

Read the paper’s limits as closely as its findings

Those questions apply to the paper’s own sourcing, too. The data partner has a commercial interest in the subject, and the relationship runs deeper than a data license. Jellyfish describes itself as an “AI Impact Platform,” and the authors have published on its blog: a Sept. 25, 2025, post by Chen and Stratton described itself as “part of our ongoing work with Jellyfish.” The paper thanks the Jellyfish team “for their partnership” and states that Jellyfish reviewed the manuscript only to check for proprietary disclosure, not for scientific content, and that the conclusions are the authors’. Its funders were the Stripe Economics of AI Fellowship, a Harvard Kennedy School program on wealth distribution and the Schmidt Sciences AI at Work Program.

Jellyfish has also promoted an earlier version of the work. A Jan. 28 post on its blog by Nicholas Arcolano called it “a preliminary version of a new paper from our collaborators at Harvard Economics, Fiona Chen and James Stratton,” based on 100,000 software engineers across 500 companies. That post, and a March 17 Jellyfish press release after it, reported that AI was making coding faster and that “code quality doesn’t seem to be suffering.” The August version, built on a larger sample running through March 2026, reads the near-doubling in change requests through its model as a possible sign of lower draft quality. The two descriptions rest on different versions and samples, so they need not conflict, but a reader relying on Jellyfish’s summary would miss the quality question the current paper raises.

The paper also carries small internal inconsistencies that do not touch the headline agent estimates. Its introduction rounds the sample to about 700 firms and 700,000 workers, and its main text describes 17 interviews where an appendix describes 21. Other limits are structural rather than clerical: the underlying data are proprietary, and use of AI tools through individual licenses goes unrecorded.

None of those caveats overturns the central result, though the March 2026 data cutoff means a revision could move the figures. What the paper offers is a standard the two legal announcements discussed here do not meet: named authors, a disclosed method, a confidence interval and a measured checkpoint. If an agent cuts 40 hours of research and drafting to a few, how many of those hours reappear on the desk of the lawyer who signs the motion?
