title: Gemini 4 Neon
content:
Introducing Gemini 4 Neon

Nov 18, 2026

|

Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion  across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

Koray Kavukcuoglu

SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google

Your browser does not support the audio element.

Listen to article

[[duration]] minutes

This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.
Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the
Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index
at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the
Vals Index
, Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new
Agent Arena Index
. Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing.
The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window.
Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in
Google AI Studio
,
Gemini for business
(via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in
Google Antigravity
, and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the
Gemini app
.

Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work
Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the
Vals Index
, it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the
Legal Research Bench
and
Tax Agent Bench
.
Neon also shows strong wins across categories on
Surge AI
, ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on
Agents' Last Exam v1.1
(75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s
AutomationBench
(56.3%) and
Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2
($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on
Arena's new Agent Arena Index
across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.
On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on
Terminal-Bench Science
(70.5%),
RiemannBench
(84.0%), and
HLE-Diamond
(71.3%).

Built for production-ready code

Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions.
Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the
Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index
(58.6), with a score of 65.2% on
Terminal-Bench 4.1
and
46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0
. For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks.

Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon.

In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets.

Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk.

In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes.

Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows
We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs.
Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting.

Built for fast, efficient, frontier-level cyber defense
As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on
AutoBaxBench
, achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%).
Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On
WebExploitBench v1.2
, Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models.
To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models.
Finding code vulnerabilities:
Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on
SEC-bench Pro
(90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge.
Validating risk through exploitation:
To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon.
Patching vulnerabilities:
Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s
CWE-bench v2
, driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon.

Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the
Fairwind Program
.

Designed for safe, dependable execution
Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our
Gemini 4 safety and security stack
— maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on:
Mitigating frontier misuse safety risks:
Because Neon brings frontier-level capabilities to a faster, lower-cost model, we paired it with strong real-time safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse comparable to our Carbon protections, while declining far less legitimate work in these areas, refusing for instance just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science.
Advancing alignment and disciplined model behavior:
In internal coding use, alert rates from our chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor remained below the already low baselines set by Carbon, suggesting improved alignment propensity for Neon — and that same monitor is deployed to protect Neon across external surfaces. Neon is trained to complete multi-step work without cutting corners, fabricating results, or overstepping user boundaries — continuing to improve the balance between following through on requests and staying within scope. It matched Carbon with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and took shortcuts on just 2.45% of tasks on our coding cheating evaluation (the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model). It also achieved a 0.09% misaligned action rate on our agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on our agent honesty evaluation.
On our agentic behavior evaluation, Neon builds on Carbon’s strong baseline by further reducing under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels.
Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks:
On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark, Neon is more resilient than other models in its class when malicious instructions are planted in the web pages, emails, documents, or code it accesses. We found that with real-time safeguards at its highest thinking level, Neon resisted every attack within this Gray Swan benchmark, matching the 0.0% attack success rate reached only by other Gemini models.

For more details, see the
Gemini 4 Neon model card
.

Built for deeper analysis
In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses.
Higher-quality writing and knowledge work:
Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs.
Reliable research and analysis:
Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data.
Faster help for tougher tasks:
Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund.

Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family
Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.

Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today
Gemini 4 Neon begins rolling out today:
For developers:
Build with the Gemini API paid tier in
Google AI Studio
and
Android Studio
, if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try Neon in
Google Antigravity
and all Pro and Ultra subscribers can try it in AI Studio.
For enterprises:
Use Gemini 4 Neon in
Gemini for business
(via the API or model drop-down) and Google Antigravity.
For consumers:
If you’re a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can select Gemini 4 Neon from the model drop-down in the
Gemini app
.
For cybersecurity defenders:
Eligible
Fairwind Program
members will begin receiving access over the next few days. To request access to the Fairwind Program, contact your Cloud account team.

At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability.

But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you run agents 24/7 doing real engineering work.

That’s why today we’re releasing a family of seven new world class models at a truly exceptional price-performance.

Here’s the lineup:

MAI Cyber 2 Flash
beats GPT-6 Astra’s quality at less than 2% of the cost per task on the CyberGym-E2E benchmark.

MAI Code 2
reaches 98% of the coding quality of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 40% of the price. And against Opus 5.5, it reaches 96% performance for just 5% of the price.

MAI Code 2 Flash
shows comparable performance  GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price, and Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the price.

MAI Image 2.7
is #1 on Artificial Analysis image editing, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price.

MAI Realtime 1
outperforms GPT-Realtime 2.1 and starts at just $0.01 per audio minute.

Dragon Copilot Transcribe
is built on MAI Transcribe 2, the world’s fastest and most accurate multilingual transcription model, and already powers 10 million patient encounters a month with multilingual error rates halved.

Decision 1.1
is the latest decision model from Microsoft, 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol.

Maia 200
, Microsoft’s second-generation AI accelerator, is now in production running our largest models, achieving 1.7x more tokens per watt.

Frontier cyber defense built to run 24/7

Security, alignment and containment are the most important priorities for agent development in 2027 and beyond. That’s our top priority. We need to run monitoring and control agents defending and patching live production systems 24/7. That’s why
MAI Cyber 2 Flash
was designed to deliver frontier intelligence at a fraction of the cost.

Built with Microsoft’s decades of proprietary data and world-class security expertise, our models help defenders stay safe in this new era where attackers have cheap and abundant offensive tools.

MAI Cyber 2 Flash builds on earlier MAI Cyber models that defenders already rely on. MAI Cyber accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, and 90% of scans that started with MAI continued to use it. Our latest model is now priced 86% lower on output tokens than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, giving existing MDASH customers a stronger model at a lower price.

Incredible coding performance at a fraction of the cost

MAI Code 2
is built for the best price-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks.  Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the price.

We’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day.  They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work.

MAI Code 2 also been tuned to generate great dashboards and visualizations. In a blind, side-by-side evaluation of frontend work, developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. Try MAI Code 2 in
GitHub Copilot
today.
Read more here
.

MAI Code 2 Flash
is designed for high-volume, everyday tasks like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. It performs comparably to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the price, respectively, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas). It’s available in
GitHub Copilot
and in a limited-access preview in
Microsoft Foundry
.

The best image and transcription models in the world

MAI Image 2.7
is the best image editing model in the world, taking the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. At text-to-image generation, our model is ranked #4, making us the second-best lab. And
MAI Image 2.7 Flash
brings world class image generation for high-volume scenarios at ~$10 per 1,000 images. Both are available in Microsoft Foundry
here
.

MAI Realtime 1
is our first live speech-to-speech model, designed for natural, low-latency conversations. In our evaluations, it outperformed GPT-Realtime 2.1 across external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. It’s priced for enterprise-scale use, starting at a budget-saving price of $0.01 per audio minute. You can try it out in
MAI Labs
and
register your interest here
.

Dragon Copilot Transcribe
, built on MAI Transcribe 2, is now live in Dragon Copilot, powering 100% of doctor–patient conversation transcriptions. It covers 10 million encounters a month, halves error rates in multilingual workflows, and is in the hands of a third of US physicians.

The leading Decision model in the market

Decision 1.1
provides model routing integrated right into your applications so that the bigger, pricier models are only used when you really need them. On the Artificial Analysis Decision Index Microsoft is ahead of Jev, Google and OpenAI, while being faster and cheaper. Used by 4,000 customers, it’s 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol.

Customize models for your business

We’ve heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model.

And if you build on open weights, can you really trust where they came from, or how they’ll behave when you use one as the foundation for your most valuable IP and data?

We heard you. We started with Custom Models. AT&T developed an MAI custom model for 5G network operation analytics and it outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at 1/50th of the cost. On complex scenarios, they found that Code 2 delivered frontier-level performance at a significantly lower price than alternatives.

Today, we’re taking a big step forward with
MAI Licensed Weights
: models under your control.

Take a frontier MAI model, customize it using your proprietary data if you want to. Then run it securely in your own Azure environment.

You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents.

So that’s MAI, a family of world class models with exceptional price performance: the world’s best image editing model; the world’s best transcription model; frontier cyber defense at 2% of the cost; and world class everyday coding models at a price you can scale.

And crucially all of it with Your IQ. Your agents. Your weights. All under your control.

This is Frontier Intelligence you can trust, from the company you can trust.

title: DaisyRose-27B: 1,200-task RL took Qwen3.8 from 5.6% to 12% on Terminal-Bench 4.1
content:
All posts
Today we are releasing
DaisyRose-27B
, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using

Miles
. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.
We are releasing

BF16
,

FP8
,
and

NVFP4

checkpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget.
DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above
1
. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes.
High-quality Training Data
We built the tasks in partnership with

Eigent AI
, starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 of them made it into the final training set. The training tasks are selected based on three criteria.
Each task targets a mistake the original model makes.
We ran the original Qwen3.8-27B on every training task and carefully redesigned each one so that it brings out the mistakes we want the model to stop making. We then tuned each task until its solve rate fell within a suitable range, neither too easy nor too hard for the model to learn from.
Every task is a long job with several problems chained together.

Each task entails a chain of interdependent problems, so an agent has to navigate through multiple stages of reasoning, planning, and execution. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in the sandbox, with more than 100 tool-calls and more than 256k output tokens.
There is no room for reward hacking.
We reviewed every task
along with the model's attempts at it. Any task that could be passed without really solving it, or that had a design flaw, was fixed or removed before training.
Efficient training backend
RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.
57% lower training cost.
On this release,
37% of each GPU's peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.
2× faster end to end.
Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.
Stable over weeks.
The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.
Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.
Robust sandbox service
During training, every attempt the agent makes runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task's environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. All of the RadixArk team's work on this release ran in sandboxes on our own service, built on the open-source

AgentENV
project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running at the same time.
Reliable as it grew.
The service grew from a single machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all of them while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded, and since late October more than 99.95% have. Getting there took a steady stream of fixes and improvements, such as keeping a machine from freezing when it runs out of memory.
80% lower cost.
Our cloud infrastructure cost for the
project's sandboxes was about 80% lower than the cost of running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to give each sandbox memory that grows and shrinks with what it actually uses. A sandbox usually uses only a small part of the memory it asks for, so each machine can run many more sandboxes.
Try DaisyRose-27B, or train your own
You can download DaisyRose-27B from

Hugging Face
, and you can train your own agents with our open source reinforcement learning framework

Miles
.
DaisyRose-27B is one example of what high-quality data and efficient infrastructure can make possible. We are bringing this approach to teams building specialized models, with a focus on improving the capabilities they need while preserving the model’s broader strengths. If you are exploring post-training for your own model, reach out at

contact@radixark.ai
.
We are deeply grateful to Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and to the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B, the foundation of our work. We also thank the Miles and
SGLang
communities, as well as other open-source projects, including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.
How we evaluated: Terminal Bench 4.1 is averaged over 8 runs per task, using our internal mini-swe-agent harness with summarization turned on. Terminal Bench 2.1 is averaged over 5 runs per task, using the Terminus 2 harness. DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE Bench Pro v2 are averaged over 8 and 5 runs per task, both using the mini-swe-agent harness. HLE (text-only) is averaged over 5 runs per problem, graded by GPT-6 Luna, with no tools. IFBench is averaged over 4 runs on each of its 300 prompts, scored by the official allenai/IFBench scorer as prompt-level loose accuracy on the final response, with the thinking left out. GPQA Diamond is averaged over 8 runs on each of its 198 questions, using the simple-evals multiple-choice template and answer extraction, with the answer order reshuffled on every run.

title: DNS resolvers are the wrong place to fight piracy
content:
On Tuesday, November 24, 2026,
Quad9
will stop answering DNS queries from France. Quad9 is the Swiss non-profit behind the free 9.9.9.9 resolver, which blocks malware and phishing domains. It is not leaving because of costs or lack of users. It is leaving because a Paris court
fined it for refusing to block
a list of pirate sports-streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With
around 20 similar cases still pending
in France, leaving the country is the only option Quad9 can afford.

Cloudflare, which runs the competing 1.1.1.1 resolver, called the departure
"a canary in the coal mine"
, and the post reached the
front page of Hacker News
. In that thread, Quad9's CTO John Todd
asked readers
to write "a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path", with plenty of sources, and to send it to policymakers. This is our attempt. Every claim below links to a primary document, a court ruling, or contemporaneous reporting.

What Quad9 is, and why it matters
​

A DNS resolver turns a name like
example.com
into an IP address your computer can connect to. Most people use their ISP's resolver without knowing it. A public resolver is one anyone can point their device or network at instead, such as Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Cisco's OpenDNS, or Quad9's 9.9.9.9.

Quad9 has a few properties that make it unusual:

It is a non-profit.
It was founded in 2017 by the
Global Cyber Alliance, IBM, and Packet Clearing House
, and
moved its legal seat to Zürich in 2021
, hosted by SWITCH, specifically so that its privacy promises would be backed by Swiss law. As John Todd put it at the time: "Privacy policies which are not backed by law are empty promises."

Security filtering is its main purpose.
Quad9 refuses to resolve domains that threat-intelligence feeds flag as malware, phishing, or botnet infrastructure. Its about page claims
670 million+ blocks a day across 230+ resolver clusters in over 110 countries
.

It keeps no user records.
Quad9 does not know who its users are, and that is the point.

Organisations have come to depend on it. Mullvad
shut down its own public encrypted DNS service on November 2, 2026
and moved Mullvad Browser users with default settings to Quad9, funding Quad9 instead. (Mullvad Browser users in France will now be migrated to a resolver that disappears three weeks later.) Quad9's announcement lists dozens of French networks it sees traffic from, including the
interministerial digital directorate DINUM, France Travail, CEA, Institut Pasteur, RENATER, EDF, SNCF, AP-HM hospitals in Marseille, France Télévisions, Thales, and Airbus's Stormshield
. Quad9 can't tell any of them it is leaving. As Cloudflare
points out
, when a resolver disappears, users don't see an error message. "Their Internet will simply stop working."

How France got here
​

The law: Article L.333-10 of the Code du sport
​

The legal basis for all of this is
Article L.333-10 of the French sports code
. It was created by
Law 2021-1382 of October 25, 2021
, the same law that merged HADOPI and the CSA into the new regulator
Arcom
. L.333-10 lets a sports rightsholder go to the president of the Paris judicial court and obtain "dynamic" blocking orders, meaning orders that cover sites already identified plus new mirror domains notified later through Arcom, against "toute personne susceptible de contribuer à y remédier" (any person able to help stop the infringement).

That last phrase is what puts DNS resolvers in scope. In
July 2026
, Parliament passed
Law 2026-725 on professional sport
, which amended L.333-10 and added an automated real-time blocking system run by Arcom. TorrentFreak
reported
that under the new system "ARCOM's agents no longer approve each block in advance." Quad9 called it "recklessly dangerous."

The cases: from ISPs to everyone
​

The timeline shows how the circle of targets has widened:

Date
What happened
Dec 2023
Canal+
sues Cloudflare, Google and Cisco
under L.333-10 to force DNS blocking of football piracy sites.
May–Jun 2024
The Paris court
orders the three resolvers to block ~117 domains
. Google complies. Cisco
pulls OpenDNS out of France
on June 28, 2024, citing a court order "issued under Article L.333-10 of the French Sport code" (
archived notice
).
Sep–Oct 2024
New orders expand blocking
by Google and Cloudflare.
Dec 2024
Canal+ wins
three orders against Quad9 and Vercara
(Premier League, Champions League, Top 14 rugby). Because it can't geolocate users, Quad9
blocks the domains for the whole world
: "we have to block these sites for all users, in all areas."
May 2025
A beIN request against Google, Cloudflare and Quad9 is
rejected for lack of evidence
. Quad9 didn't defend that case at all, citing lack of resources.
Mar 2026
The Paris Court of Appeal
rejects five appeals by Google, Cloudflare and Cisco
(RG 24/09372), the first appellate approval of DNS blocking under L.333-10: "Any filtering measure can be circumvented, and this possibility does not render the measures in question ineffective." The same month, the court issues
simultaneous orders against 19 ISPs, Google, Cloudflare, Quad9 and VPN providers
.
Apr 2026
Canal+ obtains orders against
Whalebone's EU-funded DNS4EU resolver
, which complies by blocking "globally across our resolver tiers."
May 13, 2026
beIN Sports obtains an order (RG 26/02207) requiring Quad9 to block IPTV sites showing the
WTA women's tennis tour
until the season ends on November 14. It
starts with 6 domains and grows to 58
via Arcom notifications.
Jul 2026
14 new Canal+ orders
for the 2026/27 season target ISPs, Google, Quad9, DNS4EU, Cloudflare, VPNs, and Bing.
Oct 7, 2026
The court
refuses penalties against Cloudflare, NordVPN and Surfshark
because each had made some effort to block. Cloudflare
kept 1.1.1.1 out of it
by acting through its CDN instead.
Oct 21, 2026
The court
imposes a €1,000/day penalty on Quad9
(RG 26/11882).
Oct 22, 2026
Quad9
announces it will leave France
on November 24.

The ruling itself
​

The
21 October judgment
is short and worth reading. A few details matter:

The €580,000 figure was beIN's request, not the penalty.
beIN asked for €10,000 per day
per domain
still reachable; across 58 domains that is €580,000 a day. The judge set €1,000 a day in total, running until the end of the WTA season on November 14.

The judge used Quad9's malware filtering against it.
Quad9 argued it could not implement geolocated blocking. The court (para. 16) replied that Quad9 "appears to contradict itself" because it already "applies automated filtering strictly limited to cybersecurity to neutralise malicious domains on a global scale." The fact that a resolver can drop a name for everyone was treated as proof it can drop a name for France.

Refusing to try was enough.
Paragraph 18: "Bound by an obligation of means, the Quad9 foundation states that it implements none in order to execute the decision. This circumstance alone justifies the imposition of a penalty."

€1,000 a day for three weeks is survivable, about €24,000. Twenty more cases like it, each running for a full football season with ever-growing domain lists and Arcom's new automated system feeding them, is not. Quad9
says
: "Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases."

Why Quad9 can't just comply
​

Quad9 is often asked why it doesn't just block the domains. It has three options, and none of them work.

1. Block globally.
This is what Quad9 did for Canal+ in December 2024 and what DNS4EU does today. It means a French court decides what a user in Brazil, Kenya or Germany can resolve, for the commercial benefit of one company. Quad9's
announcement
asks how France would react if other nations imposed their laws on French users through DNS. The answer is obvious, and the reverse should be too. Nothing limits this to sports either: once global blocking is accepted, every court in every country can add names to everyone's resolver.

2. Geo-block France.
Quad9 has already tried this, in Germany. In the
Sony Music v. Quad9 case
, Quad9 used geoIP blocking for German users while the case continued. Sony's lawyers used a VPN to reach the content "from Germany" anyway, the court agreed this was non-compliance, and Quad9 was fined for contempt. GeoIP is a probabilistic guess about where an IP address is, not a legal fact about where a person is. A resolver that keeps no user records has no reliable way to define a "French user." As Quad9
told TorrentFreak
: "There is no legally useful way for us to define a French user." Even the French order is geographically complicated:
heise notes
it covers the overseas departments and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon but excludes New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and French Polynesia.

3. Pay and fight.
Quad9 won in Germany. The
Dresden Higher Regional Court
held in December 2023 that DNS resolvers get the same liability privilege as access providers, and the German civil rights group GFF said "the judgement puts the onus on rights holders." But winning took "several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time," and the opposition, in Quad9's words, "has more lawyers than we have money and time." As Quad9
wrote in 2025
, compliance costs that are routine overhead for Google are, "for small, mission-driven nonprofits like Quad9, … an existential threat."

That leaves leaving.

Why DNS blocking doesn't work
​

The argument against resolver blocking isn't only about Quad9's survival. Even on its own terms, it does not do what the rightsholders want.

It doesn't remove anything.
The DNS only holds pointers. Quad9's
Dresden write-up
puts it this way: "The DNS does not contain content - it is a system designed for delivery only of pointers." The pirate server stays online and keeps serving everyone who reaches it some other way. The Internet Society's
2025 guide for legal professionals
says the same thing.

It takes seconds to bypass.
Quad9 notes there are
thousands of other open resolvers
. Users can also run their own, or use encrypted DNS over HTTPS (
RFC 8484
), which looks like ordinary web traffic. Arcom's own
December 2025 study for the National Assembly
says 20% of French internet users already use an alternative DNS resolver and 29% use a VPN. Quad9 compares DNS blocking to "holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert."

It is blunt.
DNS works at the level of whole domains. A resolver can't block one infringing stream on a shared host without blocking everything else on that name. The IAB's
RFC 7754
, the IETF's standard reference on blocking and filtering, says: "From a technical perspective, there are no perfect or even good solutions -- there is only least bad." ICANN's security committee revisited the question in
SAC127, "DNS Blocking Revisited"
(2025), warning implementers to minimise overblocking and avoid affecting users outside their jurisdiction. France's own registry operator, AFNIC, made the core point years ago in its scientific council's report on
the consequences of DNS filtering
: "Le DNS n'a pas été conçu pour filtrer les contenus." (The DNS was not designed to filter content.)

It is opaque.
When a resolver is forced to lie, the user sees a site that doesn't load. They have no way to tell whether the site is down, their network is broken, or a court ordered the block. There is a standard for being honest about this:
RFC 8914 Extended DNS Errors
defines code 16, "Censored", for answers withheld "due to an external requirement imposed by an entity other than the operator." But nothing in the French orders requires resolvers to use it.

Blocking at scale causes real collateral damage.
France is not the only test case. Italy's Piracy Shield system
blocked Google Drive for much of the country in October 2024
. A
RIPE Labs study
of Piracy Shield found more than 500 unrelated sites blocked and concluded that "IP-level blocking is an indiscriminate tool with consequences that outweigh its benefits." In Spain, LaLiga's IP blocking of shared Cloudflare addresses knocked innocent sites offline every match day, leading Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince to call the approach
"bonkers"
. The same RIPE study found most European piracy is hosted
in Europe
, which is where enforcement belongs: at the hosting provider.

Measured by its own goals, the French system has a mixed record. Arcom
reports
12,606 sports domains blocked since 2022, 6,496 of them in 2025 alone (up 71%), while piracy fell 4% in 2025 and 34% since 2021. The number of blocks is growing much faster than piracy is shrinking, and Arcom's figures don't separate the effect of resolver blocking from ISP blocking. Every one of those domains has to be found, blocked, and then found again when it reappears under a new name. OONI's
2025 measurement of French ISP blocking
found that of 542 domains tested, 291 were blocked by at least one ISP but only 132 by all four. The European Commission's own
2025 assessment
of its live-events piracy
recommendation
concluded the effects "have been limited and have not allowed to significantly curb the volume of online piracy of live events."

What France loses
​

Driving Quad9 out of France doesn't hurt pirates at all. The people who lose are the ones who chose a resolver for security.

French users lose a malware filter.
Quad9 exists to stop people resolving phishing and malware domains. Users who move to an unfiltered resolver, or to their ISP's resolver, lose that protection. Users who move to an unknown free resolver may be
trading it for one that sells their browsing data
. As Cloudflare puts it, "Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web."

Critical infrastructure may break silently.
Hospitals, utilities and local authorities on Quad9's list will lose DNS if their IT teams miss the announcement. Embedded devices with 9.9.9.9 hard-coded may be hard to fix.

The choice of resolvers shrinks.
OpenDNS left France in 2024, and Quad9 leaves now. An Internet Society report
cited by TorrentFreak
warned that small and non-profit resolvers are the most likely to be pushed out, leaving the field to the largest companies, which can afford to fight or to build per-country infrastructure. Cloudflare can satisfy the court by blocking at its CDN; Quad9 has only a resolver.

France's own digital sovereignty goals suffer.
France promotes privacy-respecting European infrastructure, yet its courts are driving out a Swiss privacy-focused non-profit while US giants remain.

It's not just France
​

Quad9 is the clearest casualty so far, but the same process is underway across Europe.

Belgium:
DAZN obtained an order against Cloudflare, Google and Cisco in March 2025, and
OpenDNS left Belgium
in April 2025 before returning when the order against Cisco was suspended. In August 2026, the Brussels business court
upheld the core of the order
, with fines of €100,000 per match day capped at €20 million per company. Cisco says its public DNS "does not allow for the implementation of selective, geolocated and dynamic blocking as required by the order." Cloudflare, Google and Cisco have
appealed
ahead of the January 2027 deadline.

Italy:
AGCOM
fined Cloudflare €14.2 million
in January 2026, 1% of its global revenue, for not blocking via 1.1.1.1. Prince threatened to pull servers and free services from Italy: "Play stupid games, win stupid prizes."

Spain:
A Barcelona court
upheld LaLiga's right
to block Cloudflare IP addresses.

Germany
is the counter-example. Courts there rejected resolver blocking for both
Quad9
and
Cloudflare
.

The EU level:
A study commissioned by the European Parliament's legal affairs committee
proposes a binding regulation
that would require blocking within 30 minutes across DNS resolvers, VPNs and CDNs. John Todd's
warning on Hacker News
is that "the EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region."

That is why France matters beyond France. If its model becomes the EU template, every public resolver in Europe will face the choice Quad9 faced: lie to all users worldwide, build unreliable geolocation infrastructure, or leave.

The counter-arguments
​

The Hacker News discussion wasn't one-sided, and the counter-arguments deserve answers.

"Hosting providers are unreachable, so courts move up the chain."

One commenter
argued that pirate hosts are bulletproof and ignore courts, so going after the intermediaries is the only lever left.
Another
asked the Quad9 CTO directly where the problem
should
be attacked. This is the strongest point. But the RIPE data shows most of the hosting is in Europe and within reach of European courts, and the commenter's logic leads to blocking at the last link in the chain that cannot fight back. That is not the same as the link that can actually stop the infringement.

"Friction works. Most people won't bother to switch."

Some argued
that DNS blocking is good
because
it nudges the majority while staying easy to bypass for those who know how. The Paris Court of Appeal used essentially this reasoning. But Arcom's numbers say a fifth of French users already use alternative DNS, the friction is gone the moment one person changes a router setting for a household, and the cost is paid by resolvers that never had anything to do with piracy.

"Cloudflare is a hypocrite."

Several commenters
pointed out that Cloudflare's CDN fronts many pirate sites. That may be true, and it is an argument about Cloudflare's CDN, which French courts can already reach and have. It says nothing about whether a resolver should lie.

"The yellow pages would be held responsible."

One commenter
asked whether we'd accept a phone directory that kept listing a drug dealer's new address. The analogy fails because a resolver is not a curated directory. It's closer to the operator who connects you to whatever number you dial. Quad9 has "no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites." Making the operator liable for every number dialled is how you end up with no operator.

What you can do
​

If you use Quad9 in France
, check whether you do at
on.quad9.net
, and switch resolvers before November 24. Check routers, VPN configs, DHCP settings, Pi-hole upstreams, and any devices with 9.9.9.9 or 149.112.112.112 hard-coded. Whatever you switch to, read its privacy policy first.

If you're in France or the EU
, do what John Todd asked:
write something long-form
, ideally in French, make it indexable, and send it to your representatives. Quad9 specifically suggests telling
Arcom
that its mandate is to balance rightsholders' interests against citizens' digital rights, and that "balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage."

If you work on infrastructure
, push for transparency wherever blocking does happen. RFC 8914's "Censored" error code exists so users can tell a court-ordered block from a broken network.

If you can afford it
, Quad9 accepts
donations
for its legal defence. Its appeal against the May order is still pending at the Paris Court of Appeal.

The canary
​

Quad9
put it this way
: "Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly." The French system started with football. It now covers tennis, rugby, MotoGP and Formula 1, has expanded from ISPs to resolvers, VPNs, CDNs and search engines, and runs through an automated system in which no human approves each block. Each step was reasonable on its own. Together, they have pushed a non-profit security service out of the country while the piracy continues.

The sports-rights industry has a real problem. DNS resolvers are the wrong place to solve it, and France is about to find out what the internet looks like when the trustworthy resolvers leave first.

title: The Magic of Partial Evaluation
content:
There are certain ideas in software that are simply beautiful. It doesn't matter if they have any practical use. It doesn't matter that you will never convince your coworkers to consider them. There is just something captivating about the way some computational systems work.

For me, the most beautiful pieces of software are those that reveal something about the nature of programming languages. Programming languages are my obsession. I have never met a problem that couldn't be solved by introducing yet another programming language. Solving a problem at the programming language level is about solving the meta problem. Instead of trying to solve a particular problem, we take a step back and ask how we can solve a whole class of problems at once.

So when I find something that makes me rethink the nature of programming languages, I start rethinking computation as a whole. One of these incredibly beautiful but tricky concepts goes by the name partial evaluation. If you are fascinated by interpreters and compilers, partial evaluation will teach you how they are related, and how you can get a compiler for free.

Partial Evaluation Easy Mode
#

Partial evaluation has been a fascination of mine for a while. But this whole thing came up when
James Long announced he had revived
Meta's partial evaluator for JavaScript called prepack. When I first heard about prepack, I had some high hopes and expectations for the project, but was sadly let down. This revival brought to light those same dreams. But sadly, just as with the original aim, prepack was not designed for beauty, but for practicality. So I figured it was time to renew my own efforts.

Yes, in some ways this is a post repping my own library I'm releasing. But I'm not doing this because I want it to be used. I'm doing this because it lets you play with the idea I find so beautiful. That is what this post is about.

Doing Partial Evaluation by Hand
#

Consider the following code:

function

factorial
(
n
)

{

if

(
n
<=

1
)

return

1
;

return
n
*

factorial
(
n
-

1
)
;

}

factorial
(
5
)
;

As a person who reads code, you can think about how this code computes and what answer it will give. But you can do more than just give the answer. You can see the expanded form of this particular code for these particular calls. This code is spiritually the same as the following expression, once we expand it out.

5

*

(
4

*

(
3

*

(
2

*

1
)
)
)

In this case, there is really nothing at all that this code needs to do at runtime. A sufficiently smart compiler will just run this code directly at compile time and give the answer. But this is a bit less clear if things come in at runtime.

function

power
(
base
,
exponent
)

{

if

(
exponent
===

0
)

return

1
;

return
base
*

power
(
base
,
exponent
-

1
)
;

}

power
(
process
.
argv
[
2
]
,

5
)

It might seem like we can't do anything here, but again, if you are used to thinking about how programs run, you can trace this out and realize this is just the same as:

process
.
argv
[
2
]

*

(
process
.
argv
[
2
]

*

(
process
.
argv
[
2
]

*

(
process
.
argv
[
2
]

*

(
process
.
argv
[
2
]

*

1
)
)
)
)

What we have done in both of these cases is called partial evaluation. In the first, it was a trivial case because everything was statically known. But in this latter case, we have reduced a program down into the essentials of its dynamic structure. There are no recursive function calls left. All of this has been expanded as far as it could till we get just the dynamic parts of the code remaining.

The Big Idea
#

This intuitive notion of partial evaluation is all you need to know to appreciate the beauty here. Partial evaluation just evaluates the part of the program we can evaluate at build time and leaves all the rest. When we do this with certain programs in certain combinations, we get some quite surprising, incredible behavior.

function

calculate
(
expr
)

{

if

(
typeof
expr
===

"number"
)

return
expr
;

switch

(
expr
[
0
]
)

{

case

"+"
:

return

calculate
(
expr
[
1
]
)

+

calculate
(
expr
[
2
]
)
;

case

"-"
:

return

calculate
(
expr
[
1
]
)

-

calculate
(

[
2
]
)
;

case

"*"
:

return

calculate
(
expr
[
1
]
)

*

calculate
(
expr
[
2
]
)
;

case

"/"
:

return

calculate
(
expr
[
1
]
)

/

calculate
(
expr
[
2
]
)
;

default
:

throw

new

Error
(
"Unknown operator"
)
;

}

}

calculate
(
[
"+"
,

1
,

[
"*"
,

2
,

3
]
]
)
;

Here we have a very simple interpreter for a language that just supports arithmetic. For the above expression, you should be able to think about how we could start "partially" evaluating it. (In this case, it can be a full evaluation.) If this kind of partial evaluation isn't quite clicking for you, I've put the steps below to hopefully help it make sense.

calculate
(
[
"+"
,

This is a simple evaluation of the code.  But what happens if we throw a value we don't know into the expression?

Here we can see that clear partial evaluation difference. We don't know how to evaluate
Number(process.argv[2])
. We have no idea what the answer to that will be. But as part of this process, we do know some partial information about it. For example, when we get to

if

(
typeof
expr
===

"number"
)

return
expr
;

we know that
Number(process.argv[2])
is indeed a number. So we can partially evaluate it further. Hopefully this is all making sense. But if you are like me, this all might seem a bit trivial and uninteresting. So let's look at a more complicated example.

The Projections
#

What we've discovered here is the first of three so-called Futamura Projections. Our partial evaluator, when applied to an interpreter and given a program, can give us a compiled version of that program. Or to put it in pseudocode.

partial_eval(interpreter, prog) -> compiled_prog

In the age of AI, perhaps less so, but I think even then many things still hold. It is quite easy to instrument an interpreter, quite a bit harder to do so for a compiler. Changing an interpreter to support new features is quite easy, less so for a compiler. Or hand-write a compiler for these schemas. But what about those schemas that exist only at runtime? Now we either need to compile those on the fly, or we have to keep both a compiler and interpreter. Having a way to partial eval lowers this burden quite a bit.

But if the Futamura projections stopped here, they would be exciting, but not quite the craziness they are. We can think of partial evaluation as a process of "specializing" a program.

Specializing the Specializer
#

Partial evaluation is a form of specialization that figures out what it should specialize on based on what input is static and what is dynamic. In many ways, a partial evaluator is a generic specializer. Given any program, we can make a specialized version of it for any input. What happens if we specialize an interpreter for a given input? We get back that interpreter for only exactly that one program. But what do we need then? Do we need all this generic dispatch? No, we know the full program. We don't need any operations we don't actually use. We can fully get rid of all the generic interpreter mechanism.

But if the specializer can specialize any program, can it specialize itself?

This leads us to the second Futamura projection. Put in our pseudo-code format, we get:

Or, to put it in our specializer language, what if we make a special version of our generic specializer? What is it specialized for? A particular interpreter. Now we have a function that, given any program, will spit out newly specialized interpreters just for that program. Or, in Java speak, we have a specialized interpreter factory.

The Third Projection
#

But we can't stop at the second projection. We have to push on and get to the final mind-bending projection. If you apply our specializer to itself as input, you get a compiler generator.

partial_eval
,
partial_eval

-
>

So now we have a generic function that will spit out compilers for any interpreter we give it!

Playing With It
#

I
have implemented
a reasonable, but still very limited partial evaluator for JavaScript in Rust. I have taken it further to try to make it work quite well for a number of different interpreters and interpreter-like programs in JavaScript. I've also tried to get limited versions of the second and third projections working. Go play with it, see what works, what doesn't, file issues, or better, use some of your tokens to help me make more cases work.

But most of all, explore. This is such a rich space. Below are some papers, blogs, and projects about partial evaluation in some way, shape, or form. There has never been a better time to play with these kinds of crazy techniques for programming languages. Don't let what is practical stop you from exploring the cool, interesting aspects of programming.

weval: the WebAssembly partial evaluator

A First Futamura Projection — Veit Heller

Partial Evaluation in Truffle — Graal documentation

Partial Evaluation of Computation Process—An Approach to a Compiler-Compiler — Yoshihiko Futamura (1971, original English translation)

Partial Evaluation and Automatic Program Generation — Neil D. Jones, Carsten K. Gomard, and Peter Sestoft

Tutorial on Online Partial Evaluation — William R. Cook and Ralf Lämmel

For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue.

Discover new Genie 3 capabilities
While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include:
Extended sessions and world chaining:

360-degree panorama image grounding:

Real-time in-world events:
Dynamically change the environment with natural-language prompts while you explore.

Create new interactive experiences

Simply describe your vision in natural language, and the agent orchestrates Google’s suite of multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing your world’s signature look, paired with custom background scores tailored to the mood.
You can also bring Gemini models into the session as you explore: it observes what is happening on screen, surfaces context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or triggers in-world events automatically as your journey unfolds.

When you just want to jump straight into exploring, the new Project Genie gallery brings together a rich collection of curated worlds alongside creative work from the community. title: The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026
content:
What Does It Mean to Be Human in the Age of AI? – Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year 2026

The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026.

The year has been defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines.
'Human' is
defined in the Cambridge Dictionary
as ‘having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines’.
In 2026, many public figures defended humans and humanity in the age of AI. Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation, made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines, in a
widely read essay
.
Commenting on the selection of ‘human’ as Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, he said: “AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human. It could help us cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most.
"But we need to make deliberate choices about how it fits into our lives, including where we want people to remain at the center. The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”
‘AI godfather’ and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton has
warned
that “we’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans.” And in his
Magnifica Humanitas
letter, Pope Leo XIV spoke of new forms of “dehumanization” and the “pressing duty to remain profoundly human”.
Actors Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, musicians Tayla Parx, LeAnn Rimes and Billie Eilish, and authors Jodi Picoult and Jonathan Franzen challenged an "assault on human creativity" as the
Human Artistry Campaign
and
Artist Rights Alliance
opposed machine-generated replicas and theft of human-generated content by large language models (LLMs).
Meanwhile, Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir has
wondered
whether he "might be among the last generation of fully human writers". The Authors Guild has launched a
‘Human Authored’ kitemark
for books, supported by Professor Dame Mary Beard and Malorie Blackman.
As AI deepfakes simulated humans, Matthew McConaughey became the first Hollywood actor to
pre-emptively protect himself against unauthorised digital reproduction
by trademarking clips of his voice, his face and even his catchphrase ‘alright, alright, alright’.  Taylor Swift followed suit,
trademarking her voice and image
in April.
Professor Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common.
“AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There’s a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them."
Dr Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge, said: “I think ‘human’ is a really interesting choice because right now our understanding of humanity is changing.
“We're trying to understand the difference between a human mind and an artificial mind, between living beings like us and artificial beings that we're creating. What sets us apart, is it consciousness, creativity or compassion?
“All the rhetoric around AI is about what's inevitably going to happen. But to young people growing up in an AI-enabled world, my advice would be that nothing is inevitable. What happens in the future of AI is up to us. It's up to you."
Lexicographer Colin McIntosh of the Cambridge Dictionary said: “AI is changing how we talk about being human. It’s this renewed interest in the idea of being human that captured the zeitgeist and made ‘human’ the Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year.”
Adapted from the
Cambridge University Press & Assessment website
.

, and on a

title: Google Gemini's "Tasks" Personal Assistant Is Now Free
content:
Put Gemini to work for you

Nov 17, 2026

|

Gemini can now make the calls, pay the bills, and finish your tasks.

Josh Woodward

Vice President, Labs, Gemini app, and AI Studio

Your browser does not support the audio element.

Listen to article

[[duration]] minutes

This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental

We’re updating Gemini to handle complex tasks like scheduling appointments, managing bills, and shopping for groceries. By connecting to your emails, calendar, and payment methods, Gemini saves you time while keeping your data secure in isolated environments. You can try these new capabilities today by switching the toggle from Chat to Task in the Gemini app, texting us on Android or iOS, or forwarding emails to gemini@google.com.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

Josh Woodward, Vice President of Labs, announces that Gemini can now manage daily tasks for you.

You can use Gemini to schedule appointments, analyze utility bills, and purchase items through integrated services.

Gemini operates within secure, hardware-isolated virtual machines to protect your private data and account information.

You can access these new features by toggling the task mode in the Gemini mobile application.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

Josh Woodward, Vice President of Labs, Gemini app, and AI Studio, explains that Gemini can now handle daily tasks like scheduling appointments, managing grocery lists, and analyzing bills. By connecting to your Google apps, it securely completes chores using your existing information. You can activate these features by switching your Gemini app to task mode, texting, or forwarding emails. This update helps you save time by managing your calendar, shopping, and household organization.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

Explore other styles:

The best assistant knows you and helps you get things done. Today, you can now hand off even more tasks to Gemini and move on with your day. We’ve built it for anyone who has tasks piling up during all the classes, meetings, and school drop-offs that fill the day. Our goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.
Starting now, this update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, using our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. We’re also rolling out a set of advanced features, starting in the U.S.
How it’s changing my daily routine
If your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards are already in the Google ecosystem, Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because this sensitive data already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.
Here’s how I’m using it.
Recently, our minivan’s check-engine light came on. Ugh. I pulled out Gemini and told it, "Our minivan is overdue for a service appointment. Please call the two nearest dealerships and figure out how to get an appointment early Friday morning over the next month or so."
Because Gemini already knows we drive a 2019 Honda Odyssey and where we live through
Personal Intelligence
, it found the nearest shops on Google Maps and called both at once

1

. Thankfully, I didn’t have to suffer through any hold music. Gemini did the job, found a time in my Google Calendar when I was free, and added the Friday early morning appointment in less than five minutes. Done. (On the dealership's end, Gemini disclosed right away that it's an AI. Businesses can
opt out
whenever they want, and Gemini won’t give out my payment or private account info unless I say so.)

In the background, Gemini called both dealerships at once, sat through the hold music for me, booked an appointment at the shop that accepts appointments vs. walk-ins only, and put Friday's appointment on my calendar without me having to check it.

Last month it saved us real money after we got hit with a surprise $389 electric bill. I gave Gemini permission to access our utility portal with the new Google Password Manager integration and asked for it to analyze our past billing statements in my email. Gemini worked for a few minutes, and then nailed it. The primary culprit was our heat pump, which it turns out was kicking on around 4 p.m., right in the middle of peak pricing. My wife and I never would have caught that digging through the PDFs and emails ourselves.
I use it for smaller stuff, too. For our upcoming holiday trip back to Oklahoma, I recently asked Gemini to give me the best options for a USB-C charger. Gemini quickly compared chargers thanks to Google’s Shopping Graph, asked me follow-up questions about the wattage and color, and then helped me check out using the new Google Pay integration. The best part: it also found a discount code so I saved an extra $10. Done.
Gemini now uses the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) to make purchases like this. We’re working with American Express (coming soon), Mastercard, and Visa to keep your purchases secure with digital tokens on supported cards. And when you shop with Gemini, you still earn your card's points, cashback, or purchase protections during checkout. You can also set a hard spending cap upfront, and Gemini is designed to stay within your budget. All of your receipts and tracking info land straight in Google Wallet, which is expanding to iOS
starting today
. Up next, we’ll integrate the
Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP)
into Gemini so everyone can expect an even faster and more reliable shopping experience from discovery to checkout.

Gemini lets you set the spending limit and still earn every airline mile, cashback point, and perk on your card.

Gemini helps with weeknight dinners, too. I recently stared down a nearly empty fridge rushing out the door in the morning, and I texted Gemini with the new RCS integration

2

: “Add lasagna, strawberries, cucumbers, and vanilla ice cream to our Instacart order.” On the walk out, I saw an empty Cheerios box in the pantry, so I snapped a photo and sent a quick follow-up: “Add this too.” Gemini added it, and then handed me off to Instacart to complete the order. Groceries were on the doorstep when we got home. Done. Today, Gemini connects with more than 60 popular apps and, as a developer, you can apply to join our
Connected Apps Platform
.
My wife and I also use Gemini to sort out medical bills, keep track of insurance renewals, and stay on top of our kids' schedules. Earlier this week, I forwarded a batch of school emails from Gmail to gemini@google.com. In less than a minute, every date was on my calendar with my wife invited. Better yet, it noticed a conflict during basketball practice and asked if I wanted to text one of the other parents to trade carpool duty.

How we protect your data
As Gemini becomes more capable, we continually advance our security defenses. When you assign Gemini a task, it uses
Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine
to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users. Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams. This sandbox is just one of multiple layers of defense, including prompt-injection filters that scan search results, webpages, and more alongside Google Safe Browsing to limit which links Gemini can open.
As Gemini works on a task, you can jump in to give it more instructions at any point, and it’s also designed to pause and check with you before critical steps. For example, Gemini is designed to ask for your confirmation or pre-approval before clicking "Buy," and will ask clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous. For routine stuff you already trust, like adding those Cheerios to your grocery cart, you can set that to “Always allow” so it doesn’t pester you.
And finally, we give you access to settings and tools that help you safeguard your data and protect your privacy. You can adjust task settings, disconnect Google and third-party apps, or delete chat history anytime. For a closer look at how we’ve implemented a multi-layer defense-in-depth security strategy, read our
technical paper
.
And please participate in our bug bounty program through Google’s
AI Vulnerability Reward Program (AI VRP)
to advance the security of agentic systems.
How you can help us improve
While we’ve tested tasks extensively to minimize mistakes, we haven't eliminated all of them. You may encounter situations where a task fails to complete or misses the mark. When you see this, please provide feedback by giving the response a “thumbs down.”
For example, the way personal assistants navigate the web is still evolving as sites are still adapting to these new use cases. On some sites, Gemini can make it most of the way through and then hand the screen back to you to click the final button. We’re partnering directly with major websites and security providers to help the web evolve so it works well for site owners and personal assistants. For decades, bots were blocked by default because most were malicious. Personal assistants require a more nuanced approach, and we believe open, verifiable standards will benefit everyone.
How to try it
Ready to hand off your next task? Open Gemini, flip the home-screen toggle from Chat to Task, and tell Gemini what you need done. Starting in the U.S., you can also forward emails to
gemini@google.com
or text Gemini by following these instructions:

title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
content:
Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN:
https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073
. It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races.
Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself.
At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans.
There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack.
Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc).
When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI.
We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead.
You can get started with `npm create factory`.
It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!
https://factory.mastra.ai
https://github.com/mastra-ai/template-factory
