title: The First Revolver: How We Got from Blackbeard's Six Pistols to the Six-Shooter
content:
The First Revolver:
How We Got From Blackbeard's Six Pistols to the Six-Shooter

Written By
Tom McHale

Handguns

Revolvers

2026

Back in 1718, the most feared man on the Atlantic had a bit of a firepower problem. He solved it according to conventional wisdom: he carried more guns.

According to Captain Charles Johnson’s
A General History of the Pyrates
, Blackbeard prepared for a fight by donning “a Sling over his Shoulders, with three brace of Pistols, hanging in Holsters like Bandaliers.” Three brace is six pistols. Of course, he carried a cutlass as well, but one has to question his mobility with all that gear.

Flintlock pistols were one-and-done affairs when they ignited. You know the black powder muzzle-loader drill. Pour powder down the barrel, ram a patched ball on top, prime the pan, close the frizzen, cock it, and pray the flint sparks and the powder is dry when you most need the thing to work. “At the range” one could do it in 20 or 30 seconds. In the middle of a battle at sea, not so much. If you wanted more shots, you brought more pre-loaded guns.

Here’s what makes the story interesting: there actually was a “fix” for Blackbeard’s problem that had been on the scene for more than a century. It just wasn’t very reliable.

Really Old Revolvers

The idea of a rotating cylinder full of pre-loaded chambers is surprisingly old. German gunsmiths in Nuremberg were building revolving matchlocks around 1580. In 1597, a Nuremberg maker named Hans Stopler built an eight-shot revolving snaphance. It’s still in a museum in Lillehammer, Norway. By the 1660s, a London gunmaker, history implies it was John Dafte, was turning out a six-shot snaphance revolver whose cylinder turned itself when you cocked it. The Royal Armouries still has one.

So why was Blackbeard still carrying a bandolier of single-shots?

Because these guns were handcrafted works of part art and part technology. Every part was hand-filed and hand-fitted. Each chamber usually needed its own priming arrangement, and loose powder near a bunch of loaded chambers is how you generate lots of undesirable excitement. The bottom line: they were expensive curiosities for rich folks, not reliable and affordable tools.

So we had the idea in concept, and it was solid. Note that we still rely on the same general plan today. The problem was with the ignition system. And that remained in the “problems to be solved someday” bucket for a long time.

A Nuremberg revolving matchlock from around 1580. The idea is more than

four centuries old. Photo: Bullenwächter / Germanisches Nationalmuseum, via Wikimedia Commons

Wait, a Lawyer Built a "Machine" Gun?

The path to that snubbie revolver in your pocket is a long and winding road.

On May 15, 1718, the same year Blackbeard was killed at Ocracoke, a London lawyer and writer named James Puckle received British Patent No. 418 for something he called the “Defence.” It was not a handgun. It was a tripod-mounted flintlock with a 1.25-inch bore. If I’m doing my math right, that’s a bit over 30mm, the bore size used on the massive gun of A-10 Warthog tank-buster planes. Of course, the ballistics are far different, but the diameter of the “bullet” was similar.

The interesting thing in the context of this story is that it relied on the same idea that all subsequent revolvers used.

Puckle’s gun had a single barrel fed by a rotating cylinder. The cylinders held anywhere from six to eleven chambers, depending on the version. The gunner turned a crank to index a loaded chamber to the barrel, fired it, and cranked to the next. When a cylinder ran dry, you replaced it with a new, preloaded one.

Puckle also had opinions. His patent drawings show two types of ammunition: round bullets for use against Christians, and square bullets for use against the Turks. Square bullets were supposed to do more damage. Ballistically, I’ll let you draw your own conclusions.

Did it work? You be the judge. In a 1722 demonstration, the gun fired 63 shots in seven minutes. A skilled infantryman might manage three shots per minute with his musket. Did I mention it was pouring rain at the time? That was normally a recipe for failure with traditional muskets.

Apparently the British Board of Ordnance wasn’t impressed as they didn’t buy it. The Puckle gun became somewhat of a joke, with leaflets claiming it was a fearsome weapon because “they’re only wounded who hold shares therein.” The Duke of Montagu did buy two for a 1722 expedition to St. Lucia and St. Vincent, and the manifest lists “2 Machine Guns of Puckles.” Original examples survive in the Montagu family collections at Boughton House and Beaulieu in England.

OK, so it wasn’t technically a “machine” gun, but remember, we’re talking early 1700s here. The important takeaway is that people were thinking about multiple-shot systems driven by revolving cylinders a very long time ago.

Puckle's "Machine" as it appeared on a 1720 satirical playing card mocking

the investment bubbles of the day. Thomas Bowles, 1720, public domain.

Americans Carry the Torch

In June 1818, Artemus Wheeler of Concord, Massachusetts, received a U.S. patent for a flintlock revolver. Bostonian Elisha Collier took the design, improved it, and patented his improved version in England later that year.

Collier’s revolver had striking similarities to more modern wheelguns. Although still a flintlock, the priming pan refilled itself from a magazine each time you closed the frizzen, and the cylinder pushed forward to seal against the barrel. He sold hundreds of them between 1819 and 1824, mostly in Britain. Officers headed to India for deployment bought them personally. to India bought them privately.

Elisha Collier's revolving flintlock, patented in England in 1818. Image: Met Museum accession 56.165.

Percussion Caps: The Bang Heard Around the World

Remember how the ignition system was holding up the show? Well, the solution arrived via a Scottish, duck-hunting clergyman. Reverend Alexander Forsyth patented a lock in 1807 that used a pinch of shock-sensitive fulminate instead of a flint and pan. A few years later, the copper percussion cap arrived, according to most accounts, by inventor Joshua Shaw.

Eureka! Now chambers were self-contained firing mechanisms. No flints or loose powder required for ignition.

One adopter of the percussion era was the pepperbox, a cluster of barrels that rotated as you pulled the trigger. Seems like a step backward from earlier systems where the rotating “magazine” shared one barrel, but Ethan Allen patented his famous version in 1837. Yes, they were heavy and didn’t impress many with accuracy. Mark Twain described a fellow stagecoach passenger’s Allen pepperbox in
Roughing It
and noted that sometimes all six barrels went off at once, “and then there was no safe place in all the region round about, but behind it.”

A cased English percussion pepperbox. Six barrels, no sights, and a reputation to match.

Smithsonian National Museum of American History, public domain.

The Inspiration of a Sailor Named Colt

In 1830, a 16-year-old Connecticut kid named Samuel Colt shipped out as a sailor on the brig
Corvo
, bound for Calcutta from Boston. According to the stories, he noticed how the ship’s capstans and windlasses worked. They turn and lock in place with a pawl. At some point, he whittled a wooden model of a revolving pistol.

To be clear, Samuel Colt didn’t invent the revolver. Rather, he worked out the mechanism that rotates the cylinder and locks it in the right place, aligned with the barrel. No more handmade mechanisms with a production run of one. These could be manufactured with machines.

He patented it in England in 1835 and in the United States on February 25, 1836. That same year, he set up the Patent Arms Manufacturing Company in Paterson, New Jersey, to build the five-shot Paterson revolver.

Strangely, the Army wasn’t interested, and the company folded in 1843 after making only a few thousand guns.

Enter the Texans. On June 8, 1844, Texas Ranger Captain Jack Hays and about 15 to maybe 20 men, armed with some of those Paterson Colts, met a 75-man Comanche war party near the Pedernales River. The lesson of the day was that the Rangers could keep shooting after they’d emptied their rifles. When it was over, the Rangers suffered one killed and four wounded while the Comanche lost 20 or more. This new revolver had made a mark.

Samuel Colt's 1836 U.S. patent drawing. Image: Public domain.

Mr. Walker's Big Gun

One of the Rangers who appreciated the Paterson revolver was Captain Samuel Walker. In 1846, with war against Mexico underway, he worked with Colt on a heavier, tougher revolver. The Paterson’s folding trigger and five-shot cylinder went away.

The result was the 1847 Walker Colt: six shots, .44 caliber, 4 1/2 pounds, and a chamber that held 60 grains of black powder. Not exactly a concealable handgun. The Colt factory was gone, so 1,100 Walkers were built at Eli Whitney Jr.’s plant in Whitneyville, Connecticut.

The Walker’s success put Colt back in business, and the Dragoons, the 1851 Navy, and the 1860 Army rolled out.

Walker Colt serial no. 1017, made at Whitneyville in 1847. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0.

Cartridges: More Simplicity

We’ve almost arrived at today’s basic revolver design. That was separating the ignition (percussion caps) from the revolver itself.

Rollin White patented the concept of a bored-through cylinder (allowed by the invention of self-contained cartridges) in 1855. Smith & Wesson licensed it and introduced the Model 1 in 1857, a tiny seven-shot .22 rimfire. It wasn’t exactly a fighting gun, but the writing was on the wall. The patent kept the other companies at bay until 1869. That’s why the Civil War was chock full of cap-and-ball revolvers.

Once the patent expired, the dam broke. In 1873, the U.S. Army adopted the Colt Single Action Army in .45 Colt. You know it as the Peacemaker.

An early "Peacemaker," Colt Single Action Army serial no. 4519, from 1874.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0.

The Execution Was the Hard Part

The ideas behind today’s revolvers date back to the 1500s. It was the technical requirements to make it work that slowed progress. In hindsight, building the actual guns was the easier part. The ignition system was arguably what held up the show.

Be thankful you’re not toting around a flintlock snubbie.

title: The x86 CPU: From 4004 to 486
content:
We already covered the main ideas behind
Real Mode & Protected Mode
in one of our previous posts. This article will build on those concepts and take a deeper look at the history and evolution of the x86 family of CPUs. But rather than simply looking at the innovations introduced with each new chip, we need to understand how the architecture
accumulated over time
, from its origins in the early 70s up until the launch of the 486.
Every time a new student starts learning x86 assembler with us, it's not rare to hear them complain that many aspects of the instruction set look
arbitrary
. An accumulator that some instructions insist on, a
base
register that is the only one allowed to point at memory, a parity flag nobody seems to use, and an addressing scheme that adds two 16-bit numbers together in a very strange way.
The majority of teaching resources out there will help you write your first lines of x86 code, assemble it, link it, and as proceed as soon as the output matches what you were expecting. I try to always explain the evolution of the x86 family of CPUs, so every aspect of our code makes a little bit more sense.
None of these things are arbitrary, of course. Each one is a decision someone made under pressure, usually to keep old software running on a new chip. If you want to
really
understand x86 (and especially if you want to program a 486 under DOS), the best place to start is not the 486 manual. It's the story.
Here is the family tree we're going to walk through:
A table like this makes the evolution look neat and planned. It wasn't. Between these rows there are cancelled projects, a customer who walked away from its own chip, a stopgap that was supposed to last a couple of years, a sales campaign, a keyboard controller wired into the address bus, and a lawsuit.
Let's travel back to 1969 and see how it all happened!
The story starts with a Japanese calculator company. In 1969,
Busicom
asked Intel (then a young memory company) to build a set of custom chips for a new printing calculator. Instead of designing many single-purpose chips, Intel's team proposed something more general: a small programmable processor that would run the calculator's logic from ROM.
The result was the
4004
, released on November 15, 1971, and designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima. It had 2,300 transistors, ran at about 740 kHz, and could address 4 KB of program ROM.
The most important line in the 4004's story is not technical, though. Busicom had paid for the design and owned the rights. When Busicom ran into financial trouble in 1971, Faggin convinced Intel's CEO Bob Noyce to lower the chip's price in exchange for Intel getting out of the exclusivity deal. Intel paid back Busicom's $60,000 development costs and won the right to sell the chip to anyone (outside the calculator market).
That deal is why "a microprocessor" became something Intel could sell, rather than a part buried inside one calculator.
At almost the same time, a second customer walked through Intel's door. In late 1969,
Computer Terminal Corporation
(CTC, later called Datapoint) asked Intel to build a chip for a programmable terminal called the
Datapoint 2200
.
This detail matters a lot:
Intel did not design the instruction set of this chip
. CTC's engineers Victor Poor and Harry Pyle did. They had already built the Datapoint 2200's processor out of dozens of discrete TTL chips, and they wanted Intel to squeeze that same design onto one piece of silicon.
Intel was slow. Texas Instruments also tried to build the chip, but its samples were buggy and rejected. Meanwhile, CTC shipped the Datapoint 2200 in 1970 with its TTL processor anyway, and later moved on to a faster design. In the end, CTC voted to walk away from the project and leave the design to Intel instead of paying the $50,000 contract. Intel renamed it the
8008
and released it in April 1972 with 3,500 transistors and 16 KB of addressable memory.
So the ancestor of every x86 chip was designed by a terminal company, for a terminal, and then rejected by that terminal company. And two of the terminal's habits are still inside your PC today.
The Datapoint 2200 processed numbers one bit at a time (a
bit-serial
design). If you're adding two numbers one bit at a time, you want to start with the lowest bit, because that's where the carry starts. So it made sense to store the lowest byte first in memory.
The 8008 copied the Datapoint's design, the 8080 kept compatibility with the 8008, and the 8086 kept compatibility with the 8080. Stephen Morse, the architect of the 8086, put it this way in his
history of the early Intel processors
:
That's why, on your 486 (and even in a more modern Core i9), this instruction:
...stores the bytes
78 56 34 12
in memory.
The second habit is the
parity flag
(PF), which tells you if the result of the last operation had an even number of 1 bits. It's one of those flags that beginners look at and wonder who on earth needs it.
The answer is: a terminal does! Morse again:
"This permits testing for transmission errors, an obviously useful function for a CRT terminal."
Data arriving over a serial line often carried a parity bit, and the Datapoint needed a fast way to check it.
Fifty years later, PF is still bit 2 of the x86 FLAGS register.
The 8008 was slow and awkward, so Intel designed a much better successor. The
8080
was released in April 1974, with Federico Faggin as its primary architect and Masatoshi Shima on the detailed design. It had about 4,500 transistors, ran at 2 MHz, and could address 64 KB of memory.
The 8080 was
not
binary compatible with the 8008, but it kept the same register set and the same "flavor." More importantly, it added several things you will recognize as an x86 programmer:
That separate I/O space is the reason why, many years later, VGA registers live at "port 3C8h" instead of at a memory address.
The 8080 powered the
Altair 8800
and became the standard CPU for
CP/M
, the most popular operating system for small business computers in the late 70s. Suddenly, there was a lot of 8080 software out there.
And then Intel got some serious competition. Faggin and Shima left Intel and went to
Zilog
, where they built the
Z80
: a chip that could run 8080 machine code, but was faster, cheaper to build a computer around, and had more instructions. The Z80 started eating Intel's market.
Intel's answer was the
8085
, released in March 1976. The "5" in the name refers to its biggest selling point: it needed a single +5 V power supply, while the 8080 needed +5 V, -5 V, and +12 V.
To fit everything into a 40-pin package, the 8085 also
multiplexed
its bus: the same eight pins carried the low byte of the address first, and then the data. Remember this trick, because the 8086 uses it too.
There's a lovely footnote here: the 8085 had 12 new instructions, but Intel made a last-minute decision to document only 2 of them. The reason? To keep things simple for the
next
chip, which was already being designed. That chip was the 8086.
In the mid 70s, Intel's big bet for the future was not the 8086. It was the
iAPX 432
, a very ambitious processor designed with object-oriented programming and high-level languages in mind. The 432 was late, and with the Z80 taking customers away, Intel needed something to sell in the meantime.
So, in May 1976, Intel started the 8086 project as a
temporary
product. Stephen Morse was the principal architect, Jim McKevitt and John Bayliss were the lead hardware engineers, and Bill Pohlman managed the project. The
8086
was released on June 8, 1978.
The brief was clear: the new chip had to address more than 64 KB, do 16-bit arithmetic, and (this is the important part) make it
easy for existing 8080 software to move over
.
The 8086 cannot run 8080 machine code. Instead, Intel aimed for
source
compatibility: you could take your 8080 assembly program and translate it, line by line, into 8086 assembly. Intel even shipped a translator called CONV86 (available from 1978) to do this automatically. Morse described the goal like this:
"the 8080 register set and instruction set appear as logical subsets of the 8086 registers and instructions."
For that translation to work, every 8080 register needed an obvious home in the 8086. And this is where the 8086's register names come from:
Here's a tiny 8080 routine and its 8086 translation side by side:
Now some of the "weird" things about x86 suddenly make sense:
The second big requirement was memory. Intel wanted 1 MB of address space, and that needs 20 address bits. But the 8086's registers were only 16 bits wide.
Morse's solution was
segmentation
. The chip has four segment registers (CS, DS, SS, and ES), and every memory access combines a segment with a 16-bit offset:
$$ \text{address} = \text{segment} \times 16 + \text{offset} $$
Multiplying by 16 is just a shift of 4 bits to the left. For example, if we want to write to pixel (160, 100) in VGA mode 13h, which lives at segment A000h:
Why 16 and not something bigger, like 256? Morse explained that with 8 bits of shift,
"segments would be forced to start on 256-byte boundaries, resulting in excessive memory fragmentation."
Segmentation was cheap (a small adder in the chip) and it worked very well with the source-compatibility goal: an 8080 program expected a 64 KB world, so you could give it one segment and it would run unchanged, wherever in memory that segment happened to be.
But it also created a rule that haunted every DOS programmer for the next 15 years:
That rule is why C compilers for DOS had
near
,
far
, and
huge
pointers, and memory models with names like
tiny
,
small
,
compact
, and
large
. It's also why mode 13h is so beloved: 320 × 200 = 64,000 bytes, which fits in one segment!
The 8086 was not an instant hit. Motorola's 68000 and Zilog's Z8000 were more elegant 16-bit designs, and many engineers preferred them.
Intel's response was a sales campaign called
Operation Crush
, launched in a meeting in December 1979. Instead of selling the 8086 on raw specs, Intel sold it as a complete solution: development tools, support chips, documentation, and support. The goal was 2,000 "design wins" (products using the chip) in one year. They got nearly 2,500.
One of them was a small project inside IBM in Boca Raton.
A year after the 8086, Intel had released the
8088
(June 1, 1979). Internally it's the same 16-bit processor, but with an 8-bit external data bus. Every 16-bit memory access takes two bus cycles, so it's slower. But an 8-bit bus meant you could build the computer with cheap, plentiful support chips designed for the 8085. Intel also offered IBM a better price and could supply more units.
The
IBM PC
was launched on August 12, 1981, with an 8088 running at 4.77 MHz. That odd number comes from television: the PC used a 14.31818 MHz crystal (four times the NTSC color carrier, which the CGA video card needed), divided by 3.
IBM made one more decision that shaped the whole industry: it required a
second source
for the CPU, so it would never depend on a single supplier. That led to a
10-year technology exchange agreement
between Intel and AMD, first signed in October 1981 and formally executed in February 1982. Keep that agreement in mind, because it comes back with the 386.
The "temporary" 8086 family was now inside the machine that would define personal computing. From this point on, every new Intel chip had to run software written for the IBM PC. Compatibility was no longer a nice-to-have.
The
80286
was released on February 1, 1982, with 134,000 transistors. IBM used it in the PC/AT in 1984, running at 6 MHz.
The 286 was designed for multitasking operating systems. Its new
protected mode
changed what a segment register means: instead of holding a paragraph number, it holds a
selector
, an index into a table of descriptors. Each descriptor says where a segment starts (anywhere in 16 MB of memory), how big it is, and who is allowed to use it. The chip checks every memory access against those rules, and runs code in one of four privilege "rings."
On paper, this was fantastic. In practice, it had three problems:
Entering protected mode was as simple as setting one bit:
But DOS and the BIOS only worked in real mode. So how did the PC/AT get back? IBM built a hack into the motherboard: the program wrote a "shutdown code" into the CMOS memory, then asked the
keyboard controller
to pulse the CPU's reset line. The CPU rebooted, the BIOS noticed the shutdown code, and jumped back into the program, now in real mode. It worked, but it was painfully slow.
Bill Gates famously called the 286 "brain-damaged," mainly because it couldn't run several DOS programs side by side under a protected-mode operating system. Most 286 machines spent their lives running DOS in real mode, as a very fast 8086.
The 286 created another, stranger problem. On the 8086, the highest address you can form is FFFF:FFFF, which is 10FFEFh. That needs 21 bits, but the 8086 only has 20 address lines, so the top bit is lost and the address
wraps around
to the bottom of memory.
Some software depended on that wraparound. DOS's CP/M-style
CALL 5
entry point relied on it to reach code at physical address C0h, and programs built with IBM/Microsoft Pascal used it as a space-saving trick. The 286 has 24 address lines, so it does not wrap, and those programs broke.
IBM's fix was to put a logic gate on address line 20 (A20), controlled by... a spare pin on the 8042
keyboard controller
. With the gate closed, the PC/AT wraps at 1 MB like an 8086. With it open, real-mode code can reach the
High Memory Area
: 65,520 bytes just above 1 MB, which is where
DOS=HIGH
loads DOS.
This hack lived much longer than anyone expected:
The 286 also had an undocumented instruction called
LOADALL
that could load the CPU's hidden segment caches directly, which tools like HIMEM.SYS used to reach extended memory without the slow reset trip. Hidden segment caches will come back very soon.
The
80386
was introduced as samples in October 1985, with mass production starting in June 1986. It had 275,000 transistors, and its chief architect was John Crawford (Pat Gelsinger, years later Intel's CEO, also worked on the project).
The 386 fixed the 286's problems one by one:
How did 32 bits fit into an instruction set designed for 16? Intel didn't add new opcodes for 32-bit operations. Instead, it added a bit to each code segment that sets the default size, plus two prefix bytes (
66h
for operand size and
67h
for address size) that flip it for a single instruction. That's why a DOS program running in real mode on a 386 can still use EAX: the assembler simply adds a 66h prefix in front of the instruction.
The 386's biggest story was not technical. Intel decided that the 386 would be
single-source
. As early as 1984, Intel had decided to stop cooperating with AMD, and it delayed and eventually refused to hand over the 386's technical details. AMD invoked arbitration in 1987, Intel cancelled the 1982 agreement, and the fight went on for years. AMD released its own Am386 in March 1991 (and sold one million of them by October of that year), and in 1994 the Supreme Court of California sided with AMD.
Then something happened that would have been unthinkable a few years before:
IBM was not first
. The
Compaq Deskpro 386
shipped in September 1986, the first time a fundamental part of the IBM PC standard was moved forward by a company other than IBM.
And one more fun detail: some early 386 chips had a bug in 32-bit multiplication. Intel marked the affected chips with
"16 BIT S/W ONLY"
, which was fine at the time because almost all software was still 16-bit anyway!
The
486
was announced at Spring Comdex on April 10, 1989, and it was the first x86 chip with more than one million transistors (about 1.2 million).
Here's the interesting part: the 486 added almost nothing to the
architecture
. A few instructions, like
BSWAP
,
XADD
, and
CMPXCHG
, and some control bits. What changed was the
engine
underneath:
Intel kept spinning variants: the 486SX (September 1991) with the FPU disabled, the clock-doubled DX2 (March 1992) that ran the core twice as fast as the motherboard, and the clock-tripled DX4 (March 1994).
For assembly programmers, the pipeline changed the rules of optimization. On the 8086, every instruction ran through microcode, and the "clever" complex instructions were often the fastest way to do things. On the 486, simple instructions became fast, and the old clever ones became the slow ones. The classic example is
LOOP
:
On an 8086,
LOOP
was the fast way to write a loop. On a 486, it's almost twice as slow as the "naive" version. If you read Michael Abrash's
Graphics Programming Black Book
, you'll see this shift everywhere: forget the microcoded tricks, use simple instructions, and keep your data inside the cache.
So why isn't the next chip called the 586? Because in 1991 Intel lost a trademark dispute over the name "386," when a judge ruled that a number was generic and could not be trademarked. AMD could call its chips "386" and "486" too.
Intel hired a branding agency and came up with a name instead of a number. The
Pentium
(from the Greek word for "five") was introduced on March 22, 1993. A few years later it would get those famous "with MMX technology" stickers, but that's
another story
.
Hopefully, by now, you can look at an x86 instruction set reference and see it as a geological record. Every layer was laid down by a specific event:
The pattern is always the same. A chip is designed quickly, often as a stopgap, with one very practical goal in mind. Software starts to depend on its exact behavior (including its accidents). And from that moment on, every future chip has to carry that behavior forward, emulate it, or work around it with a hack.
That's the real lesson of x86 history: the architecture wasn't designed, it
accumulated
. And once you know the story, the quirks stop being things you memorize and start being things you can explain.
If you're curious to dig deeper, Stephen Morse's
"Intel Microprocessors: 8008 to 8086"
is a great read straight from the architect, and Ken Shirriff's
blog
has amazing die-level reverse engineering of the 8086.
And that's it for our trip from a calculator chip to the 486. If you have any suggestions for this article, you can yell at me on
Twitter
. Also, remember to visit the
courses
page to access my lectures on retro programming.

title: When Free Software Isn't Free Enough
content:
When Free Software Isn't Free Enough

Published on 2026/11/13

If you’ve previously read my blog, it should come as no surprise that I’ve been a champion of free software for a very long time. The idea that you should be able to run, study, change, and share the programs that run your life is something I truly believe in, maybe even to an annoying degree. This past week though, a mailing list thread made me wonder whether the movement built around that idea is aiming high enough.

What happened

The thread is called “Human Emacs”, and it ran on the emacs-devel mailing list. It asks a question many projects are facing: should GNU Emacs accept LLM-generated contributions?

Brian Cully, who argued against,
posed a hypothetical
to find out where the maintainers draw their line:

if I live in a territory that permits slavery, and by law i am granted sole ownership of the products of that forced labor, and then i use that to create contributions to gnu emacs, complete with copyright assignment, and it is technically correct, and, above all, you, the emacs maintainers are aware of how this was produced, would it be ethical to accept those contributions?

As part of their response,
Eli Zaretskii said: “Our answer must be YES.”

Their reasoning was that weighing contributors’ politics, ethics, or origins would split the community along ideological lines, and that the Free Software movement addresses only problems that directly affect software freedoms. They also rejected the idea that GNU pursues liberty for all humanity, saying its goals are narrower than that.

The internet did what it did, and the story became “GNU supports slavery”, which is not a fair summary, and I want to say so plainly.
Eli later clarified that they personally don’t tolerate slavery.
Their argument was that in the context of Emacs development, the only thing that matters is the quality of the code being contributed, and that bringing personal values into those decisions would hurt the project.
Another maintainer pointed to GNU’s stated position: the project endorses only two political positions, that users should control their own computing and that basic human rights in computing should be supported. Everything else, they said, is off-topic.

Now, I don’t think anyone in that thread is a villain. I think their answers were consistent with the question they were asked, but that consistency is exactly what bothers me.

As an aside, if you’re an Emacs user, do consider checking out the
Human Emacs
website.

The case for their answer

Let’s consider the strongest version of the maintainers’ position, because I don’t think it’s foolish.

A project that tries to enforce a moral purity test on every contribution has to decide whose morality counts. Once “is this code ethically sourced?” becomes a gate, maintainers become the judges of every contributor’s life, labor, and country. That is unworkable, and it invites exactly the kind of factional fights that kill volunteer projects. There is also a fair point that rejecting the patch frees no one. The people in the hypothetical are no better off if Emacs says no.

I take that seriously, but I don’t think that it settles the question.

Where it falls short

Someone on the thread put the problem better than I can:

there is no such thing as justice for only one group of people

They went on to say that narrowly focusing on one arena is fine, as long as the work exists in the context of a larger, universal struggle. Otherwise it’s hollow.

That’s really the heart of this whole thing for me. The free software movement has a rich vocabulary of freedom and liberty, and almost all of it is about one relationship: that of the person running the software and the code they run.

To be fair, free software has never been neutral about ethics. Its founding claim is that proprietary software is an ethical wrong, and the FSF campaigns on issues like surveillance and DRM. So my complaint isn’t that the movement has no ethics. It’s where those ethics stop. They stop at one relationship: that between a person and the software on their own computer. Anything outside of that line, such as how the code was made, who was paid what, or what the finished software does to other people, gets declared off-topic. That’s the edge this thread ran into.

When “the only thing that matters is the code” is the rule, the movement has decided pre-emptively that it cannot see the labor behind the code, the data behind the models, the people who are surveilled, scored, or sorted by software they never chose and can’t inspect, or the people who can’t use any of it because they lack a computer, a language, an accessible interface, or time. A freedom that only reaches people who already have the privilege of reading source code is a narrow freedom.

I’ll note that GNU’s own stated principles include supporting basic human rights in computing. That is a real commitment, and it suggests the door is open further than the thread made it look. But a commitment that appears only when it’s convenient, and disappears when someone asks it to carry weight, doesn’t amount to much.

About the LLM question

The full case against LLMs — how they’re built on unconsented labor, sold through hype, and coercively pushed onto workers — deserves its own post, which I’ll link here once I publish it.

For now, the short version is simple: a movement built around user freedom has to ask what those freedoms are for when the tools being pushed into its codebase rely on mass extraction and coercion.

To be clear, I don’t judge people who are forced to use them at work. Most people have no say over the tools their job requires, and if the choice is between using the tool and keeping your livelihood, I don’t blame anyone for choosing their livelihood.

A volunteer contributing on their own time, or a maintainer setting a project’s rules, has a choice that an employee under a mandate doesn’t. That’s why I hold FOSS projects and their leadership to a higher standard here. My criticism is for how projects use that choice, not for people who don’t have one.

What I’d like to see

I’m not suggesting that we throw out the four freedoms. They’re foundational, and I’m not interested in burning everything to the ground to replace it with something more vague. I want to start from them and add something. Here’s where I’d start, with the small and concrete.

Projects should decide how they treat LLM contributions, in the open, instead of defaulting to “only the code matters.”
That could mean a policy that rejects them, or one that allows them with disclosure. Either way, it should be written down, argued over in public, and owned by the maintainers. Not deciding is also a decision, and it’s the one that favors whoever is pushing the hardest.

Judge the process, not the person.
I’m not asking maintainers to audit a contributor’s politics or country. That’s the unworkable version, and I think Eli is correct to fear it. A contribution policy that asks whether the code was written by a consenting human who understands and stands behind the change — rather than extracted from coerced labor or generated by a model trained on unconsented work — sets an ethical boundary without putting anyone’s personal beliefs on trial.

From there, the larger principles follow:

Freedom for users, not just programmers.
Source code access means little if you can’t read it. Real software freedom has to include usability, accessibility, documentation, and support in the languages people actually speak.

Software has a supply chain, and it’s made up of people.
Who wrote this, under what conditions, and who profits? These questions belong in the conversation, even when the answers are inconvenient.

Software has effects beyond the machine.
Systems that decide who gets a loan, a job, or bail are freedom issues, whether or not the license is permissive.

Neutrality has costs.
Declining to take a position is itself a position, and it tends to favor whoever already has power.

Solidarity over purity.
The goal isn’t a perfect test for every patch. It’s a movement that sees itself as part of a larger struggle, and shows that in how it conducts itself.

None of these are particularly new ideas. People have been arguing for a long time that struggles for justice are linked. I’m only asking that the people who build the tools of the future treat that as part of the job.

The obvious objections

“Who decides whose morality counts?”
The maintainers do, the same way they already decide everything else about a project: openly, and accountably. Setting a contribution policy isn’t a moral purity test. Every project already has standards for what it will accept.

“Doesn’t this violate freedom zero?”
I don’t think so, and I want to be careful here. Freedom zero is about what you can do with the software once you have it. A project declining a patch doesn’t stop anyone from running, changing, or sharing the code. If the policy is unpopular, anyone can fork, and that’s the system working as designed. I’m not proposing licenses that restrict who can use the software or for what. That’s a whole other thing.

At the same time, we shouldn’t pretend “just fork it” solves anything. Legally, anyone can fork any free software project. Practically though, that’s only true up to a certain point. You might be able to fork a smaller tool, but nobody is going to feasibly fork something like the Linux kernel, for example — not when it’s backed by billions of dollars in corporate hardware support and engineering resources. When foundational projects refuse to draw ethical lines, the rest of us don’t actually have a realistic exit option.

“Rejecting the patch frees no one.”
Yes, but I’d rather say so than pretend otherwise. Also, accepting a contribution isn’t neutral either. It rewards how the work was done and signals to everyone watching what the project will take. A project can’t be indifferent to its inputs and also claim to care about freedom.

Where I’m landing

I’ll be honest, it’s hard not to feel a little disillusioned with the free software movement at the moment. I’m not angry at the maintainers and I’m still going to use and appreciate the software they’ve built, but I can’t keep treating “freedom” as a word that means so much to some people and so little to everyone else.

If you feel the same way, I’d like to hear from you. What would a movement like this look like to you? What should it commit to, and what should it refuse?

And remember, nobody is free until we’re all free. That includes people who write the code, and the people who live with what it does.

title: Evidence (YC S21) Is Hiring
content:
Evidence is building the new standard for business intelligence, designed for a world where humans and AI agents work together on analytics.
At the foundation is Evidence Core, our open source framework for building reports and data products as code. On top of it, we're building Evidence Studio: a complete enterprise business intelligence platform combining an AI analytics agent with access control, enterprise security, and governance.
Thousands of organizations use Evidence, from startups to Fortune 100 companies. We've built a product people love, a substantial open source community, and a growing enterprise business.
We're now looking for someone to help us bring Evidence to a much larger audience.
You'll work directly with our cofounder and CEO to build Evidence's growth engine. We're a small team, and you'll have enormous ownership over how we reach new customers.
Our goal is to build repeatable systems that consistently generate qualified opportunities for our team.
There's a lot to work with. Our large open source community (7,000+ GitHub stars) and growing customer base give you a head start: an established audience, a steady stream of new product capabilities, and interesting customer stories waiting to be told.
Some of the things you'll work on:
You'll be encouraged to experiment, measure results, and double down on what works. We care much more about generating real customer interest than producing perfect strategies.
We move quickly, and you'll start making an impact right away.
By the end of your first month, you'll have shipped real work, learned from the results, and started building repeatable processes for reaching new customers.
This is an opportunity to build a growth function from the ground up, working directly with the founders of a growing software company.
If this sounds like you, we'd like to hear from you.
Evidence is the leading BI-as-code platform and the best way to run business intelligence with AI agents.
Evidence Core is the most popular framework for building reports, decision support tools, and dashboards with code. It powers analytics at thousands of organizations, including several Fortune 100 companies.
Evidence Studio is a complete enterprise business intelligence platform built around Evidence Core, combining an AI analytics agent with access control, enterprise security, and governance. Evidence Studio powers analytics at hundreds of organizations.
Evidence was founded in 2021 by Sean Hughes and Adam McAskill. Prior to founding Evidence, Sean and Adam built the data science team at Canada's leading private equity fund.
Evidence is venture-backed, with support from leading institutions and angels, including Y Combinator, SV Angel, A Capital, Tristan Handy (founder of dbt), and Andrew Miklas (founder of PagerDuty and YC partner).

title: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
content:
Demo:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY
There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is:
You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins.
It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem.
We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction:
1. Agent lifecycle management.
There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime.
There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up.
2. Custom environments.
Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies.
Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely.
3. Cost optimization.
If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure.
So what did we build differently?
We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents.
We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency.
As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed.
Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research.
We want your feedback.
If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build.
Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing?
Happy to answer any questions in the comments.
https://maritime.sh

title: Energy-Based Reasoners: 385x more efficient inference
content:
Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce
Energy-Based Reasoners
(
EBRs
), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

title: Just Because You Can, Doesn't Mean You Should: Re-Evaluating Galera Node Weights
content:
We all know that when using a cluster based on Galera (Codership) such as Percona XtraDB Cluster (PXC), it is recommended to deploy an odd number of nodes.
The generic answer to this recommendation is that otherwise the risk of having an inconsistent cluster (like split-brain) is higher.  (see
Get started with Percona XtraDB Cluster – Percona XtraDB Cluster
)
As a reminder, when split-brain occurs, a cluster will stop accepting queries, which is what a safe solution should do while waiting for the DBA to review and decide which of the two nodes is the leader. I do not even want to describe the infamous wsrep_provider_options=”pc.ignore_sb = yes”, which has been the cause of many, many nights spent trying to reconcile the corrupted datasets. If you have it, remove it.
However, in Galera, we also have the setting wsrep_provider_options=”pc.weight=N”. With it, we can define a specific weight in the quorum calculation for each node.

The question naturally arises:
if we can assign a different weight to each node, why can’t we have an even number of nodes and assign them different weights?

The answer to the question is simple, yes, we can.
What is not simple is to identify who should have a different weight and how to distribute it.
To understand the problem, we need to review how the quorum is calculated (I have touched on the topic long ago here
TusaCentral – Geographic replication and quorum Calculation in MySQL/Galera
) and what a View is.
In Percona XtraDB Cluster (PXC) and Galera, a
View
(or cluster view) is the agreed-upon membership of the cluster at any specific moment in time. It represents the exact list of nodes that are currently connected, synchronized, and actively communicating with each other.
Whenever a node joins the cluster, leaves gracefully, or
drops out due to a network failure
, the remaining connected nodes negotiate a new View and assign it a unique View ID.
Its relationship to the
Primary Component (PC)
is based on quorum:
Essentially, a View defines
who
is currently connected to each other, while the Primary Component is the specific View that has enough members to safely keep the database running.
The formula for calculating the quorum is:
Σ p·w  <  2·(Σ m·w + Σ l·w)
Where:

p = members of the last PRIMARY view

l = members that left gracefully (LEFT)

m = members of the component being evaluated

w = pc.weight (0–255).
In short, the total weight of the previous Primary view must be less than twice the weight of the members of the new component plus the weight of the members that left gracefully.  To be clear, a crashed / unreachable node (DOWN or in another partition) still counts in Σ p·w, so it pushes the threshold up.

A graceful leave (LEFT), instead, is credited to the new component. Also, any node that was not in the last PC is dropped from calculation, so a node that has just joined or rejoined contributes nothing to this check.
Look for the function:
(repo
https://github.com/percona/galera/tree/a6b54d887d58bae43ae3f46f5696195329405b7e
)
Now let’s assume that we have a cluster of 4 nodes, there are many possible combinations where things will work and where instead they will hit us badly.

The most common is the split-brain scenario:

To prevent this, we may decide to use one node with different weight:

Here we go, problem solved… really?
No, because changing weights may cause other issues, for example if we calculate the weights wrongly with respect to the number of nodes:

In this case one single node could bring down the whole cluster.
Of course, if we perform standard operations, or crashes happen in cascade and the cluster has time to rebuild the Primary Component, all will work well:

The problem is that:
The real question is not if we can do it but whether it is worth it: does using an odd number of nodes help or not?
The answer is partly.
Odd nodes get rid of the exact-tie case in the simple situation. They don’t completely stop the cluster losing PRIMARY state.
What matters is the parity of the total weight, not the node count.

A tie happens when present = partitioned, which means the counted weight (Σw(PC) − Left) splits exactly in half.
That is only possible when the counted weight is even. So:
Where odd nodes still lose PRIMARY:
In practice:
aim for an odd total weight in the PC and use a third site or an arbitrator for multi-DC setups. Even then, a cluster that has already shrunk can become even again, so the last-two-nodes tie can’t be designed away.
Only pc.ignore_sb or a manual bootstrap gets past it.
But you do not want to go there
.
Given this, and given that what counts is NOT the number of nodes but the balance in the weight calculation, is using weights the right way to compensate?

Well, this may be my personal opinion, but in my experience, weights make the cluster harder to manage, and the stability they add is narrow.
A weight-2 node acts like two nodes that always fail together.
Four nodes weighted 2,1,1,1 behave like a 5-node cluster where two of the nodes share one box.

We trade a split-brain tie for a single point of fate:
The set of survivable failures shifts rather than grows. We still tolerate only one arbitrary failure plus some specific splits.
What weights add to day-to-day operations:
Simple to most complex for the same goal:
Weights don’t make the cluster generally more stable, and they add operational complexity. They make sense as a deliberate tiebreaker, not as a fix for even node counts.
I stand by the evergreen KISS motto: Keep It Simple and Straightforward.

Having a PXC cluster with more than 3 nodes makes sense in very few cases, and only to scale reads or if you plan to kill 2 nodes at the same time on a cluster of 5.

Given the significant complications the increase of nodes or the use of weight brings, I do not really see why someone in a healthy state of mind should look for trouble.
Just because it can be done, it doesn’t mean “do it”, especially if the gain is minimal and the complexity increases.
Do yourself a favor: keep your cluster to the minimum, to what is really needed and do not try to stretch it. You will save yourself from spending miserable nights doing cluster recovery or worse data reconciliation.
Great MySQL to everyone.
